trackers.name: California Environmental Protection Agency (CalEPA)
trackers.desc: California’s state environmental regulator. WHO TO CONTACT for pollution complaints, permits, inspections and enforcement within California. You CAN: report suspected violations, search permits and enforcement records, and pull state monitoring data — often the front-line regulator before the federal EPA. You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL EPA (below): contact the STATE agency FIRST for anything inside state lines — routine permits, local pollution, inspections, state monitoring data; it is usually faster and more local. Go to the federal EPA regional office only to ESCALATE when the state won’t act, or when the matter crosses state lines or triggers federal law. For activists fighting a local polluter or a permit for an industrial site: this is your primary state contact and records source, frequently faster and more local than federal EPA.

trackers.name: California Public-Records Law Guide (RCFP)
trackers.desc: California’s public-records and open-meetings (‘sunshine’) law, explained by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. You CAN get: a plain-language, attorney-written guide to what records are public in California, how to request them, what exemptions and fees apply, and how to appeal a denial. You CAN’T get: the records themselves — this tells you how to demand them. For activists: your practical playbook for prying documents out of California and its local agencies — permits, emails, inspection reports — usually without needing a lawyer.

trackers.name: California Dept. of Fish & Wildlife (CDFW)
trackers.desc: California’s state fish & wildlife / natural-resources authority. WHO TO CONTACT on wildlife, habitat and state-protected species. You CAN: report habitat destruction, check state endangered-species and critical-habitat protections, and reach the agency that reviews a project’s impact on wildlife. You CAN’T: enforce the federal Endangered Species Act (that’s U.S. Fish & Wildlife). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM FEDERAL USFWS (below): the STATE agency handles STATE-listed species, state habitat review and (in states like California) the wildlife review inside state environmental-review law; USFWS handles FEDERALLY-listed species and the federal ESA. Contact BOTH — a species may be listed under state law, federal law, or both, and each listing is a separate legal tool. For activists fighting a development: a protected species or critical habitat on-site can stop or reshape it — this is the state authority that confirms and can act on it, alongside federal USFWS.

trackers.name: EPA Region 9 (San Francisco)
trackers.desc: The EPA regional office — Region 9, San Francisco — the federal environmental regulator covering California. WHO TO CONTACT: for federal enforcement, permits and cross-boundary pollution. You CAN: report violations to the federal EPA office that actually handles California, and engage on federal environmental actions. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE REGULATOR: use the federal EPA when the state agency is captured, unresponsive or lacks jurisdiction — interstate pollution, federal permits (e.g. Clean Water Act §404 dredge-and-fill), federal facilities, or national environmental law. Don’t start here for a routine local permit; the state handles that faster. For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Pacific Southwest Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Pacific Southwest Region, Sacramento CA — the federal wildlife authority covering California. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. Use the state agency for state-listed species and state review; turn to USFWS the moment a FEDERALLY protected species or designated critical habitat is in play. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: California Wildlife Conservation Board — land acquisition
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a state grant-making agency (created by the Wildlife Conservation Law of 1947) that BUYS land and rights in land on behalf of the Department of Fish and Wildlife — and, crucially, also GRANTS FUNDS TO NONPROFITS AND OTHER GOVERNMENT BODIES to do the buying themselves. Jurisdiction is statewide, across roughly 20 programmes, and it is a key vehicle for California's 30x30 commitment. USE IT: if a local land trust is willing to be the buyer, WCB money is the route — you do not need the state to hold title. TWO HARD LIMITS: every acquisition is 'WILLING SELLER' only, at fair market value appraised through the Department of General Services; and the evaluation runs 6 TO 12 MONTHS. Against an imminent sale to a developer that is too slow, so start before the land is on the market, not after.

trackers.name: Marin Agricultural Land Trust (MALT) — Marin County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the FIRST farmland land trust in the United States, founded in 1980 by a coalition of ranchers and environmentalists, and the model copied nationwide. Its method is stated bluntly: it ELIMINATES THE DEVELOPMENT POTENTIAL on farmland by acquiring agricultural conservation easements in voluntary transactions with landowners. Over 58,900 acres of Marin County farmland protected, one of the largest conservation areas in the Bay Area. USE IT: for working farmland under development pressure, an agricultural easement lets the family keep farming and keep the land while the right to build is extinguished — the objection most likely to be accepted by a reluctant landowner. Note the money route: MALT works alongside Marin County Parks, which has put $22.7 million into such easements, drawing on the county's Measure A funding, so a county ballot measure can be the funding source rather than philanthropy.

trackers.name: Sonoma Land Trust — Sonoma County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a county land trust of 50 years' standing, acquiring land AND conservation easements across Sonoma County's natural, agricultural and open lands, and restoring what it holds. Accredited by the national Land Trust Alliance. USE IT: it works closely with the SONOMA COUNTY AGRICULTURAL PRESERVATION AND OPEN SPACE DISTRICT — a public agency with its own funding — so a Sonoma site has both a private trust and a public acquisition body that can act together. Where a county has a dedicated open-space district, that pairing is usually the fastest route to a purchase, and it is worth checking whether your own county has an equivalent.

trackers.name: California Council of Land Trusts — directory of California land trusts
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the statewide association of California land trusts, with a profile page for each member covering what it protects and where. California has roughly 14 dedicated agricultural land trusts plus around ten more general open-space trusts that also protect farmland. USE IT: work down the member list to find the trust whose territory covers your site — a county or regional trust will almost always move faster on a local parcel than a national body, and several California trusts hold funding relationships with the State Coastal Conservancy that can be brought to a purchase.

trackers.name: The Land Trust for Santa Barbara County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the county land trust for Santa Barbara, conserving natural resources, agricultural land and open space — it BUYS outright as well as holding easements, having purchased the 910-acre Arroyo Hondo Preserve from the Hollister family in 2001 and protected it permanently. Also holds smaller urban sites such as the 9.3-acre Coronado Butterfly Preserve. USE IT: it takes on both large ranch-scale acquisitions and small in-town parcels, so a threatened urban lot is not automatically too small to interest it — which is not true of most trusts at this scale.

trackers.name: Peninsula Open Space Trust (POST) — San Mateo, Santa Clara, Santa Cruz
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a private land trust founded in 1977 covering the Peninsula and South Bay, credited with protecting more than 70,000 acres across San Mateo, Santa Clara and Santa Cruz counties, including Coyote Valley and Half Moon Bay farmland. Its founding purpose is the useful part: it exists to NEGOTIATE PRIVATE LAND SALES AND EASEMENTS WITH WILLING SELLERS IN CONFIDENCE — something a public open-space district cannot do, which is why it was created alongside the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District. USE IT: where a landowner will not deal publicly, a private trust can. NOTE: canonical domain not verified this session; listed on the Land Trust Alliance member directory and the California Council of Land Trusts.

trackers.name: Marin Open Space Trust (MOST) — Marin County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a volunteer-led Marin land trust (est. 2008) focused on the roughly 15,000 acres in the county's eastern urbanized corridor still at risk of development — it buys threatened properties and conservation easements, then conveys the land to Marin County Parks, the Open Space District or a town, as it did with Bald Hill, Pacheco Valle and Upper Hawthorne Canyon. USE IT: if a scenic hillside or greenbelt parcel near you is zoned for development, ask MOST to negotiate an option or purchase and to line up an agency to take permanent ownership.

trackers.name: Sonoma County Ag + Open Space — Sonoma County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Sonoma County Agricultural Preservation and Open Space District, created by county voters in 1990 and funded by a dedicated sales tax, has permanently protected more than 125,000 acres — mostly by buying conservation easements from willing landowners, sometimes by buying land outright and transferring it to a parks agency. USE IT: if farmland, ranchland or a scenic hillside near you is under development pressure, bring it to Ag + Open Space's attention; a typical easement project runs 18–24 months through evaluation, appraisal and escrow.

trackers.name: Santa Clara Valley Open Space Authority — Santa Clara County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a regional public land-conservation agency created by the California Legislature and funded by voter-approved parcel taxes, the Open Space Authority has protected roughly 30,000 acres of Santa Clara Valley hillsides, watersheds and farmland — including agricultural conservation easements bought specifically to stop farmland from being converted to subdivisions, and large ranch acquisitions in the Coyote Valley wildlife corridor. USE IT: bring a threatened parcel to the Authority's Land Conservation team against the Santa Clara Valley Greenprint priorities; it also runs Urban Grant rounds for community nature projects.

trackers.name: Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District — Santa Clara, San Mateo & Santa Cruz Counties
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: an independent special district created by Santa Clara County voters in 1972 (extended into San Mateo County in 1976, Santa Cruz in 1992 and to the San Mateo coast in 2004) with a seven-member publicly elected board, Midpen has permanently protected more than 70,000 acres of the Santa Cruz Mountains greenbelt — buying land and interests in land, prioritising parcels that connect existing protected areas into wildlife corridors and trail linkages, and on the Coastside also preserving working agricultural land. USE IT: bring a threatened parcel adjoining protected land to Midpen's Real Property Committee, whose meetings are public; Measure AA bond funds back acquisitions.

trackers.name: East Bay Regional Park District — Alameda & Contra Costa Counties
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the largest regional park district in the country (est. 1934, ~125,000 acres across 73 parks) funded for land purchase by two voter-approved bonds — Measure AA in 1988 ($225 million, which bought 34,000 acres) and Measure WW in 2008 ($500 million, 72% yes), of which 75% is dedicated to land acquisition and $125 million went to a local grant programme for city park departments. USE IT: bring a threatened parcel adjoining district land to the elected Board of Directors, which approves every acquisition in public; developer dedications and habitat-conservancy mitigation land also flow into the district.

trackers.name: Western Riverside County Regional Conservation Authority (MSHCP) — Riverside County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created in 2004 by Riverside County and 18 cities to assemble a 500,000-acre habitat reserve for 146 native species (34 of them threatened or endangered) under one of the largest habitat conservation plans in the US — it buys 'Additional Reserve Lands' inside mapped Criteria Cells using development mitigation fees and state/federal grants, and reviews development applications for MSHCP consistency. USE IT: if a project sits in a Criteria Cell, the Joint Project Review and HANS acquisition process is the lever — the land may be needed for the reserve, and the RCA can buy it instead.

trackers.name: Sustainable Agricultural Lands Conservation Program (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): a state grant programme funded from cap-and-trade auction proceeds, on the logic that paving farmland is a greenhouse-gas decision — SALC pays for permanent agricultural conservation easements and fee purchases on croplands and rangelands threatened by conversion, plus land-use planning and capacity-building grants. Roughly 244,000 acres protected or in progress since 2015. USE IT: local and regional agencies, land trusts and open space districts apply; a 10% match is normally required, but projects benefiting priority populations, tribes or socially disadvantaged farmers and ranchers can be funded at 100%.

trackers.name: Open Space Program (Measure O) — City of Davis
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Davis voters approved Measure O in November 2000 by 70% — a 30-year parcel tax running to June 2031, ringfenced by municipal ordinance for buying and maintaining open space, habitat and agricultural land and easements in the ring around the city. More than 5,900 acres protected since 1990, with 21 conservation easements co-owned with the Yolo Land Trust, which monitors them in perpetuity. USE IT: the city routinely combines Measure O money with open space development impact fees, agricultural mitigation fees required of developers, and state SALC grants — typically putting up a quarter to two-thirds of a purchase price and letting state and mitigation money cover the rest.

trackers.name: Lozeau Drury LLP — Oakland (CEQA petitioners' firm)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a small Oakland firm practising environmental law EXCLUSIVELY on the plaintiff side — its stated clients are non-profit environmental and recreational groups, labour organisations, neighbourhood associations and tribes, and its stated adversaries are oil refineries, timber companies, big developers and the agencies that permit them. Work includes CEQA and NEPA challenges, Clean Air and Clean Water Act suits and Proposition 65. Its cases include the challenge to Lake County's approval of the 16,000-acre Guenoc Valley development for inadequate wildfire, evacuation and habitat analysis, and a CEQA suit over weakened Santa Susana Field Laboratory cleanup standards. USE IT: bring them in during the comment period on a draft EIR, not after approval — CEQA claims generally must be raised in the administrative record first.

trackers.name: Carstens, Black & Minteer LLP — Hermosa Beach & San Diego (CEQA petitioners' firm)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a public interest firm founded in 1995 (formerly Chatten-Brown & Carstens), practising statewide in environmental, land use and municipal law and representing national, state and local environmental and neighbourhood groups — Sierra Club, NRDC, Planning and Conservation League, Friends of the Los Angeles River, homeowner coalitions — challenging projects that violate environmental law. It reports an over 80% success rate in reported appellate cases. Work includes the CEQA challenge to the Port of Los Angeles China Shipping terminal expansion, settled with $50 million committed to mitigation, and litigation that preserved the Lincoln Place apartments. USE IT: they take CEQA, CESA, NEPA and Section 4(f) transport cases, and also advise agencies challenging projects approved by other agencies.

trackers.name: California Business Entity Search
trackers.desc: The official registry of companies, LLCs and corporations registered in California (Secretary of State / equivalent). You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. For activists: this is how you unmask the LLC behind a local development, rezoning or mass eviction — start here to find who really controls it and whom to hold accountable.

trackers.name: CEQAnet — California CEQA document database
trackers.desc: California's State Clearinghouse database of CEQA (and NEPA) documents (formerly ceqanet.opr.ca.gov). You CAN get: full-text environmental documents and notices for most state-reviewed projects since March 2019 (summaries before that), searchable by title, location, year and lead agency — plus, via its Google-powered full-text search, every CEQA document a given consulting firm has produced statewide, with the preparer named on each. You CAN'T get: purely local projects that never reach the Clearinghouse, and there is no native 'consultant' filter. For activists: pull a firm's whole body of work, then run it through Google Scholar case law (scholar.google.com) to see which of its documents were litigated and set aside — a firm repeatedly overturned on biological resources leaves a trail you can use to challenge the next inadequate study.

trackers.name: California Attorney General
trackers.desc: California’s chief legal officer. WHO TO CONTACT for consumer fraud, environmental harm, charity and nonprofit abuse, antitrust and public corruption in California. You CAN: file complaints and tips the AG can investigate and prosecute; most AG offices have dedicated consumer-protection, environmental and charities divisions. You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: your state AG is often the most powerful — and most reachable — ally against a local corporate or official target, frequently more responsive than federal agencies.

trackers.name: Los Angeles Waterkeeper
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: one of California's most active Clean Water Act citizen-suit filers (founded 1993), targeting industrial facilities and stormwater dischargers across Los Angeles County. WHO IT SUITS: a neighborhood facing an industrial polluter or contaminated waterway in LA County. HOW A LITIGATOR/ENFORCER DIFFERS FROM THE AGENCIES above: these groups can take a polluter or an unlawful approval to court themselves — many bring Clean Water Act citizen suits. WHEN TO CONTACT: early, before a project is approved or as soon as a discharge/violation is documented; deadlines are short.

trackers.name: The Urban Wildlands Group
trackers.desc: The Urban Wildlands Group — a Los Angeles-based conservation organisation dedicated to protecting species, habitats and ecological processes in urban and urbanising areas. WHO TO ENLIST when development threatens urban habitat, wildlife corridors, native species or dark-sky/ light-pollution-sensitive ecosystems. You CAN: draw on its scientific expertise and record of CEQA and endangered-species engagement to document a project's impact on urban wildlife and build the evidence a campaign or lawsuit needs. For activists in the LA region: a specialist ally for the urban-habitat and species arguments that often carry the most legal weight.

trackers.name: San Diego Coastkeeper
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: San Diego County's clean-water watchdog (founded 1995) — pursues Clean Water Act enforcement across the county's bays, beaches and watersheds, often with the Coastal Environmental Rights Foundation, and has sued the city to fix leaking sewers. HOW A LITIGATOR/ENFORCER DIFFERS FROM THE AGENCIES above: these groups can take a polluter or an unlawful approval to court themselves — many bring Clean Water Act citizen suits. WHEN TO CONTACT: early, before a project is approved or as soon as a discharge/violation is documented; deadlines are short.

trackers.name: Law Office of Todd T. Cardiff (San Diego)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: one of California's strongest environmental / land-use LITIGATORS for fighting a destructive project in court. A San Diego environmental and land-use litigator handling CEQA, Coastal Act, water-quality and endangered-species matters for community groups and individuals across Southern California. HOW A LITIGATOR DIFFERS FROM THE AGENCIES AND NON-PROFITS above: agencies review and regulate, and conservancies organise and advocate — but when a project is approved unlawfully, only a lawyer can take it to court. WHEN TO CONTACT: early, ideally BEFORE a project is approved, so comment-letter deadlines and the administrative record are preserved — CEQA and Coastal Act deadlines are short and unforgiving.

trackers.name: Coast Law Group LLP (Encinitas)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an Encinitas public-interest firm handling environmental, CEQA, coastal and land-use litigation for community groups and individuals, with a focus on coastal San Diego and Southern California. Represents the public's side against harmful development. HOW A LITIGATOR DIFFERS FROM THE AGENCIES AND NON-PROFITS above: agencies review and regulate, and conservancies organise and advocate — but when a project is approved unlawfully, only a lawyer can take it to court. WHEN TO CONTACT: early, ideally BEFORE a project is approved, so comment-letter deadlines and the administrative record are preserved — CEQA and Coastal Act deadlines are short and unforgiving.

trackers.name: Law Office of Marc Chytilo, APC (Santa Barbara)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: one of California's strongest environmental / land-use LITIGATORS for fighting a destructive project in court. A Santa Barbara environmental firm led by Marc Chytilo with a long CEQA, land-use and natural-resources litigation record on California's central and south coast, representing environmental organisations and community groups. HOW A LITIGATOR DIFFERS FROM THE AGENCIES AND NON-PROFITS above: agencies review and regulate, and conservancies organise and advocate — but when a project is approved unlawfully, only a lawyer can take it to court. WHEN TO CONTACT: early, ideally BEFORE a project is approved, so comment-letter deadlines and the administrative record are preserved — CEQA and Coastal Act deadlines are short and unforgiving.

trackers.name: San Francisco Baykeeper
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the clean-water watchdog for San Francisco Bay and the Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta — built on Clean Water Act citizen suits (e.g. suing San Jose over trash and sewage in Coyote Creek and the Guadalupe River). Enforces against industrial dischargers, sewage spills and stormwater polluters around the Bay. HOW A LITIGATOR/ENFORCER DIFFERS FROM THE AGENCIES above: these groups can take a polluter or an unlawful approval to court themselves — many bring Clean Water Act citizen suits. WHEN TO CONTACT: early, before a project is approved or as soon as a discharge/violation is documented; deadlines are short.

trackers.name: Orange County Coastkeeper
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Orange County clean-water enforcer — brings Clean Water Act actions against facilities discharging to the San Gabriel and Santa Ana Rivers and their tributaries. WHO IT SUITS: an Orange County community fighting industrial water pollution. HOW A LITIGATOR/ENFORCER DIFFERS FROM THE AGENCIES above: these groups can take a polluter or an unlawful approval to court themselves — many bring Clean Water Act citizen suits. WHEN TO CONTACT: early, before a project is approved or as soon as a discharge/violation is documented; deadlines are short.

trackers.name: Riverkeeper, Inc.
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: New York's clean-water watchdog for the Hudson River and NYC/Hudson Valley drinking-water supply — a member-supported organization with its own legal team (and a close tie to the Pace Environmental Litigation Clinic) that brings Clean Water Act citizen suits against polluters and unlawful discharges. HOW A LITIGATOR/ENFORCER DIFFERS FROM THE AGENCIES above: these groups can take a polluter or an unlawful approval to court themselves — many bring Clean Water Act citizen suits. WHEN TO CONTACT: early, before a project is approved or as soon as a discharge/violation is documented; deadlines are short.

trackers.name: New York Lawyers for the Public Interest (NYLPI)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a civil-rights nonprofit with an active environmental-justice LITIGATION arm — co-counsel (with Earthjustice and the Pace Clinic) suing NY's DEC over CLCPA climate rules, and counsel for Southeast Queens residents in a Clean Water Act suit against waste-transfer stations. For NY environmental-justice communities: a go-to plaintiff-side litigator. HOW A LITIGATOR/ENFORCER DIFFERS FROM THE AGENCIES above: these groups can take a polluter or an unlawful approval to court themselves — many bring Clean Water Act citizen suits. WHEN TO CONTACT: early, before a project is approved or as soon as a discharge/violation is documented; deadlines are short.

trackers.name: Pace Environmental Litigation Clinic
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Elisabeth Haub School of Law (Pace) clinic — established to represent Riverkeeper and now a proven public-interest litigator in SEQRA / Article 78 challenges and Clean Water Act citizen suits (e.g. Bennett v. Troy City Council, challenging a negative declaration for a development beside the Hudson). Free representation for community groups. HOW A LITIGATOR/ENFORCER DIFFERS FROM THE AGENCIES above: these groups can take a polluter or an unlawful approval to court themselves — many bring Clean Water Act citizen suits. WHEN TO CONTACT: early, before a project is approved or as soon as a discharge/violation is documented; deadlines are short.

trackers.name: Open Space Institute
trackers.desc: Open Space Institute — a leading land trust/conservancy in New York. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good.

trackers.name: Environmental Advocates of New York
trackers.desc: Environmental Advocates of New York — a leading citizen environmental watchdog for New York. WHO TO ENLIST against harmful development, extraction, sprawl and pollution. You CAN: tap their research, organizing, litigation and lobbying to fight a specific project, and plug into local coalitions. For activists: a statewide ally that already knows the players, agencies and law — often your best first call.

trackers.name: New York Dept. of Environmental Conservation (DEC)
trackers.desc: New York’s state environmental regulator. WHO TO CONTACT for pollution complaints, permits, inspections and enforcement within New York. You CAN: report suspected violations, search permits and enforcement records, and pull state monitoring data — often the front-line regulator before the federal EPA. You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL EPA (below): contact the STATE agency FIRST for anything inside state lines — routine permits, local pollution, inspections, state monitoring data; it is usually faster and more local. Go to the federal EPA regional office only to ESCALATE when the state won’t act, or when the matter crosses state lines or triggers federal law. For activists fighting a local polluter or a permit for an industrial site: this is your primary state contact and records source, frequently faster and more local than federal EPA.

trackers.name: New York Public-Records Law Guide (RCFP)
trackers.desc: New York’s public-records and open-meetings (‘sunshine’) law, explained by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. You CAN get: a plain-language, attorney-written guide to what records are public in New York, how to request them, what exemptions and fees apply, and how to appeal a denial. You CAN’T get: the records themselves — this tells you how to demand them. For activists: your practical playbook for prying documents out of New York and its local agencies — permits, emails, inspection reports — usually without needing a lawyer.

trackers.name: New York DEC — Fish & Wildlife
trackers.desc: New York’s state fish & wildlife / natural-resources authority. WHO TO CONTACT on wildlife, habitat and state-protected species. You CAN: report habitat destruction, check state endangered-species and critical-habitat protections, and reach the agency that reviews a project’s impact on wildlife. You CAN’T: enforce the federal Endangered Species Act (that’s U.S. Fish & Wildlife). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM FEDERAL USFWS (below): the STATE agency handles STATE-listed species, state habitat review and (in states like California) the wildlife review inside state environmental-review law; USFWS handles FEDERALLY-listed species and the federal ESA. Contact BOTH — a species may be listed under state law, federal law, or both, and each listing is a separate legal tool. For activists fighting a development: a protected species or critical habitat on-site can stop or reshape it — this is the state authority that confirms and can act on it, alongside federal USFWS.

trackers.name: EPA Region 2 (New York City)
trackers.desc: The EPA regional office — Region 2, New York City — the federal environmental regulator covering New York. WHO TO CONTACT: for federal enforcement, permits and cross-boundary pollution. You CAN: report violations to the federal EPA office that actually handles New York, and engage on federal environmental actions. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE REGULATOR: use the federal EPA when the state agency is captured, unresponsive or lacks jurisdiction — interstate pollution, federal permits (e.g. Clean Water Act §404 dredge-and-fill), federal facilities, or national environmental law. Don’t start here for a routine local permit; the state handles that faster. For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Northeast Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Northeast Region, Hadley MA — the federal wildlife authority covering New York. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. Use the state agency for state-listed species and state review; turn to USFWS the moment a FEDERALLY protected species or designated critical habitat is in play. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: NY DEC — land trust grant programmes (Conservation Partnership, FCELT)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: two Environmental Protection Fund programmes DEC runs with the Land Trust Alliance. The CONSERVATION PARTNERSHIP PROGRAM has awarded grants since 2002, typically $2,000 to $100,000, for land trust capacity, transactions and stewardship. FORESTLAND CONSERVATION EASEMENTS FOR LAND TRUSTS (FCELT) offers accredited land trusts up to $350,000 to BUY conservation easements on privately owned forest — nine grants totalling $1.72 million protected 2,050 acres in the 2025 round. WHO IT SUITS: READ THE ELIGIBILITY BAR CAREFULLY. An applicant's primary mission must be conservation or stewardship of PRIVATE land; organisations focused exclusively on advocacy, education, or public land are NOT eligible. Accreditation is not required for the Partnership Program but counts in scoring, and IS required for FCELT. About 73% of New York's forests are privately owned, which is why the private-land condition is where the money goes.

trackers.name: NY Open Space Conservation Grant Program — $25m, no match required
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: $25 million from the Clean Water, Clean Air and Green Jobs Environmental Bond Act plus the EPF, to PURCHASE LAND for permanent conservation. WHO IT SUITS: municipalities, not-for-profits, AND INDIAN NATIONS OR TRIBES — a wider eligibility than most conservation funds, which usually stop at accredited land trusts. HOW IT DIFFERS: it is NO-MATCH FUNDING, so you do not need to raise a counterpart sum first — rare, and the single reason to look here before anywhere else in New York. ONE TRAP: all applicants must register in the Statewide Financial System, and not-for-profits must PREQUALIFY, which DEC advises starting well before the deadline. Begin that paperwork the day you decide to apply. This is the launch announcement; check DEC's site for the current round and closing date.

trackers.name: New York Environmental Protection Fund — Parks acquisition grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): New York's Environmental Protection Fund (EPF) offers matching grants for the acquisition, planning and development of parkland and conservation land to municipalities and not-for-profit organizations with an ownership interest (max award ~$675,000; the EPF, funded at ~$400M+/year, also supports land acquisition and farmland protection through DEC). USE IT: as a nonprofit or municipality, apply through the Consolidated Funding Application to fund the purchase of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Peconic Land Trust — Suffolk County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a Suffolk County land trust (est. 1983) that has protected more than 12,000 acres of Long Island working farms and natural lands through conservation planning, outright purchase, and the acquisition of development rights and conservation easements by gift and by purchase — then stewards them in perpetuity. USE IT: if farmland or open space near you is under development pressure, ask the Trust to assess it for a conservation easement or a bargain-sale purchase, often stacked with Suffolk County and town preservation funds.

trackers.name: Westchester County Legacy Program — Westchester County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a standing county capital-budget line for acquiring and protecting open space, credited with preserving over 2,000 acres in Westchester — from small urban parks to large rural tracts like the 200-acre Taxter Ridge, preserved with the Town of Greenburgh. Because the money is ready rather than raised project-by-project, the county can move fast when a critical parcel comes on the market, leveraging state, municipal and private funds. USE IT: get your town or a land trust to bring a threatened parcel to the County Planning Department as a Legacy partnership.

trackers.name: Partnership for Manageable Growth — Dutchess County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): created in 1999 to implement the county's Agricultural and Farmland Protection Plan, PMG puts up a local match of up to 50% of a land-preservation purchase — development rights on working farms, or fee purchase of woodland, ravines and trail corridors — and has helped protect over 6,000 acres. County money is what unlocks the much larger state Farmland Protection Implementation grants and land-trust contributions. USE IT: a land trust (Dutchess Land Conservancy, Scenic Hudson, Hudson Highlands) applies on the landowner's behalf; awards are ranked by the County Planning Board and approved by the Legislature.

trackers.name: Land preservation programmes — Suffolk County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Suffolk runs six stacked land-preservation programmes through its Division of Real Property Acquisition & Management — the Open Space Preservation Program, the Farmland Preservation Program (buying development rights on Long Island farmland), the ¼% Drinking Water Protection Program (extended by referendum, buying hundreds of acres a year), the Land Preservation Partnership and Multifaceted Land Preservation Programs, and the Legacy Fund, which requires county money to be matched from other public and private sources. USE IT: parcels approved for acquisition go onto the county's Open Space Acquisition Map, and every purchase gets a public hearing under Section 247 of NY General Municipal Law.

trackers.name: NYC DEP Watershed Land Acquisition Program — Delaware, Greene, Ulster, Sullivan, Schoharie, Putnam, Westchester & Dutchess Counties
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: to keep its water supply unfiltered, New York City is legally required by its EPA Filtration Avoidance Determination to solicit and buy watershed land upstate — over 111,000 acres of fee land and conservation easements secured since 1997 across eight counties, targeting streams, wetlands, floodplains and sensitive land ranked into Priority Areas. Purchases are willing-seller only, at independently appraised fair market value, and the City keeps paying property taxes on what it buys; the Watershed Agricultural Council runs a parallel farm easement programme. USE IT: upstate landowners can approach DEP directly — a federal drinking-water permit, not a local budget, is what funds this.

trackers.name: Super Law Group, LLC — New York City (environmental plaintiffs' firm)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a New York firm dedicated to environmental protection, representing public interest organisations, community groups and individuals — taking on, in its own words, large corporations and government agencies. Best known for Clean Water Act enforcement and the regulation of power plants; founder Reed Super has litigated public interest environmental and land use cases for over 30 years, previously running the Hudson River programme at Riverkeeper and teaching in Columbia Law School's Environmental Law Clinic. USE IT: for citizen-suit enforcement against a permitted discharger, and for intervening in state permitting proceedings — which is usually earlier and cheaper than suing after a permit issues.

trackers.name: New York Attorney General
trackers.desc: New York’s chief legal officer. WHO TO CONTACT for consumer fraud, environmental harm, charity and nonprofit abuse, antitrust and public corruption in New York. You CAN: file complaints and tips the AG can investigate and prosecute; most AG offices have dedicated consumer-protection, environmental and charities divisions. You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: your state AG is often the most powerful — and most reachable — ally against a local corporate or official target, frequently more responsive than federal agencies.

trackers.desc: The official registry of companies, LLCs and corporations registered in New York (Secretary of State / equivalent). You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. trackers.name: Blackburn & Carter (James B. Blackburn Jr., Houston)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Houston environmental-litigation firm (James B. Blackburn Jr.) with 30+ years challenging pollution, permits and harmful development to protect environmental interests across Texas and the Gulf Coast. HOW A LITIGATOR DIFFERS FROM THE AGENCIES AND NON-PROFITS above: only a lawyer can take an unlawful TCEQ permit or approval to a contested-case hearing or to court; contact early, before a permit issues, because Texas deadlines are short. NOTE: the firm has no official website we could confirm — this link is a verified directory profile; search the firm name to reach it directly.

trackers.name: Perales, Allmon & Ice, P.C. (environmental litigation)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an Austin public-interest environmental LITIGATION firm — one of Texas's strongest — that represents community groups, individuals and local governments in water, air, solid-waste and endangered-species cases, and pointedly does NOT represent companies seeking permits. HOW A LITIGATOR DIFFERS FROM THE AGENCIES AND NON-PROFITS above: agencies regulate and groups organise — but when a TCEQ permit or approval is unlawful, only a firm like this can take it to a contested-case hearing or to court. WHEN TO CONTACT: early, before a permit is granted, because Texas's contested-case and appeal deadlines are short.

trackers.name: Save Our Springs Alliance (Austin)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Austin's water watchdog since 1992 (born as the Save Our Springs Legal Defense Fund), protecting Barton Springs and the Edwards Aquifer — and increasingly a litigator, challenging highway projects, defending endangered salamanders and enforcing water-quality rules across the Hill Country. You CAN: draw on its science, organising and in-house legal muscle to fight a project threatening Central Texas water and habitat. For activists in the Austin/Hill Country region: a local group that both organises AND sues.

trackers.name: Bayou City Waterkeeper (Houston)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Houston-based water-justice group working across the 10-county lower Galveston Bay watershed since 2001, using law and science to fight water pollution, unlawful wetland development and flooding that hit Black, Brown and lower-wealth communities hardest — with a record of litigation and a $2B federal consent decree forcing Houston to fix failing sewage infrastructure. For activists on the Texas Gulf Coast: a local ally that challenges industrial pollution and wetland destruction through both organising and the courts.

trackers.name: Texas Land Conservancy

trackers.name: Texas Parks & Wildlife Dept. (TPWD)
trackers.desc: Texas’s state fish & wildlife / natural-resources authority. WHO TO CONTACT on wildlife, habitat and state-protected species. You CAN: report habitat destruction, check state endangered-species and critical-habitat protections, and reach the agency that reviews a project’s impact on wildlife. You CAN’T: enforce the federal Endangered Species Act (that’s U.S. Fish & Wildlife). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM FEDERAL USFWS (below): the STATE agency handles STATE-listed species, state habitat review and (in states like California) the wildlife review inside state environmental-review law; USFWS handles FEDERALLY-listed species and the federal ESA. Contact BOTH — a species may be listed under state law, federal law, or both, and each listing is a separate legal tool. For activists fighting a development: a protected species or critical habitat on-site can stop or reshape it — this is the state authority that confirms and can act on it, alongside federal USFWS.

trackers.name: EPA Region 6 (Dallas)
trackers.desc: The EPA regional office — Region 6, Dallas — the federal environmental regulator covering Texas. WHO TO CONTACT: for federal enforcement, permits and cross-boundary pollution. You CAN: report violations to the federal EPA office that actually handles Texas, and engage on federal environmental actions. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE REGULATOR: use the federal EPA when the state agency is captured, unresponsive or lacks jurisdiction — interstate pollution, federal permits (e.g. Clean Water Act §404 dredge-and-fill), federal facilities, or national environmental law. Don’t start here for a routine local permit; the state handles that faster. For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Southwest Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Southwest Region, Albuquerque NM — the federal wildlife authority covering Texas. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. Use the state agency for state-listed species and state review; turn to USFWS the moment a FEDERALLY protected species or designated critical habitat is in play. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: Texas Farm and Ranch Lands Conservation Program (TPWD)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to conserve working land): the Texas Farm and Ranch Lands Conservation Program (TFRLCP), administered by Texas Parks & Wildlife, provides grants to qualified easement holders — land trusts — to purchase agricultural conservation easements that protect working farm and ranch lands with high water, wildlife and agricultural value from fragmentation and development (funding is cyclical and subject to legislative appropriation). USE IT: partner with a land trust to apply for an easement grant on threatened working land.

trackers.name: Travis County Conservation Easement Program — Travis County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: approved by Travis County voters in 2012 and funded by successive bond packages, the county buys conservation easements — and accepts donated ones — on natural and agricultural land, prioritising the Wilbarger Creek, Gilleland Creek, Colorado River, Onion Creek and Pedernales River corridors, plus tracts adjoining existing preserves or holding springs and archaeological sites. In a county with no zoning authority, easements are the sharpest land-protection tool available. USE IT: landowners can approach Natural Resources staff to sell or donate an easement, including into the Balcones Canyonlands Preserve.

trackers.name: Parks and Open Space Bond — Hays County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Hays County voters approved $75 million in bonds in November 2020 (70% yes) to acquire open space, conservation land and conservation easements — explicitly to protect Edwards and Trinity Aquifer recharge, creek and river water quality, wildlife habitat and flood-prone land in one of the fastest-growing counties in the country. Projects are identified and prioritised by the citizen Parks and Open Space Advisory Commission (POSAC), and easements are typically held by a partner land trust such as Hill Country Conservancy or The Nature Conservancy. USE IT: bring a threatened karst, spring or riverfront property to POSAC with a land-trust sponsor — that is how Purgatory Creek (1,068 acres) and Sentinel Peak were stopped from being developed.

trackers.name: Floodplain Preservation & Voluntary Buyout — Harris County Flood Control District
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a special district created by the Texas Legislature in 1937 and governed by Harris County Commissioners Court, HCFCD buys land next to waterways for floodplain preservation and buys out repeatedly flooded homes from willing sellers at fair market value, demolishing them and returning the land to floodplain — about 3,100 buyouts since 1997 and 1,060 acres restored, in a county holding nearly 12% of the nation's severe repetitive loss properties. USE IT: in a county with almost no zoning, this is the main mechanism converting flood-prone land to permanent open space; buyout grants take 8–12 months to start and years to complete, so apply early rather than after the next flood.

trackers.name: Edwards Aquifer Protection Program — City of San Antonio
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: San Antonio voters approved a one-eighth-cent sales tax for aquifer land protection in 2000 and renewed it in 2005, 2010 and 2015, raising about $325 million and protecting over 187,000 acres across the Edwards Aquifer recharge and contributing zones — buying development rights instead of trying to regulate pollution after the fact. About 95% of acquisitions are conservation easements: owners keep the ranch, give up development beyond 0.5% of floor area, and are paid 30–50% of appraised market value. Easements bind all future owners and are monitored annually with the Edwards Aquifer Authority. USE IT honestly: the dedicated sales tax has since been redirected to other city programmes, with council funding the programme from the general budget instead — continued funding is a live political question.

trackers.name: Water Quality Protection Lands — City of Austin (Austin Water)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created when Austin voters approved bond funding in 1998 and sustained by five further bonds totalling roughly $230 million, the city water utility has permanently protected over 34,000 acres across the Barton Springs recharge and contributing zones in Travis and Hays counties — about 28% of that recharge zone. Roughly 22,000 acres are conservation easements, where owners keep and manage the land, are paid for the development rights and are held to about 1% impervious cover; the rest is owned outright and actively restored to grassland savanna. USE IT: the city pays appraised value and stacks purchases with NRCS and land trusts — the stated goal is keeping impervious cover under 10% across the source water protection area.

trackers.name: Lone Star Legal Aid — Environmental Justice Team, Houston
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the environmental justice team of a 501(c)(3) legal aid firm covering 72 counties across East Texas and the Gulf Coast, providing FREE legal education, advice and representation to low-income residents and community groups living beside refineries, concrete batch plants, metal recyclers, waste facilities and contaminated sites — in a region where Houston has no zoning at all. Wins include forcing Waste Management's affiliate to withdraw a landfill application at Carverdale and pausing a housing development proposed on top of a closed landfill in Alief. USE IT: they run a Community Pollution Reporting Tool and app for the whole service area — documenting odours, releases and noise builds the record their lawyers later need. Income restrictions apply.

trackers.name: Texas Business Entity Search
trackers.desc: The official registry of companies, LLCs and corporations registered in Texas (Secretary of State / equivalent). You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. For activists: this is how you unmask the LLC behind a local development, rezoning or mass eviction — start here to find who really controls it and whom to hold accountable.

trackers.name: Texas Attorney General

You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: your state AG is often the most powerful — and most reachable — ally against a local corporate or official target, frequently more responsive than federal agencies.

trackers.name: Washington Wildlife & Recreation Program (WWRP) — RCO grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): Washington's primary land-conservation grant program, administered by the Recreation and Conservation Office (RCO) — 50% matching grants to local agencies, nonprofits and tribes to acquire and protect habitat, farmland and recreation land (the Habitat Conservation account funds outright land and easement purchases). USE IT: apply, as a nonprofit or local agency, to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: King County Conservation Futures — King County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): Conservation Futures is King County's open-space acquisition grant program, funded by a dedicated property-tax levy restored to its full rate by voters in 2022 and now awarding roughly $100 million a year to buy natural lands, urban greenspaces, forests, farms, community gardens and trail corridors. Cities, tribes, park districts and nonprofits apply; a match waiver can cover up to 100% of eligible acquisition costs in under-served areas. USE IT: if a parcel in your community is threatened, get a public agency or a qualifying nonprofit to nominate it for a Conservation Futures grant — see the application and nonprofits pages.

trackers.name: Snohomish County Conservation Futures — Snohomish County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): created in 1988 under Washington's Conservation Futures statute (RCW 84.34.230) and funded by a dedicated property-tax levy, the program has directed more than $80 million into acquiring open space, farmland and timberland — recent cycles have offered up to $9–10 million a year. Grants go to public agencies and qualifying non-profits (Forterra, Washington Farmland Trust and cities have all won awards) and must secure property rights in perpetuity. USE IT: get a sponsoring agency or land trust to apply in the annual autumn round.

trackers.name: Pierce County Conservation Futures — Pierce County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): established in 1991 under Washington's Conservation Futures statute and funded by a dedicated tax levy, this grant programme buys land or development rights to preserve habitat, shorelines, farm and timber land and urban open space. Sponsors can be local governments, state or federal agencies, special purpose districts, property owners or non-profits; projects need a 10% match plus a stewardship and public access plan. USE IT: applications open every odd-numbered January, are screened by a Technical Advisory Committee in spring, then ranked by a Citizens Advisory Board in June before the County Council votes in August.

trackers.name: Thurston County Conservation Futures — Thurston County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): Thurston began collecting Washington's Conservation Futures levy in 1989 — one of the first counties to do so — and has since preserved roughly 5,900 acres of farmland, habitat, historic sites and recreation land, buying either the property or just the development rights. Eligible properties need unique or valuable wildlife habitat, agricultural, forestry, historic or recreational features. USE IT: applications run on an annual cycle and must be sponsored by a land trust or city government, so pair the landowner with a sponsor early; the Board of County Commissioners makes the final funding call on a ranking committee's advice.

trackers.name: San Juan County Conservation Land Bank — San Juan County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the only conservation land bank of its kind in Washington — islanders got the state legislature to authorise a conservation real estate excise tax, then voted it in themselves in 1990 (renewed 1999, 2011 and 2024, now running to 2038). A 1% tax paid by property purchasers at closing funds the acquisition of land and lesser interests — options, rights of first refusal, conservation easements, development and water rights — always from willing sellers, never by eminent domain, and it has leveraged roughly $53 million more in grants and partnerships. USE IT: development itself pays for the conservation; the Land Bank Commission sets an annual acquisition programme and must balance purchases geographically.

trackers.name: Transfer of Development Rights Program — King County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: instead of buying land, King County lets rural and resource landowners sell their unused development potential to developers who use it for bonus density inside urban areas — a permanent conservation easement is then recorded on the rural sending site. Over 148,000 acres (230+ square miles) protected since 1998 by moving more than 3,000 potential dwellings out of the countryside. A county TDR Bank buys, holds and resells rights as a revolving fund to catalyse high-priority conservation. USE IT: enrolment usually takes 3–4 months; landowners keep title and can keep farming or managing forest, and can reserve some rights for future use.

trackers.name: Bricklin & Newman LLP — Seattle & Spokane (land use and environmental appeals)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a small Seattle and Spokane firm whose stated focus is protecting communities and the environment from the impacts of development, pollution and logging — representing community groups, individuals and environmental organisations fighting development proposals, and intervening in the legislative and appeal process when local governments adopt zoning or development regulations that permit harm. It litigates before city and county hearing examiners, the Growth Management Hearings Boards, the Shoreline and Pollution Control Hearings Boards, the Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council, the Oregon Land Use Board of Appeals and up to the US Supreme Court; licensed in WA, OR and ID. USE IT: engage at the permit or hearing-examiner stage, where most Washington land use fights are actually decided.

trackers.name: NJ Green Acres — grants to nonprofits and local government to acquire land
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: Green Acres gives MATCHING GRANTS TO NONPROFITS to acquire land for conservation and public recreation, and grants plus ZERO-INTEREST LOANS to municipal and county governments for the same. Over 80,000 acres protected through this route alone. WHO IT SUITS: a land trust or community nonprofit that has found a willing seller — this is the money that closes the purchase. HOW IT DIFFERS: the Planning Incentive Program is the fast lane, and most New Jersey communities already qualify for it. 233 MUNICIPALITIES AND 21 COUNTIES IN NEW JERSEY LEVY AN OPEN SPACE TAX, raising $357.6 million in 2022. Where a local government has that tax AND an adopted open space and recreation plan, the plan itself serves as the application and funding runs at 50% match. Check whether your municipality already has both before assuming there is no local money.

trackers.name: NJ Green Acres — state land acquisition (and how to offer land)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created in 1961 and one of the first state land-acquisition programmes in the country, Green Acres buys land and easements FROM WILLING SELLERS by purchase, donation and bequest — over 650,000 acres preserved, contributing to New Jersey's 1.67 million acres of protected open space. Funded by a dedicated share of the Corporate Business Tax, about $156.6 million a year. USE IT: there is a direct route most people miss — a 'Sale of Land to Green Acres' offer form, so a sympathetic owner can put a parcel forward themselves rather than waiting to be approached. The programme's Appraisal Review Section walks applicants through valuation, which removes the usual first obstacle. Note Green Acres does not keep what it buys: land is assigned to Parks and Forestry, Fish and Wildlife, or the NJ Natural Lands Trust to manage.

trackers.name: New Jersey Green Acres — DEP land-acquisition grants & loans
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): New Jersey DEP's Green Acres program provides matching grants and low-interest loans to local governments AND to nonprofit land trusts (50% match statewide, up to 75% in urban-aid areas) to acquire open space for conservation and recreation — it has protected 725,000+ acres. USE IT: apply as (or partner with) a nonprofit, or work through your municipality or county, to fund the purchase of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Eastern Environmental Law Center (EELC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST (environmental lawyers): New Jersey's only nonprofit public-interest environmental law firm (Newark), representing environmental, conservation and community groups — typically those who cannot otherwise afford counsel — to defend New Jersey's open space, watersheds and wildlife habitats from encroaching development, hold polluters and agencies accountable, and advance environmental justice. USE IT: contact them to get legal representation challenging a project that threatens your community's land, water or health.

trackers.name: Monmouth County Open Space Trust Fund — Monmouth County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): Monmouth was the first New Jersey county to create an Open Space Trust Fund (1987, expanded by referendum five times), and its Municipal Land Preservation Incentive Program will match up to 75% of the acquisition cost a town cannot cover with state Green Acres money — 47 of the county's 53 municipalities have drawn on it. USE IT: get your municipality to apply through the Park System's Acquisition and Design Office; applications are taken year-round, first come, first served.

trackers.name: Morris County Open Space Preservation — Morris County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): the Morris County Preservation Trust Fund, in place since 1994, has preserved over 18,000 acres by giving grants to the county's 39 municipalities and to qualified non-profit conservancies for acquiring land or water areas for conservation — parkland, greenways, ecologically sensitive areas and passive open space. USE IT: applications run in an annual spring cycle; the Open Space Trust Fund Committee makes site visits and scores projects on environmental value and community benefit before recommending them to the County Commissioners, so get your township or a land trust to sponsor the parcel.

trackers.name: Burlington County Farmland Preservation — Burlington County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: New Jersey's farmland preservation programme began in Burlington County, which still leads the state with more than 67,000 acres permanently preserved — the County Agriculture Development Board buys development rights, deed-restricting land to agriculture forever while the owner keeps title, and the county pairs this with outright open-space purchases (as at the Van Wagoner Farm, previously targeted for a large housing development). A 2025 policy change waived the municipal cost share in most cases, removing the main barrier for small towns. USE IT: farm owners apply through the CADB; the annual acquisition targeting list shows what the county is chasing.

trackers.name: Burlington County Municipal Park Development Program — Burlington County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): funded by Burlington County's dedicated Open Space, Recreation, Farmland and Historic Preservation Trust Fund tax (raising roughly $28 million a year), this grant programme gives partner municipalities money to acquire locally important open space, to cover their share of a farmland preservation deal, or to build and improve parks. USE IT: your township applies by council resolution — useful when a specific threatened parcel matters locally but is too small or too municipal to reach the county's own acquisition list.

trackers.name: Somerset County Open Space Preservation — Somerset County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by a county open space trust fund tax voters created and then doubled in 1997, Somerset has assembled more than 24,000 acres of preserved land — buying fee simple, buying or accepting donated conservation easements and development rights, and cost-sharing with municipalities, land trusts and the state Green Acres programme. Priorities run along river greenways, the Second Watchung ridgeline, Sourland Mountain and the Millstone Valley, and the county has bought out development-threatened sites including a 402-acre golf course on Sourland Mountain. USE IT: bring a parcel to county planning staff, ideally with your township and a land trust attached.

trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: one of the oldest and largest transfer-of-development-rights markets in the world, covering the 1.1-million-acre Pine Barrens. Nearly 56,000 acres permanently preserved. The state-chartered PDC Bank issues certificates, keeps the registry of buyers and sellers, and can buy and retire credits itself. USE IT: sellers keep title and any permitted non-residential use; municipalities are legally required to allow credits to be used.

trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Ozaukee County's Planning & Parks Department protects priority natural areas identified in its Park and Open Space Plan and Farmland Preservation Plan through fee-simple purchase, land donations and easement acquisition — recent additions include the 134-acre Clay Bluffs Cedar Gorge Nature Preserve (Lake Michigan clay bluffs, coastal gorge, 0.7 miles of shoreline) and floodplain and wetland parcels bought outright. It uses a GIS ecological prioritisation tool to rank habitat and aquatic-connectivity projects and partners with the Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District, which holds easements on some parcels. USE IT: the Park and Open Space Plan update runs public open houses — that is where a parcel gets onto the acquisition list.

trackers.name: Greenseams — Milwaukee, Ozaukee, Washington & Waukesha Counties (MMSD)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District runs a flood-management programme that buys undeveloped private land and conservation easements — from willing sellers only — along streams, shorelines and wetlands across a 720-square-mile, six-watershed, four-county area, specifically targeting water-absorbing hydric soils in places expected to see major development. Over 5,000 acres acquired since 2001, with a goal of 10,000 more acres of river buffer; one protected acre can store up to 651,000 gallons. The Conservation Fund runs the transactions. USE IT: a wetland or floodplain parcel facing development is worth putting to MMSD as flood infrastructure, not just habitat.

For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Mountain-Prairie Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Mountain-Prairie Region, Lakewood CO — the federal wildlife authority covering Colorado. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: Great Outdoors Colorado (GOCO) — Land Acquisition program
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy land): a competitive grant programme that has helped conserve more than 1.4 million acres in Colorado, funding fee-simple purchases and — where tax credits are insufficient or impractical — conservation easements. Priorities include wildlife habitat and migration corridors, watersheds and riparian systems, scenic viewsheds and greenways, and open space serving disproportionately impacted communities. WHO IT SUITS: Colorado cities, towns and counties, Title 32 special districts, and LAND CONSERVATION ORGANISATIONS — so a land trust can apply, an unincorporated neighbourhood group cannot. HOW IT DIFFERS: eligible fee-simple projects must PROVIDE PUBLIC ACCESS, so a pure no-access habitat purchase is a poor fit for this window; pitch the easement route instead.

trackers.name: Boulder County Parks & Open Space — Boulder County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Boulder County's voter-funded open-space program (a county sales-and-use tax first passed in 1993) has conserved 100,000+ acres — buying land outright and holding conservation easements to keep farms, ranches, wildlife habitat and community buffers from being developed. USE IT: if you own threatened land in Boulder County, contact the Real Estate Division about selling or donating a conservation easement; if you're fighting sprawl, point to the program as the local tool for permanent protection.

trackers.name: Jeffco Parks & Open Space — Jefferson County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created in 1972 by a half-percent county sales tax — the first sales-tax-funded county open space program in the country — Jeffco Parks & Open Space has preserved more than 58,000 acres, buying land and easements from willing sellers under published Land Acquisition Criteria and its Conservation Greenprint. USE IT: nominate a threatened property to the Open Space Department against those criteria, and take the case to the Open Space Advisory Committee, whose public meetings feed acquisition recommendations to the Board of County Commissioners.

trackers.name: PLAN Jeffco — Jefferson County
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the citizen nonprofit that drafted and won the 1972 Open Space Resolution and later the 1998 $160 million open-space bond, and that has since acted as the watchdog on the program — monitoring Open Space Advisory Committee meetings, keeping residents informed, and training citizens in how to advocate for open space against Front Range development. USE IT: bring them a Jefferson County parcel worth protecting or a proposal that would erode the Open Space Program, and use their classes and OSAC presence to get a local campaign heard.

trackers.name: Larimer County Open Lands — Larimer County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by the voter-approved Help Preserve Open Spaces quarter-cent sales tax (1995, extended 1999 and 2014), Larimer County has conserved over 55,000 acres through outright purchase and conservation easements on working ranches and foothills habitat. A 12-member citizen Natural Resources Advisory Board reviews possible acquisitions in monthly public meetings. USE IT: landowners can sell or donate an easement through the Landowner Conservation pages; communities can take a threatened property to the Advisory Board, whose recommendations go to the County Commissioners.

trackers.name: Douglas County Open Space & Natural Resources — Douglas County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by a sixth-of-a-cent open space sales and use tax approved by Douglas County voters in 1994 and extended for 15 more years in 2022, the programme has protected roughly 65,000 acres on the fast-developing Front Range — about 70% of it through conservation easements on private land, the rest county-owned — and it leverages $2.92 in partner money for every $1 of county tax. USE IT: bring a threatened ranch or corridor to Open Space staff or to the Douglas Land Conservancy, which co-holds many of the easements; recent deals include the 2,038-acre Sandstone Ranch.

trackers.name: Pitkin County Open Space and Trails — Pitkin County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: founded in 1990 by a voter-approved dedicated property tax — reauthorised three times, most recently through 2040 — Pitkin County OST has conserved nearly 30,000 acres of the Roaring Fork watershed through outright purchase and conservation easements, including the $34 million Snowmass Falls Ranch buy that stopped development on 650 acres ringed by wilderness. USE IT: acquisitions are recommended by the five-member Open Space and Trails Board of Trustees before going to the County Commissioners, so that board is where a case for a threatened property gets made in public.

trackers.name: Eagle County Open Space and Natural Resources — Eagle County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by a 1.5-mill property tax approved by Eagle County voters in 2002 and extended to 2040, the programme has helped conserve well over 15,000 acres through fee-simple purchases, conservation easements, and — usefully — by paying the transaction costs of easements that other conservation partners will hold. An Open Space Advisory Committee evaluates and recommends projects. USE IT: if a land trust is close to a deal but stuck on survey, appraisal and legal costs, Eagle County money can close that gap; bring ranch and river-corridor parcels to OSAC.

trackers.name: Summit County Open Space & Trails — Summit County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by open space mill levies Summit County voters approved in 1993, 1999, 2003, 2008 and 2019, the programme has protected nearly 18,000 acres through roughly 400 acquisitions since 1995 — buying land at fair market value, taking donated conservation and access easements, and leveraging each county dollar into about $3 of protected land via Great Outdoors Colorado and town partnerships. Priorities include community buffers, growth limitation, scenic corridors, wetlands and wildlife habitat. USE IT: landowners can sell, donate, or partially donate; the department works from the Open Space and Trails Master Plan's acquisition priorities.

trackers.name: Purchase of Development Rights Program — Routt County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: approved by Routt County voters in 1996, amended in 2005 and reauthorised through 2035, the PDR programme uses a 1.5-mill property tax (up to about $1.25 million a year) solely to buy development rights and cover easement costs — nearly 70,000 acres of ranchland, river corridor and wildlife habitat conserved for roughly $32 million, typically paying only part of an easement's value with landowners, Great Outdoors Colorado, land trusts and USDA covering the rest. USE IT: proposals go to the citizen PDR Advisory Board in two tiers (proposal evaluation, then due diligence) before the County Commissioners vote; a land trust such as CCALT usually carries the project.

trackers.name: Open Space & Mountain Parks — City of Boulder
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: in 1967 Boulder voters approved a 0.40-cent sales tax to buy and manage open space — the first time residents of any US city taxed themselves specifically for it, passed by 57%. The programme now holds more than 46,640 acres forming a development buffer around the city, roughly 90% funded by sales and use tax, with a 1971 charter amendment allowing bonds for acquisition and a 1986 charter amendment (77% yes) giving open space permanent protection. USE IT: land comes in by purchase, by joint acquisition with Boulder County, and by dedication during annexation or development — that last route is the one a community can invoke when a project needs city approval.

trackers.name: Natural Areas Department — City of Fort Collins
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a small group of residents put a quarter-cent sales and use tax on the ballot by citizens' initiative in 1992; voters renewed it in 2002 as 'Open Space, Yes!'. Over 55,000 acres conserved and 114 miles of trails, stacked with the separate Larimer County 'Help Preserve Open Space' tax and Great Outdoors Colorado grants. USE IT honestly: the funding has an expiry date, which is why residents keep having to run renewal campaigns, and about 71% of the protected acreage lies outside city limits — a live local argument about whether taxpayers without a car can actually reach what they paid for. The Land Conservation and Stewardship Board advises Council and is the place to raise both points.

trackers.name: Colorado Attorney General
trackers.desc: Colorado’s chief legal officer. WHO TO CONTACT for consumer fraud, environmental harm, charity and nonprofit abuse, antitrust and public corruption in Colorado. You CAN: file complaints and tips the AG can investigate and prosecute; most AG offices have dedicated consumer-protection, environmental and charities divisions. You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: your state AG is often the most powerful — and most reachable — ally against a local corporate or official target, frequently more responsive than federal agencies.

trackers.name: Colorado Business Entity Search
trackers.desc: The official registry of companies, LLCs and corporations registered in Colorado (Secretary of State / equivalent). You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. For activists: this is how you unmask the LLC behind a local development, rezoning or mass eviction — start here to find who really controls it and whom to hold accountable.

trackers.name: Environmental Law Clinic — University of Denver Sturm College of Law
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a student law office clinic whose stated work is protecting impacted communities, wild places and wildlife from pollution, exploitation and OVERDEVELOPMENT. Student attorneys litigate under NEPA, the Endangered Species Act, the National Forest Management Act, the Clean Air and Clean Water Acts and the Administrative Procedure Act — including citizen-enforcement suits. Record includes suing Xcel Energy over the Comanche 3 coal unit at Pueblo and the Lamar Light and Power plant on behalf of WildEarth Guardians, and the Windy Gap Firming Project settlement. USE IT: clinics run on a semester cycle and take limited cases, so approach before a deadline is on top of you.

trackers.name: Western Pennsylvania Conservancy
trackers.desc: Western Pennsylvania Conservancy — a leading land trust/conservancy in Pennsylvania. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good.

trackers.name: PennFuture
trackers.desc: PennFuture — a leading citizen environmental watchdog for Pennsylvania. WHO TO ENLIST against harmful development, extraction, sprawl and pollution. You CAN: tap their research, organizing, litigation and lobbying to fight a specific project, and plug into local coalitions. For activists: a statewide ally that already knows the players, agencies and law — often your best first call.

trackers.name: Chesapeake Bay Foundation (CBF)
trackers.desc: The largest conservation organization dedicated to the Chesapeake Bay watershed. WHO TO ENLIST on development, runoff, wetlands and water-quality fights in the region. You CAN: draw on their science, advocacy, litigation and local networks to challenge harmful projects. For activists: a deep regional ally focused on protecting land and water from destructive development.

trackers.name: Pennsylvania Dept. of Environmental Protection (DEP)
trackers.desc: Pennsylvania’s state environmental regulator. WHO TO CONTACT for pollution complaints, permits, inspections and enforcement within Pennsylvania.
