You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL EPA (below): contact the STATE agency FIRST for anything inside state lines — routine permits, local pollution, inspections, state monitoring data; it is usually faster and more local. Go to the federal EPA regional office only to ESCALATE when the state won’t act, or when the matter crosses state lines or triggers federal law. For activists fighting a local polluter or a permit for an industrial site: this is your primary state contact and records source, frequently faster and more local than federal EPA.

trackers.name: Pennsylvania DCNR Community Conservation Partnerships Program (C2P2)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): DCNR's C2P2 program (~$50M/year, funded by the Keystone Recreation, Park and Conservation Fund and the Environmental Stewardship Fund) makes grants to local governments, nonprofit conservation organizations and pre-qualified land trusts to acquire land and conservation easements for critical habitat, open space, parks and trails (50% match typical). USE IT: apply, as a land trust, nonprofit or municipality, to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Lancaster County Agricultural Preserve Board — Lancaster County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: established in 1980 under Pennsylvania's Act 442/Act 43, the Preserve Board runs the county's agricultural conservation easement purchase program — landowners apply to sell their development rights, the Board ranks applications, commissions appraisals and makes formal offers using combined county and state funds, then monitors the perpetual easement recorded on the deed. It has preserved roughly 91,000 acres across more than 1,100 farms. USE IT: farm owners facing development pressure apply to the Board; the recorded easement binds all future owners.

trackers.name: Chester County Preservation Partnership Program — Chester County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): since 1989 Chester County's Open Lands division has given grants to municipalities and non-profit land conservation organizations for fee-simple purchases and conservation easements — over 20,000 acres preserved through this program alone, with recent awards including 204 acres at Crebilly and 493 acres added to William Penn State Forest. Preference goes to projects that leverage state or federal money. USE IT: an eligible land trust or your township applies in the annual spring grant cycle; a community campaign works by getting one of them to sponsor the parcel.

trackers.name: Bucks County Agricultural Land Preservation — Bucks County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: established in 1989 under Pennsylvania Act 43 and funded by county, state and municipal money, the Bucks County Agricultural Land Preservation Board buys conservation easements that permanently extinguish development rights on productive farmland, ranking farms by soil quality, location, conservation practices and threat of development. A Municipal Partnership Program added in 2025 lets townships put their own money alongside the county's. USE IT: farm owners apply through the county board; townships can top up the county offer to reach full easement value.

trackers.name: Montco Forever Green Open Space Grant Program — Montgomery County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): launched in 2025 as the successor to Montgomery County's 1993 and 2003 open space programmes, Montco Forever Green gives municipalities and qualified non-profit land conservation organisations up to $500,000 per project toward fee-title purchases or conservation easements — any open land in the county, any size, rural to urban, with only a 25% match (down from the old dollar-for-dollar requirement). USE IT: applications are taken on a rolling basis by the County Planning Commission, reviewed by the Open Space Board, then voted by the County Commissioners.

trackers.name: Agricultural Conservation Easement Program — Berks County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Berks ranks second in Pennsylvania and among the leaders nationally for farmland preservation, with over 65,000 acres protected since 1989 — the nine-member county Agricultural Land Preservation Board buys perpetual agricultural conservation easements with combined county and state money, deliberately building large contiguous clusters of preserved farms rather than isolated parcels. Townships can join a purchase alongside the county and state. USE IT: landowners apply free of charge by 31 December each year with no commitment to proceed; applications are scored on the LESA system, which weights soil quality and development pressure.

trackers.name: Fair Shake Environmental Legal Services — Pittsburgh (nonprofit law firm)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a 501(c)(3) nonprofit law firm founded in 2013 to close the environmental legal services gap in the Appalachian Basin, representing residents, grassroots groups and nonprofits on a PRO BONO or sliding-scale, income-based fee — explicitly so that people can act regardless of means. Practice covers oil and gas, land use and zoning, eminent domain, mine reclamation, landfill regulation, stormwater, land conservation and land trusts, citizen suits under the Clean Air and Clean Water Acts, and nonprofit incorporation. It also runs Community Democracy training on civic engagement and organising. USE IT: they publish free guidance on how municipalities rezone quietly for data centres, warehouses and industrial facilities — ring them BEFORE the rezoning hearing.

trackers.name: Florida Forever — state land acquisition programme
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: one of the largest PUBLIC land-acquisition programmes in the United States, run by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. It buys environmentally significant land outright (fee simple) OR buys a conservation easement over it (less-than-fee, so the owner keeps the land but development is barred). Florida Forever and its predecessor Preservation 2000 have together protected more than 2.6 million acres. USE IT: two hard gates decide whether your site is eligible — there must be a WILLING SELLER, and the project must be on the Florida Forever Priority List, which the ten-member Acquisition and Restoration Council ranks. Anyone can sponsor a project: government agencies, conservation organisations or private citizens. Getting a threatened parcel onto that list is the actual fight. Land trusts often act as the intermediary with the owner.

trackers.name: Florida Forever — how to get a parcel considered (FAQ)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the state's own answers on eligibility, sponsorship and process — how projects get onto the Priority List, who ends up owning and managing acquired land (title vests in the Governor and Cabinet as Board of Trustees, held in trust for the people of Florida), and how a landowner can request REMOVAL of their property from a project boundary. USE IT: read this before pitching a site, and note the removal route — a hostile owner can use it, so speed matters. It also names the companion programmes for smaller or local acquisitions: Florida Communities Trust, the Land and Water Conservation Fund, and the Florida Recreation Development Assistance Program.

trackers.name: Earthjustice — Florida Regional Office
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST (environmental lawyers): the Florida regional office of Earthjustice, the nation's premier nonprofit environmental law organization, with attorneys in Tallahassee and Miami providing free legal representation to citizen groups and conservation organizations — it has defended the Everglades and Florida's waters and wetlands for 35+ years and overturned the state's takeover of federal wetlands permitting. USE IT: contact them, or partner with a local group they represent, to challenge a project threatening Florida's land, water or wildlife.

trackers.name: Alachua County Forever — Alachua County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created by a 2000 bond referendum and now funded by the voter-renewed Wild Spaces Public Places half-cent sales tax, Alachua County Forever has protected more than 36,000 acres by buying land outright and by purchasing conservation easements from willing landowners; condemnation is not permitted. USE IT: anyone can nominate a property using the program's one-page nomination form — staff score it on a 25-question matrix (water, habitat, species, social value) and the Land Conservation Board ranks it onto the acquisition list.

trackers.name: Jan K. Platt ELAPP — Hillsborough County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Environmental Lands Acquisition and Protection Program, created by Hillsborough County voters in 1987 and expanded by referendum in 1990 and 2008, has acquired or helped protect roughly 62,000 acres of environmentally sensitive land. It is voluntary and non-regulatory — it buys only from willing sellers — and citizen volunteer committees run every key stage. USE IT: anyone can nominate a site, which triggers a staff assessment and a public ELAPP committee evaluation and ranking; a threatened wetland, scrub or river corridor in Hillsborough belongs in that queue.

trackers.name: Environmentally Endangered Lands (EEL) Program — Miami-Dade County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by a property tax Miami-Dade voters approved in 1990, the EEL Program has brought more than 20,700 acres of pineland, hardwood hammock, salt marsh and wetland into public ownership, buying only from willing sellers and stretching its money with matching grants and acquisition partners. USE IT: the program considers newly proposed sites twice a year — staff and the citizen-volunteer Land Acquisition Selection Committee inspect each one and, after a public hearing, recommend sites to the County Commission, so a threatened natural area can be put into that pipeline from outside.

trackers.name: Environmentally Sensitive Lands Protection Program — Sarasota County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: approved by Sarasota County voters in 1999 and extended to 2029 in 2005, ESLPP (with the companion Neighborhood Parkland program) has protected more than 42,000 acres by outright purchase and conservation easement — including three easements totalling 8,060 acres on Longino Ranch in the Eastern Ranchlands priority site. Purchases require a willing seller. USE IT: any resident can submit a land nomination form to landnominations@scgov.net; staff screen it, then the Environmentally Sensitive Lands Oversight Committee reviews it before the County Commission votes.

trackers.name: Volusia Forever — Volusia County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a dedicated 0.2-mill county tax approved by Volusia voters in 2000 and renewed for another 20 years in 2020, funding purchase of environmentally sensitive land, water-resource land, outdoor recreation land and now working forests and farmland — nearly 60,000 acres protected countywide with its predecessor programme. USE IT: the county accepts nominations “from any government entity, conservation organization, corporation or individual” for any property in the county, whether or not you own it (it is a willing-seller programme); the nine-member Volusia Forever Advisory Committee visits sites and recommends to the County Council. A separate Small Lot programme absorbs parcels in nine antiquated subdivisions with no survey or appraisal required.

trackers.name: Environmentally Endangered Lands (EEL) Program — Brevard County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by a Brevard County referendum in 1990, reaffirmed in 2004 and extended again in 2022, EEL has protected more than 28,000 acres of scrub, wetland, woodland and lagoon-buffering habitat, buying from willing sellers and leveraging state and St. Johns River Water Management District money. Current acquisition focus: the Brevard Coastal Scrub Ecosystem and the North Indian River Lagoon Blueways projects. USE IT: parcels are nominated for public acquisition and reviewed by the eight-member volunteer EEL Selection & Management Committee — seven of them scientists — and only land the committee recommends can be bought with EEL funds, so that committee is where a campaign lands.

trackers.name: Conservation 20/20 — Lee County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: approved by Lee County voters in 1996, Conservation 20/20 has protected more than 31,000 acres of Southwest Florida wetlands, uplands and wildlife corridors, buying from willing sellers. Anyone can nominate a property; the citizen Conservation Land Acquisition and Stewardship Advisory Committee (CLASAC) ranks nominations into Tier I and Tier II priority lists in monthly public meetings, and purchases go to the County Commissioners for final approval. NOTE: county staff declined to replenish the acquisition fund in the 2025 budget round, so roughly $19 million remains against far more in nominated properties — tier ranking now decides what actually gets bought. USE IT: nominate the parcel anyway and turn out at CLASAC.

trackers.name: Preservation Project — City of Jacksonville
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: launched in 1999 as a $300m+ 'greenprint for growth' and the largest land acquisition programme in Florida's history, buying environmentally sensitive land across five priority corridors (St Johns River, the Southeast Greenbelt, the Intracoastal Waterway and others) explicitly to steer development away from them. Tens of thousands of acres protected; combined with National Park Service and state park land through a tri-governmental partnership it forms the largest urban park system in the contiguous US. USE IT: the city worked through the Trust for Public Land and a nonprofit intermediary to negotiate with landowners, and recovered millions via Florida Communities Trust grants — the model is city money plus a land trust doing the deals plus state grant reimbursement.

trackers.name: Florida Business Entity Search
trackers.desc: The official registry of companies, LLCs and corporations registered in Florida (Secretary of State / equivalent). You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. For activists: this is how you unmask the LLC behind a local development, rezoning or mass eviction — start here to find who really controls it and whom to hold accountable.

trackers.name: Florida Attorney General
trackers.desc: Florida’s chief legal officer. WHO TO CONTACT for consumer fraud, environmental harm, charity and nonprofit abuse, antitrust and public corruption in Florida. You CAN: file complaints and tips the AG can investigate and prosecute; most AG offices have dedicated consumer-protection, environmental and charities divisions. You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: your state AG is often the most powerful — and most reachable — ally against a local corporate or official target, frequently more responsive than federal agencies.

trackers.name: Everglades Law Center — nonprofit public interest law firm
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a nonprofit law firm founded in 1995 representing the public interest in ENVIRONMENTAL AND LAND USE matters, working with 30+ national, state and local groups. Record of stopping things: blocked expansion of nearly 20,000 acres of lime rock mines in the Everglades Agricultural Area; prevented a commercial airport between two national parks; defeated a proposal to deepen and widen the Lake Worth Inlet that would have destroyed corals and manatee seagrass beds; and successfully challenged numerous developments that violated Florida's growth-management laws. USE IT: they appear not only in court but before WATER MANAGEMENT DISTRICTS AND COUNTY COMMISSIONS — the bodies that actually approve most Florida development.

trackers.name: Openlands
trackers.desc: Openlands — a leading land trust/conservancy in Illinois. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good.

trackers.name: Illinois Environmental Council
trackers.desc: Illinois Environmental Council — a leading citizen environmental watchdog for Illinois. WHO TO ENLIST against harmful development, extraction, sprawl and pollution. You CAN: tap their research, organizing, litigation and lobbying to fight a specific project, and plug into local coalitions. For activists: a statewide ally that already knows the players, agencies and law — often your best first call.

trackers.name: Environmental Law & Policy Center (ELPC)
trackers.desc: The Midwest’s leading public-interest environmental legal advocacy organization. WHO TO ENLIST against polluting facilities, pipelines, factory farms and dirty-energy projects across the region. You CAN: get legal and policy advocacy to challenge projects and permits. For activists: regional legal muscle and clean-energy expertise to fight harmful development.

trackers.name: Illinois Environmental Protection Agency (IEPA)
trackers.desc: Illinois’s state environmental regulator. WHO TO CONTACT for pollution complaints, permits, inspections and enforcement within Illinois. You CAN: report suspected violations, search permits and enforcement records, and pull state monitoring data — often the front-line regulator before the federal EPA. You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL EPA (below): contact the STATE agency FIRST for anything inside state lines — routine permits, local pollution, inspections, state monitoring data; it is usually faster and more local. Go to the federal EPA regional office only to ESCALATE when the state won’t act, or when the matter crosses state lines or triggers federal law. For activists fighting a local polluter or a permit for an industrial site: this is your primary state contact and records source, frequently faster and more local than federal EPA.

trackers.name: Illinois Public-Records Law Guide (RCFP)
trackers.desc: Illinois’s public-records and open-meetings (‘sunshine’) law, explained by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. You CAN get: a plain-language, attorney-written guide to what records are public in Illinois, how to request them, what exemptions and fees apply, and how to appeal a denial. You CAN’T get: the records themselves — this tells you how to demand them. For activists: your practical playbook for prying documents out of Illinois and its local agencies — permits, emails, inspection reports — usually without needing a lawyer.

trackers.name: Illinois DNR — Wildlife
trackers.desc: Illinois’s state fish & wildlife / natural-resources authority. WHO TO CONTACT on wildlife, habitat and state-protected species. You CAN: report habitat destruction, check state endangered-species and critical-habitat protections, and reach the agency that reviews a project’s impact on wildlife. You CAN’T: enforce the federal Endangered Species Act (that’s U.S. Fish & Wildlife). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM FEDERAL USFWS (below): the STATE agency handles STATE-listed species, state habitat review and (in states like California) the wildlife review inside state environmental-review law; USFWS handles FEDERALLY-listed species and the federal ESA. Contact BOTH — a species may be listed under state law, federal law, or both, and each listing is a separate legal tool. For activists fighting a development: a protected species or critical habitat on-site can stop or reshape it — this is the state authority that confirms and can act on it, alongside federal USFWS.

trackers.name: EPA Region 5 (Chicago)
trackers.desc: The EPA regional office — Region 5, Chicago — the federal environmental regulator covering Illinois. WHO TO CONTACT: for federal enforcement, permits and cross-boundary pollution. You CAN: report violations to the federal EPA office that actually handles Illinois, and engage on federal environmental actions. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE REGULATOR: use the federal EPA when the state agency is captured, unresponsive or lacks jurisdiction — interstate pollution, federal permits (e.g. Clean Water Act §404 dredge-and-fill), federal facilities, or national environmental law. Don’t start here for a routine local permit; the state handles that faster. For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Midwest Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Midwest Region, Bloomington MN — the federal wildlife authority covering Illinois. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. Use the state agency for state-listed species and state review; turn to USFWS the moment a FEDERALLY protected species or designated critical habitat is in play. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: Illinois OSLAD — Open Space Lands Acquisition & Development grant (IDNR)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): IDNR's OSLAD program, funded by a dedicated share of the state Real Estate Transfer Tax, gives grants (up to 50%, or up to 100% for distressed communities) to local units of government to acquire land for public parks, open space and natural-resource preservation. USE IT: work through your municipality or park district to apply for an acquisition grant on a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County — Cook County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Forest Preserves of Cook County — the largest forest preserve district in the U.S. (est. 1914, ~70,000 acres) — has a statutory mandate to acquire and permanently protect open space, prairies, woodlands and wetlands across metropolitan Chicago, funded by a county tax levy and bonds. USE IT: alert the District to a threatened natural parcel that fills a gap in its holdings, or partner with allied groups to push for its acquisition.

trackers.name: Lake County Forest Preserves — Lake County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Illinois's second-largest forest preserve district (est. 1958) protects nearly 31,000 acres in the county with the most threatened and endangered species in the state, and in November 2024 county voters approved a $155 million bond of which $65 million is earmarked specifically for buying more land. USE IT: bring a threatened natural parcel to the district's Planning and Land Preservation staff — all acquisitions are approved in public by the elected Board of Commissioners, so a community campaign can press the case there.

trackers.name: Forest Preserve District of DuPage County — DuPage County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: established by referendum in 1915 and funded by a county property-tax levy and bonds, the district's statutory mission is to acquire and hold forests, prairies, wetlands and restorable land — nearly 26,000 acres, about 12 percent of DuPage County, in one of Illinois's most developed areas. It keeps buying: a $12 million, 35-acre purchase beside Danada Forest Preserve closed in 2024. USE IT: flag a threatened parcel that would fill a gap in or buffer an existing preserve; acquisitions are approved in public by the elected Board of Commissioners.

trackers.name: McHenry County Conservation District — McHenry County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: established by countywide referendum in 1971 under the Illinois Conservation District Act — one of only five such districts in the state (with Boone, Macon, Putnam and Vermilion) — it protects roughly 25,800 acres including 17 dedicated State Nature Preserves, in a county holding some of Illinois's highest-quality remaining wetlands. Its statutory purpose is acquiring land by purchase, lease, gift or easement, funded by a dedicated tax levy plus referendum-approved bonds ($141.5 million across two open space referenda). USE IT: bring a parcel to the seven-member Board of Trustees.

trackers.name: Forest Preserve District of Kane County — Kane County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: founded in 1925 and now holding more than 23,000 acres of Fox Valley woodlands, wetlands and prairies, the district buys land only from willing sellers — either additions to existing preserves or entirely new sites — funded by successive voter referenda (1999, 2011, 2017, and a 2024 levy increase passed 125,219 to 87,811 to add up to 125 acres of new preserve a year). Its board is the Kane County Board sitting as forest preserve commissioners, with a standing Land Acquisition committee. USE IT: bring a threatened river-corridor or watershed parcel to that committee.

trackers.name: Greater Chicago Legal Clinic — Environmental Law Program
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a legal services provider for low-income Chicagoans whose Environmental Law Program exists specifically so that people confronting urban environmental problems have equal access to justice — free representation for residents and neighbourhood groups who would otherwise be unrepresented in matters affecting their family's health and safety. It runs the Chicago Environmental and Energy Law Clinic jointly with Chicago-Kent College of Law, appearing in rulemaking, permitting, remediation and enforcement cases at local, state and federal level under every major environmental statute. USE IT: the clinic states it does not impose an agenda on clients but responds to community-directed concerns — so bring your own objective, whether that is stopping a permit, forcing a cleanup or being heard in a rulemaking.

trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Harvard Law School's environmental clinic, working on litigation, administrative, legislative and policy projects with scientists, medical professionals and public interest organisations at federal, state and local level. Output includes briefs, comment letters, model legislation and guidance documents written for NON-LAWYERS. WHO IT SUITS: be clear-eyed about the fit — this clinic leans policy, regulatory drafting and expert-facing work, and its clients include government bodies as well as NGOs. For a single contested application you likely want a plaintiff-side firm or a representation-focused clinic; for a rule, a permit programme or a technical comment that needs to withstand scrutiny, this is the stronger call.

trackers.name: Massachusetts Division of Conservation Services — land acquisition grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): the Massachusetts EEA Division of Conservation Services (DCS) runs several land-acquisition grant programs — the Conservation Partnership Grant reimburses nonprofit land trusts up to 50% (max ~$175k) to acquire land or conservation restrictions; the LAND grant funds municipal conservation-land purchases; and Landscape Partnership and Drinking Water Supply Protection grants fund larger acquisitions. USE IT: as a land trust or municipality, apply to fund the purchase or restriction of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Community Preservation Act (CPA) — local open space funds
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (town by town): a 2000 state law (MGL c.44B) letting any Massachusetts city or town vote in a property-tax surcharge of up to 3% to create a local Community Preservation Fund for open space protection, historic preservation, affordable housing and outdoor recreation — with an annual match from a statewide trust fund financed by Registry of Deeds fees. At least 10% of revenue each year must go to open space. Over 200 municipalities have adopted it and none has ever revoked it. USE IT: adoption is by ballot referendum, so this is the mechanism a community organises for where no county programme exists; spending is then decided each year by a local Community Preservation Committee and Town Meeting or council.

trackers.name: Nantucket Islands Land Bank
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the first land bank of its kind in the United States — recommended by Nantucket Town Meeting in 1983 by 446 votes to 1, authorised by special act of the Massachusetts legislature, and confirmed by the island's voters in 1984. It levies a 2% fee on most real estate transfers in Nantucket County, paid by the buyer, and uses it to buy and hold open space, farmland and recreation land. Over 3,475 acres owned plus 500 more under conservation restriction, more than $420 million spent, and with other conservation groups nearly half the island is now permanently protected. USE IT: five commissioners are directly ELECTED, so acquisition priorities are answerable at the ballot box; first-time homebuyers are exempt on a threshold raised annually (recently $1.2 million).

trackers.name: Martha's Vineyard Land Bank Commission
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created by island voters in 1986 after Nantucket's model, funded by a 2% surcharge on most real estate transfers across the Vineyard's six towns and charged with reversing the loss of farmland, trails and public access during a building boom. About 4,200 acres conserved. The commission is admirably blunt that this is only 7% of the island and that its revenue is modest against need. USE IT: the last item of business at every commission meeting (most Mondays at 3pm) is public input, letters are accepted any time, and a formal public input session runs every other autumn — the acquisition list is genuinely open to residents proposing land.

trackers.name: Clean Ohio Green Space Conservation Program (OPWC)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): the Clean Ohio Green Space Conservation Program, a voter-approved state bond program administered by the Ohio Public Works Commission (OPWC) through 19 local Natural Resources Assistance Councils, provides grants for up to 75% of costs to acquire open space and easements — land for parks, forests, wetlands, natural areas and stream corridors — open to local governments, park districts and nonprofit conservation organizations. USE IT: apply through your district NRAC to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Cleveland Metroparks — Cuyahoga County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Cleveland Metropolitan Park District (est. 1917, now over 25,000 acres across 49 communities) has statutory power to acquire land inside or outside the district for conservation, and its Natural Resources Division evaluates tracts for protection by purchase, easement or other means — aggressively targeting the remaining major river valleys of Northeast Ohio, often alongside Western Reserve Land Conservancy and West Creek Conservancy. USE IT: flag a threatened stream corridor or woodland adjoining a reservation; donations of land, easements and life estates are accepted through the Land Protection Fund.

trackers.name: Columbus and Franklin County Metro Parks — Franklin County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: an independent political subdivision created in 1945 under Ohio Revised Code 1545 to conserve natural resources, now protecting over 28,000 acres across seven Central Ohio counties, funded primarily by a 10-year 0.95-mill levy Franklin County voters approved in 2018 that explicitly covers acquiring additional land for future preservation. Its parks were built river-corridor first, so stream and floodplain land is its core interest. USE IT: bring a threatened river or stream corridor parcel to the Board of Park Commissioners; the district has been assembling such land continuously since 1947.

trackers.name: Summit Metro Parks — Summit County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a levy-funded park district (est. 1921) managing roughly 14,000 acres in Summit County, including six conservation areas held purely for natural-resource protection rather than public recreation — stream corridors, kettle-hole bog, mature forest and rare-species habitat, some of it acquired specifically to stop subdivisions. It routinely partners with the Trust for Public Land, Western Reserve Land Conservancy and the Northeast Ohio Regional Sewer District, stacking Clean Ohio Fund and Ohio EPA water-quality money against local levy dollars. USE IT: bring a threatened wetland or headwater parcel to the park district and to those land trusts together.

trackers.name: Five Rivers MetroParks — Montgomery County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Montgomery County park district protects more than 3,000 acres through conservation easements on privately owned land — headwater streams, large forest tracts and farmland adjoining its parks — alongside outright purchases, with roughly half its land-protection money coming from state and federal grants (chiefly the Clean Ohio Fund, plus LWCF, the Farm and Ranch Lands Protection Program and Ohio EPA's Water Resource Restoration Sponsor Program). Landowners keep ownership. USE IT: bring a stream-corridor or forest parcel to MetroParks' conservation staff; its three-member board approves all land acquisition in public.

trackers.name: Fair Shake Environmental Legal Services — Akron (nonprofit law firm)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the same nonprofit law firm serving Ohio from an Akron office, alongside Pennsylvania and West Virginia. It provides pro bono and sliding-scale representation to individuals, families, grassroots groups and nonprofits directly affected by environmental harm — oil and gas, zoning and land use, landfills, mine reclamation, water and air citizen suits, land conservation and nonprofit formation — and trains new lawyers specifically to serve modest-means environmental clients. USE IT: it is one of very few places in the Ohio River Valley where a community with no money can get an environmental lawyer, and it partners with regional nonprofits for workshops and legal clinics.

trackers.name: Ohio Business Entity Search
trackers.desc: The official registry of companies, LLCs and corporations registered in Ohio (Secretary of State / equivalent). You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. For activists: this is how you unmask the LLC behind a local development, rezoning or mass eviction — start here to find who really controls it and whom to hold accountable.

trackers.name: Ohio Attorney General
trackers.desc: Ohio’s chief legal officer. WHO TO CONTACT for consumer fraud, environmental harm, charity and nonprofit abuse, antitrust and public corruption in Ohio. You CAN: file complaints and tips the AG can investigate and prosecute; most AG offices have dedicated consumer-protection, environmental and charities divisions. You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: your state AG is often the most powerful — and most reachable — ally against a local corporate or official target, frequently more responsive than federal agencies.

trackers.name: Freshwater Land Trust
trackers.desc: Freshwater Land Trust — a leading land trust/conservancy in Alabama. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good.

trackers.name: Alabama Rivers Alliance

You CAN: tap their research, organizing, litigation and lobbying to fight a specific project, and plug into local coalitions. For activists: a statewide ally that already knows the players, agencies and law — often your best first call.

trackers.name: Southern Environmental Law Center (SELC)
trackers.desc: The Southeast’s leading nonprofit environmental law organization. WHO TO ENLIST when a development, highway, pipeline, landfill or polluting plant threatens your area. You CAN: get expert legal representation and advocacy to challenge permits and projects in court — SELC takes major regional cases at no charge to communities. For activists: proven legal firepower that has stopped and reshaped countless Southeastern projects.

trackers.name: Alabama Dept. of Environmental Management (ADEM)
trackers.desc: Alabama’s state environmental regulator. WHO TO CONTACT for pollution complaints, permits, inspections and enforcement within Alabama. You CAN: report suspected violations, search permits and enforcement records, and pull state monitoring data — often the front-line regulator before the federal EPA. You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL EPA (below): contact the STATE agency FIRST for anything inside state lines — routine permits, local pollution, inspections, state monitoring data; it is usually faster and more local. Go to the federal EPA regional office only to ESCALATE when the state won’t act, or when the matter crosses state lines or triggers federal law. For activists fighting a local polluter or a permit for an industrial site: this is your primary state contact and records source, frequently faster and more local than federal EPA.

trackers.name: Alabama Public-Records Law Guide (RCFP)
trackers.desc: Alabama’s public-records and open-meetings (‘sunshine’) law, explained by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. You CAN get: a plain-language, attorney-written guide to what records are public in Alabama, how to request them, what exemptions and fees apply, and how to appeal a denial. You CAN’T get: the records themselves — this tells you how to demand them. For activists: your practical playbook for prying documents out of Alabama and its local agencies — permits, emails, inspection reports — usually without needing a lawyer.

trackers.name: Alabama Wildlife & Freshwater Fisheries (DCNR)
trackers.desc: Alabama’s state fish & wildlife / natural-resources authority. WHO TO CONTACT on wildlife, habitat and state-protected species. You CAN: report habitat destruction, check state endangered-species and critical-habitat protections, and reach the agency that reviews a project’s impact on wildlife. You CAN’T: enforce the federal Endangered Species Act (that’s U.S. Fish & Wildlife). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM FEDERAL USFWS (below): the STATE agency handles STATE-listed species, state habitat review and (in states like California) the wildlife review inside state environmental-review law; USFWS handles FEDERALLY-listed species and the federal ESA. Contact BOTH — a species may be listed under state law, federal law, or both, and each listing is a separate legal tool. For activists fighting a development: a protected species or critical habitat on-site can stop or reshape it — this is the state authority that confirms and can act on it, alongside federal USFWS.

trackers.name: EPA Region 4 (Atlanta)
trackers.desc: The EPA regional office — Region 4, Atlanta — the federal environmental regulator covering Alabama. WHO TO CONTACT: for federal enforcement, permits and cross-boundary pollution. You CAN: report violations to the federal EPA office that actually handles Alabama, and engage on federal environmental actions. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE REGULATOR: use the federal EPA when the state agency is captured, unresponsive or lacks jurisdiction — interstate pollution, federal permits (e.g. Clean Water Act §404 dredge-and-fill), federal facilities, or national environmental law. Don’t start here for a routine local permit; the state handles that faster. For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Southeast Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Southeast Region, Atlanta GA — the federal wildlife authority covering Alabama. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. Use the state agency for state-listed species and state review; turn to USFWS the moment a FEDERALLY protected species or designated critical habitat is in play. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: Alabama Forever Wild Land Trust (ADCNR)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): Forever Wild is Alabama's only state fund dedicated to land conservation (voter-established 1992, extended to 2032), funded by a portion of the Alabama Trust Fund (oil and gas royalties) — ADCNR's State Lands Division uses it to acquire wildlands, nature preserves, recreation areas and wildlife management areas (284,000+ acres), often leveraging federal and nonprofit funds and partner-nominated tracts. USE IT: nominate a threatened tract, or partner with ADCNR or a land trust, to fund its purchase and permanent protection.

trackers.name: County Soil & Water Conservation Districts — Alabama Soil and Water Conservation Committee
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Alabama has 67 soil and water conservation districts — ONE IN EVERY COUNTY — each a legal subdivision of state government governed by a five-member board of supervisors serving without pay, with staff and a working agreement giving them NRCS technical support. Their stated role includes erosion control, water protection on private land, helping landowners reach USDA conservation programmes, and serving as the local voice ensuring state and federal programmes meet local needs. USE IT: the district is the nearest public body with soil and water expertise in any Alabama county, and its supervisors are listed publicly by county — approach them for technical evidence and for a local institutional voice.

trackers.name: Pima County Conservation Lands Acquisitions — Pima County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: under the Sonoran Desert Conservation Plan and voter-approved bond elections, Pima County has assembled a portfolio of over 250,000 acres — land owned outright plus conservation easements, grazing leases and other agreements — and the Board of Supervisors continues to appropriate funding for new acquisitions that fill gaps in the Conservation Lands System. USE IT: if a biologically important parcel is threatened, ask Conservation Lands & Resources to evaluate it against Conservation Lands System priorities for acquisition; landowners can also donate land or an easement to the County.

trackers.name: Coalition for Sonoran Desert Protection — Pima County
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an alliance of roughly 30 conservation and neighborhood member groups (formed 1998) that is the regional leader on land-use fights in eastern Pima County — it uses science-based advocacy, habitat conservation planning, wildlife-linkage protection and community science to oppose destructive development and to hold Pima County to the Sonoran Desert Conservation Plan. USE IT: bring them a proposed project that would cut a wildlife corridor or eat into Conservation Lands System land; member-group status connects a local campaign to a countywide advocacy network.

trackers.name: Floodprone Land Acquisition Program — Pima County Regional Flood Control District
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a distinct route to protection from the county's conservation bonds — the Regional Flood Control District buys flood-prone land outright to preserve natural floodplain function, then manages it as open space under a Land Stewardship Program with watershed-by-watershed management plans, supporting both the Sonoran Desert Conservation Plan and the county's Multi-Species Conservation Plan obligations. USE IT: if the parcel you are defending sits in a floodplain or riparian corridor, this is often the stronger argument and the better-funded buyer, because flood-risk reduction and lower flood insurance costs justify the purchase independently of habitat value.

trackers.name: Parks & Preserve Initiative / Sonoran Preserve — City of Phoenix
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Phoenix voters approved a dedicated sales tax for preserve acquisition in 1999 and renewed it in 2008 by 83% for a further 30 years — one cent per $10 of purchases, with 40% of proceeds dedicated to acquiring and developing the desert preserves and 60% to parks. The Sonoran Preserve in north Phoenix has grown to over 9,600 acres, and preserve land is protected by Chapter 26 of the City Charter. USE IT: the citizen Sonoran Preserve & Mountain Parks/Preserves Committee meets quarterly and recommends ordinances affecting the preserves and the development around them, and a separate oversight committee audits annually whether spending matches the ballot language voters approved.

trackers.name: McDowell Sonoran Preserve — City of Scottsdale
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: volunteers formed a land trust in 1991 with a dream of a connected desert corridor; Scottsdale voters then approved a 30-year sales tax for land purchase in May 1995 and a second in 2004, funding over 30,580 acres inside a defined 34,000-acre Recommended Study Boundary — the largest municipal land preserve in the country, about a quarter of the city's total area, owned outright by the city and co-managed with the McDowell Sonoran Conservancy. USE IT honestly: the original 0.20% acquisition tax expired on 30 June 2025 and voters replaced it in November 2024 with a 0.15% tax for maintenance, parks and protection rather than new acquisition — the buying phase has largely closed, and a citizen task force process decided that.

trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Earthjustice represents clients at no charge and has acted for the Tohono Oʼodham Nation, Pascua Yaqui Tribe and Hopi Tribe in blocking a company's attempt to open a mile-wide copper mine on sacred lands south of Tucson — a ruling with precedential weight for ancestral lands elsewhere. USE IT: where a project touches ancestral or sacred land, tribal consultation failures under federal law are usually a stronger and faster ground than state permitting arguments.

trackers.name: Arkansas Natural & Cultural Resources Council (ANCRC)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): the ANCRC administers a grants-and-trust fund (from the state real-estate transfer tax) for the acquisition, management and stewardship of state-owned natural areas and recreation lands — grants go to state agencies such as the Natural Heritage Commission and State Parks, which use them to buy natural areas (e.g., the 4,230-acre Cossatot River corridor). USE IT: partner with, or advocate to, the Arkansas Natural Heritage Commission or State Parks to nominate a threatened tract for acquisition through an ANCRC grant.

trackers.name: Buffalo River Watershed Alliance
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: formed in 2013 by a former pig farmer and neighbours with two stated goals — close the C&H swine CAFO permitted beside a Buffalo National River tributary, and win a permanent ban on future CAFO permits in the watershed. They achieved both: after six years of permit challenges, intervention petitions, expert karst-geology testimony and appeals brought with the Ozark Society, Arkansas Canoe Club, National Parks Conservation Association and Earthjustice, the state bought out the farm for $6.2 million in 2019, took a conservation easement over the land, and the legislature approved a permanent moratorium in 2025. USE IT: BRWA publishes its entire permit-fight document trail — objection letters, technical attachments, motions to intervene — which is a working template for anyone contesting an agricultural or industrial permit.

trackers.name: County conservation districts — Arkansas Association of Conservation Districts
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Arkansas passed the first soil conservation district law in the nation (Act 197 of 1937) and districts are POLITICAL SUBDIVISIONS OF THE STATE, created by popular vote of resident landowners, covering the whole state since 1955. Act 197 gives districts specific authorities including to CONSTRUCT, IMPROVE, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN WORKS OF IMPROVEMENT, to cooperate with other districts, and to ORGANISE AN IRRIGATION, DRAINAGE OR WATERSHED DEVELOPMENT DISTRICT to build and run dams, levees and ditches. USE IT: for a community facing a water or erosion threat, the district is a standing unit of local government with construction and watershed powers — and it can partner across district lines when a problem crosses county boundaries.

trackers.name: Iowa Resource Enhancement & Protection (REAP)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): Iowa's REAP program (funded by state gaming receipts) provides grants and cost-share for land acquisition — competitive City Park & Open Spaces grants to cities, 100% County Conservation grants to counties for land purchases and easements, and Open Space acquisition where REAP pays up to 75% and a private partner such as a land trust provides 25%. USE IT: work through your city or county, or partner with a land trust, to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Polk County Water & Land Legacy Bond — Polk County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): Polk County voters approved a $50 million conservation bond in 2012 and renewed it at $65 million in 2021, running through 2032, with a dedicated share for land and habitat acquisition administered by the Polk County Conservation Board — it lets the county move fast when open land in the growing Des Moines metro comes up for sale before a developer takes it. USE IT: bring a threatened parcel to Polk County Conservation; the board publishes progress reports and buys both proactively and opportunistically.

trackers.name: Linn County Conservation — Linn County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: one of the 99 county conservation boards Iowa created under Chapter 350 of the Code of Iowa (Linn's was established by popular vote in 1958), statutorily empowered to acquire, develop and hold conservation areas, parks and preserves — Linn manages over 9,000 acres and voters approved a $40 million Water and Land Legacy bond to keep buying, including a 485-acre creek-corridor purchase south of Squaw Creek Park. USE IT: bring a threatened natural area to the Conservation Board, whose meetings and agendas are public; every Iowa county has an equivalent board with the same acquisition power.

trackers.name: Iowa's 99 county conservation boards — find yours (IACCB)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Iowa is the only state where every single county has a voter-established conservation board with statutory power to acquire and hold land — created by Chapter 350 of the Code of Iowa in 1955, the 99 boards now own or manage nearly 200,000 acres across more than 1,850 areas. The Iowa Association of County Conservation Boards runs this statewide directory of them. USE IT: find your county's board, then take a threatened natural area to it — board meetings are public and the board itself decides what to buy.

trackers.name: Purchase of Development Rights (PDR) — Lexington-Fayette County

Roughly $2 million a year of local money is matched with federal NRCS easement funds. USE IT: farms of 20+ acres (or adjoining tracts totalling that) apply to the PDR office in the annual cycle; a Small Farm Program extends the same deal to smaller holdings.

Their stated purposes include protecting and restoring the coastal zone as a natural storm barrier, flood control and water filtration system and as wildlife habitat, and resolving conflicts between competing uses. USE IT: if your parish has an approved LCP, the coastal use permit hearing is a LOCAL hearing you can attend and object at; if it does not, adopting one is the way to bring that decision home.

trackers.name: Maine Inland Fisheries & Wildlife

trackers.name: Land for Maine's Future (LMF)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): Land for Maine's Future is the state's primary land-conservation funding program — it provides land-acquisition funding to state agencies, municipalities and private land trusts to purchase land and easements of statewide, regional or local significance from willing sellers (farmland, water access, working waterfronts, wildlife habitat), and in 2026 gained ongoing dedicated funding. USE IT: partner with a Designated State Agency, or as a land trust or municipality, to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Land for Maine's Future (LMF)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): Maine's primary land conservation fund, created when voters approved a $35 million bond in 1987 and replenished by further bonds in 1999, 2005, 2007, 2010 and 2012, then appropriated $40 million in 2021 after nearly a decade without new money. Over 300 projects funded, protecting farmland, water access, working waterfront and recreation land — roughly 90% of Maine is privately owned, so public access depends on it. LAND TRUSTS AND MUNICIPALITIES can apply, not just state agencies. USE IT: awards go up to 50% of appraised value and you must secure matching funds at least equal to the award, so line up your other sources first — LMF publishes a partner-funding checklist showing which programmes stack with it.

trackers.name: Town conservation commissions — Maine Association of Conservation Commissions
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a municipal advisory board established by a Maine town, city or plantation through its legislative body, which advises planning and select boards, conducts natural resource surveys, develops open space plans, PROPOSES ORDINANCES, monitors development and stewards public land. The association exists to help citizens form new commissions as well as support existing ones. USE IT: in a state with weak county government this is the standing body a community can join or create to get conservation into the town plan and to watch permit applications — ring the association if your town has no commission and you want to start one.

trackers.name: Program Open Space (Maryland) — county-allocated land acquisition money
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: Maryland's land programme since 1969, funded by a 0.5% STATE REAL ESTATE TRANSFER TAX — so it is not a budget line that competes each year, it flows with property sales. Over 7,100 projects and 422,700 acres. Two arms: STATESIDE buys large tracts by fee simple and conservation easement for State Parks, Forests and wildlife management areas; POS LOCAL funds county and municipal acquisition and development. WHO IT SUITS: the local arm is the one most communities can actually reach. HOW IT DIFFERS, AND THIS IS THE POINT: POS Local funds are ALLOCATED ANNUALLY TO ALL 23 COUNTIES AND BALTIMORE CITY BY FORMULA. Money is already earmarked for your county — what it gets spent on is decided locally, entered in the county's POS Local Annual Program and then sent to the Board of Public Works. So lobby the county, not the state. Separately, the Rural Legacy Program covers 36 locally designated areas where land trusts acquire easements over working landscapes.

trackers.name: Maryland Program Open Space (DNR)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): Maryland's Program Open Space, funded by the state real-estate transfer tax since 1969, funds land acquisition and conservation easements — its Stateside component acquires large tracts and easements for state parks, forests and wildlife areas, and its Local component and Rural Legacy program give grants to county and municipal governments and to land trusts to plan, acquire and protect recreational and conservation land (422,700+ acres protected). USE IT: work through your county or municipality, or a Rural Legacy land trust, to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Montgomery County Agricultural Land Preservation — Montgomery County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Montgomery County has preserved more than 70,000 acres — the highest share of farmland under easement of any county in the nation — through seven stacked programs anchored on the 93,000-acre Agricultural Reserve: the county Agricultural Easement Program buys development rights outright, while Transferable Development Rights and Building Lot Termination easements permanently cap or extinguish residential density on a property. USE IT: landowners facing development pressure can apply to the county Agricultural Easement Program (typically 6–12 months, no state approval needed); communities can cite Ag Reserve zoning and recorded TDR easements when opposing a subdivision.

trackers.name: Baltimore County Land Preservation — Baltimore County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: with nearly 70,000 acres already under easement, Baltimore County's Planning Department runs a county Agricultural Protection Program alongside the state MALPF and Rural Legacy programs, and funds easements and outright purchases itself within five designated Rural Legacy Areas — targeting farm and forest land, stream valleys and reservoir watersheds. USE IT: landowners inside a Rural Legacy Area apply through the land trust that sponsors it (Land Preservation Trust for Piney Run, The Manor Conservancy for Manor, the county itself for the Coastal area); easements can be sold or donated.

trackers.name: Harford County Agricultural Preservation — Harford County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a nationally recognised farmland preservation leader since 1977 with more than 64,000 acres preserved, Harford County runs its own Agricultural Land Preservation Program (HALPP) buying development rights under Chapter 60 of the county code, alongside the state MALPF programme, the Maryland Environmental Trust and the Deer Creek Rural Legacy Area (nearly 67,000 acres of watershed) which the county administers. USE IT: landowners with agricultural or forest land, at least one spare development right and qualifying soils apply competitively through Planning and Zoning; easements are perpetual.

trackers.name: Installment Purchase Program — Frederick County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created in 2002 and funded by a dedicated share of the county's recordation tax, Frederick County's IPP buys permanent agricultural easements using installment purchase agreements — paying the farmer tax-free interest over 10 to 20 years with a lump-sum principal at the end, which for many families beats a single taxable payout. More than 24,000 acres preserved across 172 properties, alongside the county's MALPF and Critical Farms programmes. USE IT: apply through the Office of Agriculture; you need 50+ acres (or adjacency to protected land), qualifying soils and remaining development rights.

trackers.name: Agricultural & Woodland Preservation — Anne Arundel County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Anne Arundel runs a stack of easement programmes — its own local programme (from 1990, open to parcels of 50+ acres, 6,583 acres protected), the state MALPF programme (5,485 acres), and the Anne Arundel South Rural Legacy Area, a 37,381-acre corridor between the Patuxent and Rhode Rivers where the explicit goals include creating a greenway and extinguishing development rights. Recent easement offers have run $8,000–$10,000 per acre with cash at settlement. USE IT: deadlines differ by programme (MALPF 1 May; local 1 November and 1 April; Rural Legacy 1 December) — landowner interest drives the county's annual capital budget ask, so applying is itself the lobbying.

trackers.name: Rural Legacy Program — Maryland DNR
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): enacted in 1997 explicitly to discourage sprawl, Rural Legacy funds county governments and private land trusts — not the state directly — to buy conservation easements from willing owners inside locally designated Rural Legacy Areas, of which there is at least one in every Maryland county. Over 130,000 acres preserved, with annual awards recently running $15–35 million. USE IT: a local sponsor (your county or a land trust) applies each year to the Rural Legacy Board, and can also apply to expand an existing Rural Legacy Area or designate a brand-new one — so a community can get its landscape onto the map, not just individual parcels.

USE IT: work with your city, county or township to apply for an acquisition grant on a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Ottawa County Parks & Open Space — Ottawa County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Ottawa County Parks manages over 7,700 acres of parks, dunes, greenways and open space, bought and stewarded with a dedicated voter-approved Parks & Open Space millage renewed for ten years in 2026 — the money buys land and easements outright (the 353-acre Ottawa Sands dune purchase, ongoing Macatawa and Grand River Greenway acquisitions) and is routinely stacked with Michigan Natural Resources Trust Fund grants. USE IT: bring a threatened parcel adjoining an existing park or greenway to Park Planning staff; acquisitions go before the Parks and Recreation Commission in public.

trackers.name: Natural Areas Preservation Program (NAPP) — Washtenaw County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: established in 2000 by county ordinance and funded by a countywide quarter-mill NAPP millage (renewed by voters repeatedly), the programme buys natural areas outright for public nature preserves and, since 2010, also buys agricultural conservation easements — with 93% of millage revenue required by ordinance to go to land acquisition rather than overheads. It is run by the Washtenaw County Parks and Recreation Commission and has co-funded dozens of easements held by townships and land trusts. USE IT: landowners nominate their own land for purchase or for a purchase of development rights through the programme's application page.

trackers.name: Purchase of Development Rights (PDR) — Kent County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a voluntary county programme that pays farmland owners the difference between their land's unrestricted market value and its value as farmland, in exchange for a permanent deed restriction barring non-agricultural development — in one of Michigan's most agriculturally productive counties (over $231 million of annual output). Values are set by independent appraisal and negotiated farm by farm; the owner keeps title, can still sell the land as farmland, and can still borrow against it. USE IT: farmers facing development pressure apply to the county; the cash typically goes to debt reduction, expansion or generational transfer, which is what keeps the farm operating rather than selling out.

trackers.name: Greenbelt & Bluebelt Program — City of Ann Arbor
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Ann Arbor voters passed a 30-year, 0.5-mill Open Space and Parkland Preservation millage in 2003 to buy development rights on farmland and natural areas — mostly OUTSIDE the city limits — protecting nearly 8,000 acres with Washtenaw County and surrounding townships, and in 2024 adding a second 'Bluebelt' boundary covering the Huron River watershed upstream of the city's drinking water intake. USE IT: two features are worth copying. Removing development rights lowers land price, which the city uses deliberately to get beginning farmers onto land; and its buy-protect-sell initiative buys a farm, attaches an easement, then resells it cheaply to income-qualified small farmers who own no land, recycling the proceeds back into the fund.

USE IT: applications go to the county's Open Lands Citizen Advisory Committee, which recommends to the County Commission; a land trust such as Five Valleys usually carries the project.

USE IT honestly: Bold is an organiser, not a law firm, and it has at times negotiated community benefit agreements instead of opposing a project outright.

USE IT: because the board is elected and the district follows your watershed, this is the most accessible and most watershed-relevant body of government in Nebraska — attend board meetings, stand for election, and raise land and water threats there.

You CAN: report habitat destruction, check state endangered-species and critical-habitat protections, and reach the agency that reviews a project’s impact on wildlife. You CAN’T: enforce the federal Endangered Species Act (that’s U.S. Fish & Wildlife). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM FEDERAL USFWS (below): the STATE agency handles STATE-listed species, state habitat review and (in states like California) the wildlife review inside state environmental-review law; USFWS handles FEDERALLY-listed species and the federal ESA. Contact BOTH — a species may be listed under state law, federal law, or both, and each listing is a separate legal tool. For activists fighting a development: a protected species or critical habitat on-site can stop or reshape it — this is the state authority that confirms and can act on it, alongside federal USFWS.

trackers.name: EPA Region 9 (San Francisco)
trackers.desc: The EPA regional office — Region 9, San Francisco — the federal environmental regulator covering Nevada. WHO TO CONTACT: for federal enforcement, permits and cross-boundary pollution. You CAN: report violations to the federal EPA office that actually handles Nevada, and engage on federal environmental actions. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE REGULATOR: use the federal EPA when the state agency is captured, unresponsive or lacks jurisdiction — interstate pollution, federal permits (e.g. Clean Water Act §404 dredge-and-fill), federal facilities, or national environmental law. Don’t start here for a routine local permit; the state handles that faster. For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Pacific Southwest Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Pacific Southwest Region, Sacramento CA — the federal wildlife authority covering Nevada. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. Use the state agency for state-listed species and state review; turn to USFWS the moment a FEDERALLY protected species or designated critical habitat is in play. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: Conservation and Resource Protection Grant Program (Question 1) — Nevada Division of State Lands
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or protect land): Nevada voters approved Question 1 in 2002, authorising up to $200 million in bonds for land conservation — water quality, lakes, rivers, wetlands, open space and wildlife habitat — administered by the Division of State Lands and ranked by staff and the programme administrator. The legislature followed with Assembly Bill 84 in 2019, authorising a further $217 million in bonds over ten years. Crucially the programme includes a dedicated category for NONPROFIT ACQUISITIONS OF LAND AND WATER, so a land trust or community organisation can apply directly rather than only through a government sponsor. USE IT: money is released in metered rounds rather than all at once, deliberately so smaller applicants have time to prepare — watch for the next round opening.

trackers.name: Conservation districts — Nevada DCNR Conservation Districts Program
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Nevada has 28 LOCALLY ELECTED conservation districts, governmental entities under NRS Chapter 548 described by the state as working 'much like school boards'. In a state where the federal government manages more than 85% of the land, the state's own strategic plan identifies their most distinctive power: districts can WORK ACROSS THE BOUNDARY BETWEEN PUBLIC AND PRIVATE LAND, and cooperate with neighbouring districts to address problems on a WATERSHED basis, which is why federal and state agencies route natural resource projects through them. USE IT: elected volunteer boards, so both winnable and open — and the cross-boundary role makes a district a rare local body that can engage on federal land decisions.

trackers.name: Nevada Attorney General
trackers.desc: Nevada’s chief legal officer. WHO TO CONTACT for consumer fraud, environmental harm, charity and nonprofit abuse, antitrust and public corruption in Nevada. You CAN: file complaints and tips the AG can investigate and prosecute; most AG offices have dedicated consumer-protection, environmental and charities divisions. You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: your state AG is often the most powerful — and most reachable — ally against a local corporate or official target, frequently more responsive than federal agencies.

trackers.name: Nevada Business Entity Search
trackers.desc: The official registry of companies, LLCs and corporations registered in Nevada (Secretary of State / equivalent). You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. For activists: this is how you unmask the LLC behind a local development, rezoning or mass eviction — start here to find who really controls it and whom to hold accountable.

trackers.name: New Hampshire LCHIP — Land & Community Heritage Investment Program
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): LCHIP, an independent New Hampshire state authority, awards matching grants to NH municipalities and nonprofits to conserve land and interests in land (and to preserve historic resources) — 290,000+ acres conserved, funded through state document-recording fees. USE IT: as a land trust or town, apply for a matching grant to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Land and Community Heritage Investment Program (LCHIP)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): an independent state authority created by the legislature in 2000 (RSA 227-M) making matching grants directly to NEW HAMPSHIRE TOWNS, CONSERVATION COMMISSIONS AND NON-PROFITS — not only to state agencies — to conserve natural, cultural and historic resources. Over $68 million in 646 grants across 210 communities since 2001, conserving more than 247,000 acres of farmland, timberland and habitat. Each LCHIP dollar reportedly leverages several more in local, private and federal money, and grants are routinely stacked with the state's Drinking Water and Groundwater Trust Fund. USE IT: funded by a fee on real estate recordings, so its budget is fought over each biennium — in 2019 a fee increase passed the legislature and was vetoed. Watch the appropriation.

trackers.name: Town conservation commissions — NH Association of Conservation Commissions
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: under RSA 36-A a New Hampshire town or city may establish a conservation commission with power to ACQUIRE CONSERVATION LAND OR EASEMENTS, hold a municipal Conservation Fund fed by appropriations and tax-deductible donations, accept gifts of land, and comment on state wetlands permit applications. Under RSA 36-A:4-a, adopted by warrant article, a town can additionally authorise its commission to buy land OUTSIDE its own boundaries and to contribute Conservation Fund money to land trusts even where the town takes no property interest. USE IT: municipal ownership alone does not protect land in perpetuity — NHACC advises adding a deed restriction or an easement held by another conservation body, which also stops a future town board eyeing the parcel for a car park.

trackers.name: New Mexico Natural Heritage Conservation Act (EMNRD)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): the NHCA program, run by EMNRD's Forestry Division and funded by the Land of Enchantment Legacy Fund, is New Mexico's only dedicated funding source for conservation and agricultural easements — competitive grants to qualified entities (state agencies, tribes, local governments and conservation nonprofits) to protect forests, watersheds, natural areas, wildlife habitat and working farms and ranches. USE IT: as a land trust, tribe or local government, apply to fund an easement or acquisition on a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Santa Fe County Open Space, Trails and Parks Program — Santa Fe County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the county buys land and accepts donations for open space under procedures set by Resolution 2009-206, managing roughly 9,400 acres — and recent purchases have been driven from below, including the 2,650-acre Bobcat Crossing Ranch in a wildlife corridor between the Sangre de Cristos and the Galisteo Basin. USE IT: anyone can file a Property Acquisition Application with the Open Space and Trails Planner; applications are scored partly on demonstrated community support, so letters, petitions and turnout at COLTPAC meetings materially change the outcome.

trackers.name: Open Space Program — Bernalillo County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: begun through a grassroots campaign that won a 1998 mill-levy referendum (renewed in 2000), Bernalillo County's Open Space Program bought and now manages 17 properties totalling roughly 1,150 acres from the Sandia Mountains to the Rio Grande valley — land the county says would very likely have been developed otherwise — and has partnered on the acquisition of about 780 acres more, including the Valle de Oro National Urban Wildlife Refuge, the first urban refuge in the Southwest. USE IT: the county is still buying (a South Valley acquisition was approved in 2026); acquisitions and open space master plans go to the County Commission in public.

trackers.name: Open Space Division — City of Albuquerque
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Albuquerque has been buying land for preservation since 1963 and now manages over 30,000 acres of Major Public Open Space — foothills, West Mesa volcanoes, Rio Grande bosque and five working farms bought to stop valley farmland disappearing. Voters approved a temporary quarter-cent tax in 1997 that raised about $36 million for acquisition, and the city recently raised the open space set-aside in its general obligation bond package from 2% to 3%, roughly $6 million every two years, with a stated goal of buying everything on the priority acquisition list by 2034. USE IT: the citizen Open Space Advisory Board sets acquisition priorities and also reviews any proposal to sell, lease or build on open space — so it is the body to petition both to protect land and to stop its disposal.

trackers.name: North Carolina Land and Water Fund (NCLWF) — acquisition grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): the NC Land and Water Fund makes grants to local governments, state agencies and nonprofit conservation organizations — land trusts and watershed groups — to acquire land and easements that protect water quality, ecological diversity, natural areas and historic or military-buffer lands (no match strictly required, though matched projects rank better). USE IT: as a land trust, nonprofit or local government, apply (annual March 1 deadline) to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Wake County Open Space Program — Wake County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: funded by successive voter-approved general obligation bonds, Wake County buys land and conservation easements in targeted conservation areas set out in its Consolidated Open Space Plan, using a voluntary reverse-auction 'Solicitation of Interest' in which landowners offer to sell, donate, or place an easement. Recommendations run through the Open Space and Parks Advisory Committee to the Board of Commissioners. USE IT: landowners can offer a parcel in the annual solicitation; recent projects stacked county open-space and farmland-preservation money with Triangle Land Conservancy easements.

trackers.name: Lands Legacy Program — Orange County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: enacted in 2000 and backed by $10 million in bond money county voters have approved since 1997, Lands Legacy buys land outright for parks and nature preserves and buys or accepts donated conservation easements — over 3,000 acres protected, including 28 working farms and “Forever Wild” easements on stream corridors in the Jordan Lake watershed. Local money has pulled in over $5 million in state and federal grants, and projects run with Triangle Land Conservancy, the Eno River Association and the NC Land and Water Fund. USE IT: every two years the County Commissioners adopt an Action Plan setting acquisition priorities — that adoption is the public moment to get a threatened parcel named.

trackers.name: Floodplain Buyout Program — Mecklenburg County (Charlotte-Mecklenburg Storm Water Services)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a joint county-and-municipal stormwater utility funded by impervious-area fees, which since 1999 has voluntarily bought and demolished more than 450 flood-prone properties, returning 185 acres to undeveloped public open space and greenway — over $67 million invested, an estimated $25 million in damage already avoided and $300 million in future losses prevented. Crucially it sets its own eligibility criteria and can make offers within months of a flood using local fee money, instead of waiting years for FEMA. USE IT: it identifies high-risk properties before floods happen, so ask to be on the priority list early; leaseback arrangements are available case by case.

trackers.name: Mountain Revolving Loan Fund — Conservation Trust for North Carolina
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (bridge finance and the costs nobody funds): CTNC runs revolving loan funds holding several million dollars, lending at minimal interest to North Carolina land trusts so they can buy conservation land and easements in the mountains before their own fundraising closes — and as loans are repaid the money is lent again. A share of the fund is given away each year as grants of up to $25,000 that do NOT have to be repaid, deliberately aimed at the hardest money to raise: surveys, appraisals, attorney fees, project administration and long-term stewardship. USE IT: transaction costs are the usual reason a landowner's intended donation or bargain sale collapses — this is the fund that covers them.

USE IT: eligible applicants are the county, any municipality in it, county or municipal agencies, federal agencies, and any 501(c)(3) land-conservation or historic-preservation charity empowered to hold land — so a local land trust can carry a community's parcel into the grant round.

trackers.name: Center for Heirs' Property — clearing title to family land
