It is the single most fragile form of ownership: ANY heir can force a court sale of the whole property, or sell their fractional share to an outside buyer such as a developer, who can then do the same. USE IT: ring for a free one-hour consultation; they also run family meetings to help relatives reach agreement.

You CAN: get legal advocacy, litigation and organizing support to fight projects and enforce environmental law. For activists: a regional powerhouse with the lawyers and track record to take on big projects.

trackers.name: Vermont Dept. of Environmental Conservation (DEC)
trackers.desc: Vermont’s state environmental regulator. WHO TO CONTACT for pollution complaints, permits, inspections and enforcement within Vermont. You CAN: report suspected violations, search permits and enforcement records, and pull state monitoring data — often the front-line regulator before the federal EPA. You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL EPA (below): contact the STATE agency FIRST for anything inside state lines — routine permits, local pollution, inspections, state monitoring data; it is usually faster and more local. Go to the federal EPA regional office only to ESCALATE when the state won’t act, or when the matter crosses state lines or triggers federal law. For activists fighting a local polluter or a permit for an industrial site: this is your primary state contact and records source, frequently faster and more local than federal EPA.

trackers.name: Vermont Public-Records Law Guide (RCFP)
trackers.desc: Vermont’s public-records and open-meetings (‘sunshine’) law, explained by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. You CAN get: a plain-language, attorney-written guide to what records are public in Vermont, how to request them, what exemptions and fees apply, and how to appeal a denial. You CAN’T get: the records themselves — this tells you how to demand them. For activists: your practical playbook for prying documents out of Vermont and its local agencies — permits, emails, inspection reports — usually without needing a lawyer.

trackers.name: Vermont Fish & Wildlife Dept.
trackers.desc: Vermont’s state fish & wildlife / natural-resources authority. WHO TO CONTACT on wildlife, habitat and state-protected species. You CAN: report habitat destruction, check state endangered-species and critical-habitat protections, and reach the agency that reviews a project’s impact on wildlife. You CAN’T: enforce the federal Endangered Species Act (that’s U.S. Fish & Wildlife). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM FEDERAL USFWS (below): the STATE agency handles STATE-listed species, state habitat review and (in states like California) the wildlife review inside state environmental-review law; USFWS handles FEDERALLY-listed species and the federal ESA. Contact BOTH — a species may be listed under state law, federal law, or both, and each listing is a separate legal tool. For activists fighting a development: a protected species or critical habitat on-site can stop or reshape it — this is the state authority that confirms and can act on it, alongside federal USFWS.

trackers.name: EPA Region 1 (Boston)
trackers.desc: The EPA regional office — Region 1, Boston — the federal environmental regulator covering Vermont. WHO TO CONTACT: for federal enforcement, permits and cross-boundary pollution. You CAN: report violations to the federal EPA office that actually handles Vermont, and engage on federal environmental actions. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE REGULATOR: use the federal EPA when the state agency is captured, unresponsive or lacks jurisdiction — interstate pollution, federal permits (e.g. Clean Water Act §404 dredge-and-fill), federal facilities, or national environmental law. Don’t start here for a routine local permit; the state handles that faster. For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Northeast Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Northeast Region, Hadley MA — the federal wildlife authority covering Vermont. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. Use the state agency for state-listed species and state review; turn to USFWS the moment a FEDERALLY protected species or designated critical habitat is in play. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: Environmental Advocacy Clinic — Vermont Law and Graduate School
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the environmental advocacy clinic at Vermont Law and Graduate School, which trains and supervises students on environmental and natural resource matters. WHO IT SUITS: the school runs an unusually broad clinic suite alongside this one — environmental justice, energy, food and agriculture, and transnational environmental law — so if your matter is really an energy siting or agricultural land question, ask which clinic fits rather than assuming the general one. Clinic capacity follows the academic year, so approach early in a semester rather than mid-summer.

trackers.name: Vermont Housing & Conservation Board (VHCB)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): an independent Vermont state funding agency that uses property-transfer-tax revenue to make grants and loans to nonprofits, land trusts, towns and state agencies to acquire and permanently conserve farmland, forestland, natural areas and recreational land (it has helped conserve 431,000+ acres, 746 farms). USE IT: apply, or partner with a land trust applying, to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Town conservation commissions — Association of Vermont Conservation Commissions
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Vermont towns can establish a conservation commission with real powers — managing municipally owned land and town forests, working with the planning commission on the town plan, PURCHASING LAND for the town's conservation needs, and establishing a local land conservation fund. The association publishes a handbook chapter on how to pay for it, with worked examples: Middlesex won a $271,000 VHCB award covering about 83% of its town forest acquisition, Huntington $125,000 toward another. USE IT: this is the route in a state with no county government — form or join your town's commission, get a conservation fund established at Town Meeting, then use it as the local match VHCB requires (33%, which can include in-kind services or donated land value).

trackers.name: Vermont Attorney General
trackers.desc: Vermont’s chief legal officer. WHO TO CONTACT for consumer fraud, environmental harm, charity and nonprofit abuse, antitrust and public corruption in Vermont. You CAN: file complaints and tips the office can investigate and prosecute; most have dedicated consumer-protection, environmental and charities divisions. You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: often the most powerful and reachable ally against a local corporate or official target.

trackers.name: Vermont Business Entity Search
trackers.desc: The official registry of companies, LLCs and corporations registered in Vermont (Secretary of State / equivalent). You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. For activists: this is how you unmask the LLC behind a local development, rezoning or mass eviction — start here to find who really controls it and whom to hold accountable.

trackers.name: Virginia Land Conservation Foundation (VLCF) — DCR grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): the Virginia Land Conservation Foundation, a state-funded competitive grant program run by the Department of Conservation and Recreation (DCR), gives 50% matching grants to nonprofit land trusts, localities, public bodies and Tribes (state agencies 100%) to purchase land and conservation easements ($137M+ awarded, 167,900+ acres). USE IT: as a land trust or locality, apply to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Albemarle County ACE program — Albemarle County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Acquisition of Conservation Easements (ACE) program, established under Virginia's Open-Space Land Act in 2000, buys open-space easements from Albemarle landowners — paying up to 100% of appraised easement value on a sliding income scale, ranking applicants on 17 criteria including threat of conversion to development and adjacency to already-protected land. The companion Albemarle Conservation Easement Authority also accepts donated easements. USE IT: apply by the annual 31 October deadline; the application is non-binding and can be withdrawn any time before closing.

trackers.name: Loudoun County Conservation Easement Assistance Program — Loudoun County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to lock the land down): Loudoun County reimburses up to $25,000 of the upfront costs — survey, appraisal, legal and baseline documentation — of putting a property under conservation easement with a qualified land trust, with $150,000 available annually on a rolling, first-come basis. Over 85,000 acres in the county are already under easement. USE IT: pick a land trust (Land Trust of Virginia, Northern Virginia Conservation Trust, Old Dominion Land Conservancy, Piedmont Environmental Council or the Virginia Outdoors Foundation) and have them apply on your behalf; the cost barrier is what stops most easements.

trackers.name: Purchase of Development Rights (PDR) — Fauquier County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: established by the Board of Supervisors in 2002 under Virginia's Open-Space Land Act, Fauquier's PDR programme pays landowners a set $60,000 per development right to extinguish it permanently while the owner keeps title and keeps farming — more than 13,000 acres preserved, more than any other locality in Virginia, with a further 5,600 acres protected through donated easements since 2006. Applications are scored on parcel size, development risk, road frontage, soil quality and proximity to already-protected land. USE IT: land must be 50+ acres and zoned Rural Agricultural or Rural Conservation.

trackers.name: Conservation Easement Authority — Clarke County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created by county ordinance in 2002, the Conservation Easement Authority runs Clarke County's Easement Purchase Programme — buying perpetual easements on farm and forest land with county money matched by annual Virginia VDACS farmland preservation grants, and accepting donated easements (over 40 landowners have donated since 2002). Its Easement Value Criteria deliberately target low- and middle-income landowners who cannot use a donation's tax benefits, paying up to $25,000 per dwelling-unit right retired. USE IT: the Authority meets publicly on the second Friday of each month; landowners apply through the county's conservation planner.

It also handles black lung benefits and mine-safety retaliation claims. USE IT: where the fight is against an operator's permit history rather than a single decision, its violation analyses are the evidence base.

USE IT: partner with a West Virginia land trust to apply for a grant to buy or place a permanent easement on a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Appalachian Mountain Advocates (Appalmad)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST (environmental lawyers): a nonprofit public-interest environmental law and policy firm (est. 2001) based in Lewisburg, WV, with a record of precedent-setting Clean Water Act and permitting cases against mountaintop-removal mining, pipelines and power plants across West Virginia. USE IT: contact them to get legal counsel or representation to challenge a harmful project.

trackers.name: County Farmland Protection Boards — Voluntary Farmland Protection Act
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: West Virginia's 2000 Act lets the County Commission in any county establish a FARMLAND PROTECTION BOARD that runs a local programme and holds conservation easements, and a 2002 amendment lets each county with such a board fund it through a REAL ESTATE TRANSFER TAX — a genuinely local, self-sustaining source. Landowners apply directly to their county board to sell or donate an easement; where no funded board exists, the offer goes instead to the state Agricultural Land Protection Authority. Easements can be co-held with a land trust, which the state notes gives the landowner extra protection. USE IT: county boards partner with The Nature Conservancy, Potomac Conservancy, WV Land Trust and others, and NRCS matches county board money — but landowners cannot apply to NRCS directly.

trackers.name: County conservation districts — cooperating agency status (Teton example)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Wyoming's conservation districts are SPECIAL DISTRICT GOVERNMENT ENTITIES with locally elected boards of supervisors — and crucially they are eligible for COOPERATING AGENCY STATUS under the Council on Environmental Quality, which gives them a formal seat inside federal environmental reviews rather than a comment slot outside them. Teton Conservation District has used it in the Upper Snake River Wild and Scenic Plan and EIS, Bridger-Teton National Forest fuels management, Shoshone National Forest plan revision and the Wyoming Public Lands Initiative, and it feeds science-based recommendations into the county's Land Development Regulations. USE IT: ask your district to seek cooperating agency status on a federal project affecting your area — it is the strongest formal position a local body can hold in a NEPA process.

trackers.name: Hawaii Legacy Land Conservation Program (DLNR)

USE IT: as a land trust or agency, apply to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST (environmental lawyers): Earthjustice's Mid-Pacific office (est. 1988, Honolulu) provides free legal representation across Hawai‘i on water rights (establishing that water is a public trust), Native Hawaiian cultural rights, endangered species, land use and clean energy — winning landmark cases including a U.S. Supreme Court Clean Water Act ruling against Maui County. USE IT: contact them, or partner with a community group they represent, to challenge a project threatening Hawai‘i's land, water or wildlife.

trackers.name: Public Access, Open Space & Natural Resources Preservation Fund — Kauaʻi County
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): a dedicated county fund written into the Kauaʻi County Charter (Section 19.15) and Chapter 6 Article 14 of the county code, holding several million dollars for acquiring land, property entitlements and public access-ways — it has funded conservation easements and acquisitions including the Waipā Foundation's purchase of the Halulu Fishpond access. A nine-member citizen Commission, drawn from each district, recommends the priority list to the County Council. USE IT: submit a site through the Commission's open-space survey and public-input process, then turn out for its meetings.

trackers.name: Alaska Conservation Foundation — grants to Alaskan conservation groups
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a statewide grantmaker funding Alaska-based organisations working to protect public lands and waters — general operating support as well as project money, awarded to front-line groups including regional conservation councils, river coalitions, Native-led organisations and legal advocates. Named funds target particular fights, among them a Mining Impacts and Prevention Fund supporting groups resisting hardrock mining. Donor-advised funds let supporters direct money to a specific group or issue. USE IT honestly: awards are modest — typically $10,000–30,000 for operating support, and its small Discovery Grants for grassroots groups ran $500–2,000 and were suspended pending redesign, so check what is open before planning around it.

trackers.name: Soil & Water Conservation Districts — Alaska DNR / Natural Resource Conservation and Development Board
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Alaska has twelve soil and water conservation districts under a law passed in 1947, in territorial days, each run by a board of five supervisors ELECTED from their membership in annual elections run by the state board. Crucially the twelfth district covers ALL AREAS OF THE STATE NOT SERVED BY A LOCAL DISTRICT, and the state Natural Resource Conservation and Development Board oversees those unserved portions — so there is a conservation body with jurisdiction even in the unorganised borough, where there is no municipal government at all. USE IT: in a state where most land is federal, state or Native corporation held and local government is patchy, the district is often the only elected local body dealing with land and water.

trackers.name: BC First Nations Justice Council (BCFNJC)
trackers.desc: Indigenous-led council advancing First Nations self-determination over justice in British Columbia and implementing the BC First Nations Justice Strategy. Through a province-wide network of Indigenous Justice Centres (and a virtual centre), it provides free, culturally grounded legal advice and representation to Indigenous people in criminal-defence and child-protection matters — available regardless of legal-aid eligibility — along with Gladue reports, diversion and healing plans, and wraparound supports (housing, mental-health and addictions, employment) that address the causes of criminalisation. Its work responds to the drastic over-representation of Indigenous people in the justice system and to the Truth and Reconciliation and MMIWG Calls to Action.

trackers.name: Alliance of Canadian Land Trusts (ACLT)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the national body representing roughly 150 local and regional Canadian land trusts — charities that conserve private land through donation, acquisition and conservation agreements (easements and covenants) held in perpetuity. USE IT: to find the land trust covering your area, and to understand which instrument (sale, donation or easement) fits the parcel you are trying to save.

trackers.name: East Coast Environmental Law (ECELAW) — Atlantic Canada
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: provides public-interest environmental law services throughout Atlantic Canada, running an inquiry line, legal and policy research and workshops on environmental assessment, water, mining, energy, protected places and species at risk. WHO IT SUITS: anyone in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, PEI or Newfoundland and Labrador — the regional first call, where Ecojustice and CELA have less reach.

trackers.name: Indigenous Leadership Initiative — Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: works at Nation, territorial, provincial and federal level to secure recognition and long-term funding for IPCAs — lands and waters where Indigenous governments hold the primary role in protecting ecosystems through their own laws, governance and knowledge systems. IPCAs are central to Canada's commitment to protect 30% of lands and waters by 2030. USE IT: for the funding and recognition side of standing up an IPCA, and for the national argument that Indigenous-led conservation delivers better ecological outcomes.

trackers.name: CPAWS BC — Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas explainer
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a plain guide to what an IPCA is and, critically, what legal footing it stands on. THE KEY POINT: no federal or provincial statute currently recognises IPCAs. Indigenous Peoples have the right to self-determination and CAN establish an IPCA in their territories WITHOUT recognition from non-Indigenous governments — the Tsilhqot'in National Government declared Dasiqox Tribal Park in 2014 on that basis, following the Supreme Court of Canada's recognition of their Aboriginal title. USE IT: recognition from BC or Canada is not required to declare, but where it is given it helps ensure management plans are respected and prohibited activities such as mining, logging or bottom-trawling are actually limited. Know which of the two you are asking for.

trackers.name: Environmental Damages Fund (Canada) — fines redirected to the affected area
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a federal fund holding money from FINES, PENALTIES, COURT ORDERS AND VOLUNTARY PAYMENTS FOR ENVIRONMENTAL VIOLATIONS, which is then spent on projects benefiting the natural environment — USUALLY IN THE AREA WHERE THE VIOLATION OCCURRED. Over $255 million across 600+ projects since 1995. Four categories: restoration, environmental quality improvement, research and development, and education and awareness. WHO IT SUITS: communities living with the consequences of a prosecuted polluter — the geographic tie is the point. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is the polluter's own money paying for the remedy on the ground they damaged, so if there has been a conviction or settlement near you, ask where that money went. Generally one to two calls for applications a year; requirements vary by call, so read the current Applicant Guide rather than assuming.

trackers.name: Environment and Climate Change Canada — environmental funding programs
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the federal department's index of its grants and contributions programs, covering species-at-risk recovery, freshwater quality, habitat protection, ecologically sensitive land, and community action. Indigenous communities, landowners, environmental groups, schools, other levels of government and businesses are all eligible applicants across the suite. WHO IT SUITS: start here rather than at a single programme page — the right fit is often not the obvious one. HOW IT DIFFERS: it also links the EcoAction Community Funding Program, which has run since 1995 for community-based non-profits and typically requires that at least half your project value come from non-federal sources, so line up matching support first.

trackers.name: ATRIS — Aboriginal and Treaty Rights Information System
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a web-based geographic information system giving access to the documents and maps used to work out who must be consulted about activity on a given piece of land — data co-developed with Indigenous communities, in one interactive platform. USE IT: to establish, before anything else, which Indigenous groups hold or assert rights over the site in question, and therefore who the Crown was obliged to consult. If a project has been approved and a rights-holding group on ATRIS was never properly consulted, that is the gap a challenge is built on. Training is available and a government account can be requested.

trackers.name: Réseau de milieux naturels protégés (RMN) — Québec conservation network
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Québec network of conservation organisations — national, regional and local groups, plus municipalities and MRCs — supporting voluntary conservation of natural areas on PRIVATE land across the province. Members protect somewhere between 66,000 and 80,000 hectares, and RMN maintains the Répertoire des sites de conservation volontaire du Québec, which has passed 1,500 registered protected sites covering roughly 75,000 hectares. USE IT: the site carries a search tool to find a conservation organisation near you, which is the fastest route in — you do not need to know which group covers your area.
