trackers.name: Pracownia na rzecz Wszystkich Istot (Workshop for All Beings)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Polish association that has spent since 1990 forcing its way into administrative proceedings and winning — a civil suit against Lasy Państwowe over the Białowieża Forest logging, brought under art. 323 of the environmental protection act, produced an interim order banning felling in the most valuable fragments; the Gliwice administrative court confirmed its right to be a party in the environmental proceeding for a Pilsko chairlift; the Kraków court fined a building inspectorate for a 54-month delay over an illegally expanded resort. Publishes 'Paragrafy dla przyrody', a watchers' handbook on joining a proceeding as a party and appealing the decision. WHO IT SUITS: a group facing a road, ski lift, resort or logging plan that needs standing first and arguments second.

trackers.name: Klub Przyrodników — wykup gruntów i tworzenie rezerwatów
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: buys ecologically valuable ground and then gets the state to protect it — land it purchased was, on the Klub's own application, given nature-reserve status, which is the whole sequence a community needs and the reason this is more than a land trust. It has been buying since close to its founding: xerothermic grassland at Owczary, land in the Obra valleys, then peatlands and grasslands scattered across the country from the Odra to the Rospuda, passing 150 hectares owned or co-owned, latterly with WWF Polska under a privately-protected-areas programme. USE IT: two doors. If a parcel is for sale, this is the buyer of last resort for peatland, fen and dry grassland in particular. And its current programme exists precisely to bring local organisations, activists and enthusiasts into the creation of NEW nature reserves, working from a database of sites that qualify for reserve protection — so if your site is good enough, the route is to get it onto that list rather than to fight the development on its own terms.

trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Tirana organisation that brought the first environmental lawsuit ever heard in Albania's Administrative Court — and won it twice. In December 2016 it went to court against the Poçem hydropower plant on the Vjosa together with RiverWatch, EuroNatur and 38 affected residents as co-plaintiffs, arguing the environmental impact assessment was inadequate and the affected community had not been consulted, in breach of Albanian law and international conventions. The court struck the project down in 2017 and recognised the residents' standing; the Administrative Court of Appeal confirmed the annulment in 2024. Its own account calls that the case that opened the door for every environmental claim brought since. WHO IT SUITS: communities facing hydropower, and anyone whose project's paperwork is thin — the winning grounds were procedural. Worth copying its other habit too: when the government announced Vjosa protection in 2020, EcoAlbania read the actual public documents and found the designation was a protected landscape, not a national park. Always check which status was really granted.

trackers.desc: The association of more than fifty environmental organisations across Moldova, including Transnistria, and Ukraine, built around the transboundary Dniester basin and registered under Moldovan law. WHO TO ENLIST: use it as the switchboard — if there is a local group anywhere in the basin, it is probably a member, and reaching the network is faster than finding one cold. You CAN: draw on its compilation of Moldovan environmental legislation, published in volumes on its own site, and on its scientific capacity, which is unusual for an NGO here — it developed a methodology for assessing hydropower impacts on river ecosystems and has surveyed riverbank erosion. It sits on the Dniester river commission it helped create, so it has a seat where basin decisions are taken. For activists: it has form on access to information, having pursued a case internationally under the Aarhus Convention after a state service demanded a very large fee for environmental data — worth citing if you are quoted a price for records.

It gives free legal assistance on environmental matters and has supported court actions on access to information, public participation and the protection of natural resources — reportedly more than fifty consultations across 2024-2025 — and it does not wait to be visited: in 2024 its teams reached 182 of the 187 localities in its target districts to offer free legal help on the spot. WHO IT SUITS: rural communities above all, and local councils, since it also drafts local environmental regulations covering grazing, mowing, recording of offences and transparency in decision-making. Two things that improve your odds: it runs the environmental-cases programme for judges and prosecutors at the National Institute of Justice, so the bench has been trained on exactly these questions, and it moderates a platform of over 230 environmental organisations and experts if the expertise you need is not in-house.

trackers.name: Natural Justice: Lawyers for Communities and the Environment
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an African public-interest law organisation — lawyers and paralegals working with communities facing mining, oil and gas, logging and large infrastructure, combining legal empowerment, community protocols, policy work and litigation. Hubs in Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, staff in Madagascar, Botswana and Guinea, and country programmes in Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal and South Africa. It also runs the Environmental Lawyers Collective for Africa and an EIA Process Tracker. WHO IT SUITS: an Indigenous or rural community whose land, water or customary rights are threatened by an extractive or infrastructure project. trackers.name: African Environmental Defenders Fund (emergency grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the African Environmental Defenders Fund — an emergency grant fund run by Natural Justice with the International Land Coalition Africa, ICCA Consortium, PACJA, Oxfam Novib, FEMNET and others, giving up to US$5,000 to land and environmental defenders anywhere in Africa who are under threat because of their activism. It can cover the cost of legal representation where a defender is arrested, summoned or prosecuted, plus relocation and other short-term transitional costs. WHO IT SUITS: an individual frontline defender who is a citizen or legal resident of an African country, facing an imminent threat, and not already supported by another body — it is not project or core funding, and routine office and administrative costs are excluded. HOW IT DIFFERS: applications are rolling, by email or helpline, not to a grant round. Natural Justice's own site names Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa and Botswana as its country programmes, which is where this entry is placed; the fund's stated eligibility is any African country, so apply from elsewhere on the continent too.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)

WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

Several of the agreement types are formally declared as protected areas under the Protected Areas Act 57 of 2003, which gives long-term legal security to the site, and since 2016 a landowner declaring a Nature Reserve or National Park can deduct 4% of the land value from taxable income each year for 25 years (per UNDP South Africa). USE IT: to find out which agreement type gives real statutory protection rather than a non-binding partnership, before approaching your provincial authority about land you are trying to keep out of development.

It also develops tourism, ethical hunting and natural-resource ventures so protected land can pay for itself. USE IT: when you have land worth protecting but need someone who has done the declaration paperwork before.

Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly.

trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Tanzania's first public-interest environmental law organisation, founded in 1994 — legal and social-policy research, advocacy and selected public-interest litigation on mining and extractives, land, water, forests and wildlife. It supported Rufiji Delta residents in the constitutional petition that helped stop a 10,000-hectare prawn farm, and has acted for households facing demolition on utility way-leaves. A member of ELAW and of Friends of the Earth International. WHO IT SUITS: a Tanzanian community or residents' association fighting an extractive project, an eviction or a major land-use decision — LEAT litigates selectively, so expect a case-selection conversation rather than open legal aid.

trackers.name: Legal and Human Rights Centre (LHRC)
trackers.desc: Tanzania's largest human-rights NGO, running free legal-aid centres alongside public-interest litigation. WHO TO ENLIST: legal aid through the Kinondoni (Dar es Salaam), Arusha and Dodoma offices and the Haki Kiganjani mobile legal-aid service. You CAN: get free advice and representation, and draw on LHRC's annual human-rights reporting; it was a co-applicant in the 2026 East African Court of Justice judgment that struck down Tanzanian restrictions on who may bring public-interest litigation. For activists: the practical route to a lawyer when a land or environment dispute becomes a rights case.

It petitions the High Court against coastal privatisation, oil-shale projects and ministerial inaction; its legal action has forced the Ministry of Environmental Protection to publish new conditions on businesses, won a ruling that Dead Sea Works must pay for the water it uses, and helped save the Bat Yam cliff. WHO IT SUITS: residents and local environmental groups facing a planning decision or a polluting facility. It is membership-based and picks strategic cases, and its planning team is often more use early than its litigators are late.

WHO TO ENLIST: the office in your own country. Its Good Water Neighbors programme works with communities on either side of a shared water problem, pairing them across the border rather than treating each in isolation. You CAN get community-level organising support and technical and advocacy weight on water, sewage and Jordan Valley development. You CAN'T get a litigator — EcoPeace works by cross-border cooperation, research and advocacy, not by suing proponents, so a community that needs a permit or an approval challenged in court should look elsewhere. For activists: in Jordan and Palestine this was the only substantial environmental organisation with an office and a named national director that could be verified on its own domain.

trackers.name: RTI Portal (India)
trackers.desc: You CAN get: any record, file noting, order, inspection report or status report held by a public authority, under the Right to Information Act 2005, on payment of a ₹10 fee — waived for BPL applicants. Any Indian citizen may ask; you do not have to say why. The Public Information Officer must ordinarily answer within 30 days. Know which site does what: rti.gov.in is the GATEWAY — use it to identify the right PIO and First Appellate Authority and to read proactive disclosures. Filing happens at rtionline.gov.in. You CAN'T get: state records through that filing portal. It covers CENTRAL ministries, departments and public authorities only, and an application wrongly filed there against a state body — including the Government of NCT of Delhi, which runs its own portal — is returned WITHOUT REFUND. State authorities need the relevant state portal or a postal application. An online first appeal can only follow an online application. For activists: this is how you get an environmental clearance file, a public-hearing record or project correspondence from MoEFCC or a central regulator — but a State Pollution Control Board is a state body, so check the tier before paying. If the PIO misses the 30 days or answers badly, appeal to the First Appellate Authority within 30 days, then to the Central Information Commission within 90; the Commission can order disclosure and fine the officer.

You CAN'T get: reliable machine access — the interfaces change and dataset endpoints have been dormant. For activists: the public-hearing stage is the statutory intervention point, EAC minutes reveal exactly which objections registered, and clearances can be appealed to the National Green Tribunal within its strict deadlines.

Awarded the Right Livelihood Award in 2021. WHO IT SUITS: a community or CSO challenging a clearance, a public hearing or an EIA anywhere in India — support is free to the communities it takes on, but it works case by case, not on demand.

trackers.desc: You CAN get: records held by the Philippine EXECUTIVE branch — national departments, bureaus, government-owned and -controlled corporations, state universities and colleges and local water districts — filed online through the portal and tracked there, with agencies required to answer within 15 working days (extendable, with notice, where the request is voluminous or needs consultation). If the agency does not hold the record but another executive agency does, a 2021 memorandum circular requires it to refer your request on rather than deny it. You CAN'T get: anything from Congress or the courts — there is no enabling statute covering all branches, so the order reaches the executive only. Critically for a local fight, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS ARE MERELY ENCOURAGED to follow it, not bound, so a barangay, municipal or provincial record may need a local FOI ordinance instead. Records are also withheld under national-security, privacy and banking confidentiality exceptions. For activists: this is the route to an EIA, a permit file, a procurement record or project correspondence held by DENR, DPWH or a GOCC. Use it early — a denial can be appealed to the agency head within 15 calendar days, then to the Office of the President or by petition for mandamus, and that clock is slower than most project timetables.

trackers.name: National Secretary of Social Action (NASSA)
trackers.desc: The National Secretary of Social Action was established in 1966 as a humanitarian and advocacy arm of the Catholic Bishops’ Conferences of the Philippines (CBCP). The aim of NASSA is to address poverty alleviation, sustainable agriculture, empowerment of women and children, and ecological protection.

trackers.name: Environmental Legal Assistance Center (ELAC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Philippine environmental law NGO founded in 1990 — lawyers, paralegals, researchers and community organisers, backed by volunteer lawyers and scientists, working from offices in Palawan, Cebu, Bohol and Leyte. It provides free legal representation in environmental court cases against deforestation, mining and other destructive projects and coastal degradation, trains community paralegals and forest, wildlife and fish wardens, and litigates on forest, coastal and land-tenure disputes. WHO IT SUITS: a community or indigenous group in its coverage areas, especially Palawan, facing an extractive or large development project — it is a small office under political and corporate pressure, so cases are chosen, not queued.

trackers.name: The Samdhana Institute — grants programme
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a Southeast Asian grantmaker giving micro to medium-sized grants, plus urgent-action grants, directly to Indigenous peoples and local communities, community-based and civil-society organisations, informal groups and individual activists — for land and territorial rights, natural-resource governance, and community-led climate and livelihood work. Its own site names offices only in Bogor, Indonesia and in Cagayan de Oro and Quezon City, Philippines, which is where this entry is placed; it describes its remit as Southeast Asia generally, so groups elsewhere in the region should still ask. WHO IT SUITS: groups that cannot get money from conventional donors — Samdhana states its grantmaking principle as funding the "un-fundable", and an unregistered informal group is not disqualified. HOW IT DIFFERS: it supplies environmental conflict mediation and technical support alongside the grant rather than only writing cheques.

trackers.name: Foundation for the Philippine Environment (FPE)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: an endowment-based Philippine grantmaker for biodiversity conservation and sustainable development, with small grants of up to PHP 500,000 and a youth stream of up to PHP 100,000. Its grant framework (CARES) explicitly includes Environmental Defense and advocacy alongside research, constituency building and site work. WHO IT SUITS: civil-society organisations, people's organisations, Indigenous peoples' organisations and academic institutions — not individuals. Much of the money is site-focused: FPE identifies a priority conservation site and invites organisations based there to apply, so check whether your area is currently one before writing anything. HOW IT DIFFERS: FPE has also served as implementing partner for the GEF Small Grants Programme in the Philippines, so one relationship can reach more than one pot.

trackers.name: Forest Foundation Philippines
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a Philippine grantmaker for forest protection, running microgrants for community-led work to reduce deforestation and forest degradation, conserve high-conservation-value forest and improve ecosystem connectivity — concentrated in priority landscapes including the Mindoro and Eastern Mindanao Biodiversity Corridors. WHO IT SUITS: duly registered individuals, organisations and firms — NGOs, social enterprises, professionals and consultancy groups — working on forest protection and conservation in the Philippines. HOW IT DIFFERS: programmes open and close, and the Foundation openly lists past programmes that are no longer accepting proposals, so write to the proposals address and confirm what is live before preparing a submission.

trackers.name: Friends of the Earth Asia Pacific
trackers.desc: The Asia Pacific regional structure of Friends of the Earth International, formed in 2008, whose member groups work on community-based struggles against destructive projects, particularly mining and other extractive industries, alongside Indigenous peoples, peasant farmers, fisherfolk and trade unions. WHO TO ENLIST: the national member group nearest the project. In this region Friends of the Earth International's own directory names groups in Bangladesh (BELA, the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers' Association), India, Indonesia (WALHI), Japan, Malaysia (Sahabat Alam Malaysia), Nepal, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines (the Legal Rights and Natural Resources Center), South Korea and Sri Lanka. You CAN: reach an organisation that already works community-side in your own country, and draw regional weight onto a local fight. For activists: in several of these countries the Friends of the Earth affiliate is the most experienced community-side environmental body there is.

trackers.name: Legal Rights and Natural Resources Center — Kasama sa Kalikasan (LRC-KsK)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Philippine public-interest law centre founded in 1987 by four young lawyers, one of them now a Supreme Court Justice, working for recognition and protection of the rights of Indigenous peoples and upland rural poor communities to land and natural resources. It runs three programmes — research and policy development, direct legal services, and advocacy and campaigns support — and was instrumental in drafting the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997 and defending its constitutionality, the statute under which ancestral domain is recognised in the Philippines. It campaigned to repeal the Mining Act of 1995 and still petitions against it. For partner communities it runs paralegal training and field briefings, supplies documentary research, and files cases in court. WHO IT SUITS: an Indigenous or upland community facing mining, logging or encroachment. The model is supporting a community's own campaign rather than taking a client, so it suits a group that is already organised, and it works through partners rather than open intake.

For activists: check a project's ECC status and its EIA documents.

trackers.name: EcoLur Informational NGO
trackers.desc: Armenia's environmental information organisation, built around a repeatable model rather than a single campaign: it runs named S.O.S. campaigns site by site — Amulsar, Teghout, Akhtala, Qajaran, Kapan, Agarak, Sotq, Ararat and others — acting as the information coordinator for residents living beside a mine or a polluter. WHO TO ENLIST when what you need is the evidence and the timetable rather than a lawyer. You CAN: use its independent-experts library, which collects geologists' and geomorphologists' opinions, social-impact surveys of affected communities and reports on new circumstances in an ESIA — the material that turns an objection into an argument. It also publishes notices of scheduled public hearings on exploration and mining permits and reports the council votes on them, which is the single hardest thing for a rural community to learn in time. For activists: it works with CEE Bankwatch and other Armenian groups on complaints to development-bank accountability mechanisms, so it is a route to the financing side as well as the permit.

trackers.name: FPWC — Caucasus Wildlife Refuge (Foundation for the Preservation of Wildlife and Cultural Assets)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: gives a community an alternative buyer for its own land. FPWC built the Caucasus Wildlife Refuge from 2011 by taking on land from more than a dozen communities across Ararat and Vayots Dzor — mostly by lease, with the payments going back to the villages for their own improvements — and it now covers around 30,000 hectares buffering the Khosrov Forest State Reserve, the first privately protected area in the South Caucasus. It employs local rangers and funds part of the work through ecotourism rather than donations alone. USE IT: this is the counterparty when someone else wants your community's land. Gnishik gave its land to the refuge under pressure to lease it as a hunting ground instead; another community turned down a company's cash offer and ceded the land for conservation. If a concession, a hunting lease or a mine is being dangled at your council, FPWC is the competing offer that keeps the ground intact and still pays. Note it is lease-based, so the community keeps title.

trackers.name: EPBC Act Public Portal — federal referrals
trackers.desc: Australia's public list of every project referred for federal environmental approval under the EPBC Act (administered by the new National EPA from mid-2026), with each referral's documents and a public comment window. You CAN get: every proposed action touching nationally protected matters — the proponent, location, documents, decisions, and 10 business days to comment on whether it's a 'controlled action'. You CAN'T get: projects with only state-level impacts — those sit with state EPAs. For activists: the comment window opens the moment a referral is published, so watching this portal for your region is how campaigns get ahead of a mine or development while the federal decision is still open.

trackers.desc: Accountability source (FOI request platform); Right To Know — civic Freedom-of-Information request platform (Alaveteli/mySociety network) — lets citizens file public-records requests and publishes the requests and the authorities’ responses in a public archive.

trackers.name: Bush Heritage Australia — buying land for conservation
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a national not-for-profit that BUYS bushland outright to protect it permanently — 44 reserves covering over 1.4 million hectares, bought, gifted or bequeathed, each locked down with a conservation covenant that binds every future owner in perpetuity (no subdivision, no clearing, no building). USE IT: if land you are trying to save has outstanding conservation value, pitch it to them as an acquisition target, or partner with them on a purchase.

trackers.name: Australian Government (DCCEEW) — conservation organisations directory
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the federal environment department's own list of the conservation organisations that buy and manage land for the National Reserve System — Bush Heritage, Australian Wildlife Conservancy, Tasmanian Land Conservancy, Trust for Nature and others. USE IT: the official starting point for finding which body might acquire or covenant the land you are defending.

trackers.name: Environmental Defenders Office (EDO) — public-interest environmental law
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the largest environmental legal centre in the Australia-Pacific and an accredited Community Legal Centre — runs litigation for community groups defending their area from destructive development, and gives free expert legal advice. Its lawyers have fought some of Australia's biggest environmental battles, from the Adani mine to drilling in the Great Australian Bight. WHO IT SUITS: community groups, farmers, Traditional Owners and residents anywhere in Australia or the Pacific — never proponents. If you are not yet at the litigation stage, their online Legal Help Gateway carries free fact sheets.

trackers.name: Australian Wildlife Conservancy (AWC)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: acquires land and partners with other landholders to establish sanctuaries for threatened wildlife — the largest private owner and manager of land for conservation in Australia, covering 31 sanctuaries and partnership sites across more than 6.5 million hectares. USE IT: pitch a threatened parcel with high wildlife value as an acquisition or partnership target.

trackers.name: National Native Title Tribunal — future acts and Indigenous land use agreements
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Tribunal mediates and arbitrates the FUTURE ACT process — the statutory procedure triggered when a government proposes to grant a mining tenement, exploration licence or other interest over land where native title exists or is claimed. Native title parties get procedural rights: notification, a right to be consulted, and in defined cases a right to negotiate, with s. 31 agreements recorded. WHO IT SUITS: this is a right to be AT THE TABLE and to negotiate, not a general veto — be precise about which it is in a given case. The Tribunal also publishes dedicated guidance for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, mining and exploration, cultural heritage and land acquisitions.

trackers.name: GrantConnect via DCCEEW — how to catch every Commonwealth environment grant
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: individual Australian environment grant rounds open and close constantly — the Environment Restoration Fund ran 2019-2023, the Communities Environment Program closed in 2019 — so chasing a named programme is the wrong strategy. ALL Australian Government grant opportunities are published on GRANTCONNECT, the Commonwealth's grants information system, where you can register free and set a self-defined notification profile covering both live and FORECAST opportunities. WHO IT SUITS: any Australian community or environment group. HOW IT DIFFERS: the forecast feed is the real advantage — it tells you a round is coming before it opens, which is the only way to have a proposal ready in time. Funding continues through the Natural Heritage Trust, a $1.1 billion commitment running to the end of 2027-28.

trackers.name: National Landcare Program — Environment Small Grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: grants of $5,000 to $50,000 for projects improving the local environment through natural resource management, COVERING UP TO 100% OF PROJECT COSTS — no matching contribution required, which is unusual and makes this reachable for groups with no reserves. Eligible activities include weed treatment, pest and disease management, fencing, erosion management, revegetation, access management, community education, Indigenous land and sea country planning, and recording Indigenous ecological knowledge. WHO IT SUITS: community and environment groups. HOW IT DIFFERS: the 100% cost coverage and the explicit inclusion of Indigenous knowledge and country planning set it apart from co-funded programmes. Check the current guidelines — rounds and amounts change.

trackers.name: Landcare Australia — grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a national body that works with governments, corporate partners, philanthropic organisations and donors to build grants programmes for hands-on environmental projects — habitat restoration, sustainable land management, biodiversity. WHO IT SUITS: landcare and community groups doing on-ground work rather than campaign or legal work. HOW IT DIFFERS: rounds are intermittent and the site states plainly when nothing is open, so subscribe to the newsletter rather than checking hopefully; the money is raised from partners, so timing follows their cycles, not a government calendar.

trackers.name: DCCEEW — revolving funds by state and territory
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the federal environment department's own directory of the state-based revolving funds — the bodies that buy conservation land, covenant it and sell it on so the capital can be reused. Lists the responsible organisation and contact details for New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania and Victoria. USE IT: the fastest way to find the acquiring body for your state, and the route to South Australia's Nature Foundation, which is named here. ONE CAUTION: the directory carries at least one transposed web address for a listed fund, so use the phone numbers and email addresses to confirm, or search the organisation's name directly, rather than typing a URL straight off the page.

trackers.name: NSW Biodiversity Conservation Trust — private land conservation
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a statutory body under the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016 that negotiates in-perpetuity conservation agreements with private landholders AND PAYS THEM to manage the land for conservation. It holds 2,644 agreements over 2.17 million hectares, with 616,494 hectares protected forever; NSW has invested more than $356 million, and the median annual payment is about $102.50 per hectare. USE IT: more than 80% OF NSW LAND IS PRIVATELY MANAGED, so a private agreement often reaches ground that national-park designation never will. Payment eligibility is geographic — the Biodiversity Conservation Investment Strategy ranks NSW into five priority investment areas, and land in a high-priority area attracts funding support. BE AWARE OF THE CONFLICT: the same Trust also runs a biodiversity OFFSETTING service that compensates for biodiversity lost to development elsewhere, so it sits on both sides of the development ledger. That does not make an agreement any less permanent, but know it before you treat the BCT as an ally against a specific project.

trackers.name: NSW BCT — pathways to a private land conservation agreement (which type to ask for)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: compares the three agreement types, which is the decision that matters. CONSERVATION AGREEMENTS are permanent and attract either annual payments under the Conservation Management Program or grants under the Conservation Partners Program. WILDLIFE REFUGE AGREEMENTS are the entry-level option for a landholder who wants to protect biodiversity but is NOT ready to commit permanently. BIODIVERSITY STEWARDSHIP AGREEMENTS are permanent and let the landholder generate and sell biodiversity credits under the Offsets Scheme. USE IT: if a sympathetic owner is hesitating, the wildlife refuge route is the low-commitment way in — get the land into the system now and the permanent agreement can follow.

trackers.name: Trust for Nature (Victoria) — permanent protection on private land
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Victoria's statutory private-land conservation body — places permanent conservation covenants on private property and works on strategic conservation planning and on-ground protection. USE IT: if the parcel under threat is private Victorian land, a covenant is the instrument that protects it without a sale.

trackers.name: Environmental Justice Australia — legal support (Victoria)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Victoria's public-interest environmental law organisation (formerly EDO Victoria), acting for communities on environmental and planning matters. WHO IT SUITS: Victorian residents and community groups — outside Victoria, go to EDO instead. Their legal-support page also routes you to the other bodies that take these cases if they cannot act for you themselves.

trackers.name: Queensland Trust for Nature — the Revolving Fund
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: runs a REVOLVING FUND — it buys ecologically significant land, restores it, locks it down with a conservation covenant as a legally binding nature refuge, then RESELLS it on the private market and recycles the capital into the next purchase. Operating since 2004, over 100,000 hectares protected. USE IT: two reasons this matters in Queensland. First, about 85% of the state is privately owned or managed, so public reservation reaches very little of it. Second, the economics are extraordinary — because the money revolves, QTFN reports preserving roughly 104,000 hectares at an effective cost of about $1.32 per hectare, against single National Park acquisitions in Queensland that generally exceed $28 per hectare. If you are arguing for public money to save a Queensland site, that comparison is your strongest card. They also list properties currently for sale, so a sympathetic buyer can acquire land that is already covenanted.

trackers.name: National Trust WA — Conservation Covenant and Stewardship Program
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a statutory authority running WA's longest-established private-land covenanting scheme — begun in 1999, now 189 covenants protecting more than 18,000 hectares of bushland, registered over 340 land titles. Covenants bind the land, not just the current owner. USE IT: for WA bushland on private title, this is the route with the most experience behind it, and stewardship support continues after signing rather than ending at registration. BE AWARE WA HAS FIVE OVERLAPPING COVENANT PROGRAMMES delivered by three different bodies — this one, DBCA's Nature Conservation Covenant Program, Land for Wildlife, the Biodiversity Conservation Covenant Program and DPIRD's Soil Conservation Covenant Program. They are not interchangeable, and the same parcel can end up under more than one. Ask which fits before committing.

trackers.name: DBCA — Nature Conservation Covenant Program (Western Australia)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the WA Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions negotiates voluntary, legally binding covenants registered ON THE LAND TITLE, restricting activities that would threaten the land's conservation values. Each one is INDIVIDUALLY NEGOTIATED between the department and the landowner, so terms can reflect how the owner actually uses the land. USE IT: the reason to pick the departmental route over a trust is stated on the page — the department provides ongoing management advice, advocacy, AND ENFORCEMENT AS A LAST RESORT. If you expect the covenant to be tested by a future owner or a neighbouring development, a covenant the State will enforce is the stronger instrument. Contact the Species and Communities branch direct.

trackers.name: Nature Foundation — Bushbank Revolving Fund (South Australia)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: South Australia's revolving fund — it BUYS properties with conservation value, rejuvenates them, then sells them to new owners who are OBLIGED TO MAINTAIN THEM UNDER CONSERVATION STATUS, recycling the proceeds into the next purchase. Run by Nature Foundation (est. 1981), South Australia's largest private land conservancy, which also owns and manages seven nature reserves totalling over 500,000 hectares. USE IT: two routes in. Pitch a threatened South Australian property as an acquisition target; or, if someone in your network is looking to buy rural land, buying THROUGH the fund puts a conservation obligation on the title permanently and frees the Foundation's capital to save the next site. Donated land works the same way — the donor knows it stays protected and the proceeds buy more.

trackers.name: Tasmanian Land Conservancy — buying land for protection
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: conserves and protects Tasmania's natural environment by PURCHASING and managing land, holding it as private reserve. Has deductible-gift-recipient status, so donations toward an acquisition are tax-deductible. USE IT: to propose a threatened Tasmanian parcel for purchase, or to channel fundraising into an actual buy.

trackers.name: Conservation Council ACT Region
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the peak environment body for the ACT, advocating and campaigning on local environmental issues and acting as the umbrella for Canberra's environment groups — ParkCare and similar community groups sit under it, and it runs the annual ACT Environment Awards. WHO IT SUITS: anyone facing development in the ACT. In a jurisdiction this small the peak body is close to the ground, engaging directly on specific sites and on ACT Government budget and policy decisions, so it is a realistic first call rather than a national office to petition.

trackers.name: Environment Centre NT (ECNT)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the peak community-sector environment organisation in the Northern Territory, working since 1983 on land clearing, mining rehabilitation, biodiversity and stronger environmental legislation. TWO THINGS THAT MAKE IT USABLE. First, it is LEGALLY REPRESENTED — Environmental Justice Australia acts for ECNT, so its objections arrive as legal submissions rather than letters. Second, NT Environment Protection Authority guidance on stakeholder engagement treats ECNT as a body proponents SHOULD consult on referrals, which means a proponent that has not contacted them has a visible gap in its process. USE IT: for NT land clearing and mining referrals, get ECNT engaged early enough to be inside the assessment process, not commenting after it.

trackers.name: Office of the Privacy Commissioner
trackers.desc: Office of the Privacy Commissioner — New Zealand’s independent data-protection / information commissioner, overseeing how public bodies handle personal data and enforcing access and privacy rights. — Holds to account: officials handling public information & personal data — find rulings, guidance and complaint channels.

trackers.desc: New Zealand Legal Information Institute: free judgments and legislation. · Find here: free New Zealand legislation and court and tribunal decisions (NZLII).

trackers.desc: Independent officer handling complaints under New Zealand's Official Information Act. · Find here: New Zealand's Ombudsman — complaints and Official Information Act reviews.

trackers.desc: Māori Land Court — tribunal (New Zealand).

trackers.name: FYI — FOI requests (NZL)
trackers.desc: Accountability source (FOI request platform); FYI — civic Freedom-of-Information request platform (Alaveteli/mySociety network) — lets citizens file public-records requests and publishes the requests and the authorities’ responses in a public archive.

trackers.name: QEII National Trust (Ngā Kairauhī Papa) — open space covenants
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: an independent STATUTORY body (QEII National Trust Act 1977) that protects private land forever by registering an open space covenant — the landowner keeps and manages the land, and the protection binds every future owner even after sale. Over 5,000 covenants protect more than 180,000 ha. Roughly 70% of New Zealand is privately owned, so this is the main instrument for protecting lowland habitat. USE IT: if a sympathetic owner holds the threatened land, a covenant locks it down without anyone having to buy it. There are 30 QEII regions each with a local rep.

trackers.name: Environmental Defence Society (EDS)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a not-for-profit founded in 1971 by law students and scientists, combining law, science and planning, with a long record of litigating environmentally significant cases under the Resource Management Act — and it publishes its case studies. Its landmark win, EDS v New Zealand King Salmon [2014] NZSC 38, established that the New Zealand Coastal Policy Statement sets FIRM ENVIRONMENTAL BOTTOM LINES that must be given effect to, displacing the earlier 'overall broad judgment' approach under which environmental harm could simply be balanced away against economic benefit. WHO IT SUITS: cases with precedent value, especially coastal and landscape matters — if a decision-maker is balancing away an outstanding natural landscape, King Salmon is the authority to cite.

trackers.name: Forest & Bird (Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: New Zealand's largest independent conservation organisation, which litigates — jointly with EDS it filed High Court judicial review proceedings challenging 99 of the Minister of Conservation's decisions on West Coast stewardship land, covering roughly 365,345 of the 644,000 hectares reviewed, on the ground that the Minister issued bare 'proceed / do not proceed' decisions with no reasons. WHO IT SUITS: public conservation land and species matters. USEFUL TO KNOW: about 30% of public conservation land is held as STEWARDSHIP land — over 2.7 million hectares, 9% of New Zealand's land area — a weaker protective category than national park, and the category most exposed to reclassification and disposal.

trackers.name: Ngā Whenua Rāhui Fund — protection of indigenous biodiversity on Māori land
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a contestable Ministerial fund (established 1991, administered by the Department of Conservation) that funds voluntary protection of indigenous biodiversity on Māori-owned land while honouring the rights guaranteed under Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Covers remnant forest, waterways and riparian margins, wetlands, tussock, coastal dunes and saltmarsh on Māori freehold, customary land, Māori reservation, or General land owned by Māori. WHO IT SUITS: Māori landowners — the fund's design point is that owners KEEP full ownership and management, and retain their tikanga and tino rangatiratanga; a kawenata is a 25-year renewable agreement tailored to the whenua, not a transfer. HOW IT DIFFERS: three statutory instruments are available and which one applies depends on the land's management structure — Ngā Whenua Rāhui Kawenata (s77A Reserves Act 1977 or s27A Conservation Act 1987) for long-term protection of Māori freehold land, and an Agreement for the Management of Land (s29 Conservation Act 1987) for smaller blocks. Funding also covers pest and weed control and landowner capability.

trackers.name: Waitangi Tribunal — claims process
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a standing commission of inquiry under the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 that hears claims that the Crown has breached the Treaty through an Act, regulation, policy, practice, act or omission, and that Māori suffered prejudice as a result. ANY MĀORI MAY SUBMIT A CLAIM. Registered claims receive a 'Wai' number, and the Crown and other interested parties are notified. WHO IT SUITS: where the harm traces to Crown action or inaction rather than a private developer — resource consents, statutory regimes, and Crown land and water decisions. CRUCIALLY: once a claim is registered it becomes ELIGIBLE FOR LEGAL AID, applied for through the Legal Aid Services Treaty team by a legal representative. That funding route is the practical reason to register early rather than late.

trackers.name: Te Puni Kōkiri — whenua Māori resources
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Ministry of Māori Development's directory of the agencies and tools that bear on Māori land — Ngā Whenua Rāhui and Mātauranga Kura Taiao funds at DOC; Kāhui Taiao at the Ministry for the Environment, which advises on Treaty issues in environmental and resource-management policy and on Waitangi Tribunal claims involving natural resources; and the Environmental Protection Authority's Treaty obligations. USE IT: as the map of who to approach before committing to one route. It also points to Māori Land Online, the Ministry of Justice's definitive ownership, trustee and block record for land under the Māori Land Court's jurisdiction per Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993 — the place to establish who actually holds a block.

trackers.name: Banks Peninsula Conservation Trust
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a community-driven trust set up by peninsula landowners in 2001 — notably, following a mediated settlement of landowner appeals to the Environment Court — that protects biodiversity on private land by voluntary rather than statutory means. THE KEY POINT: it holds COVENANTING AUTHORITY STATUS, so it can itself place a legally protective covenant in perpetuity over areas of high biodiversity and landscape value. Most regional groups can only refer you elsewhere; this one can do the protecting. USE IT: for Banks Peninsula and wider Canterbury land, it is a local alternative to a national covenant, run by people who live there. It also works at landscape scale through the Wildside project alongside Christchurch City Council, DOC and Environment Canterbury, and runs practical workshops on weed control, biodiversity and fire-risk mitigation.

trackers.name: Tiaki Tāmaki Makaurau — guide to the legal protection of land (Auckland)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Auckland's conservation portal, with a practical guide to every route for legally protecting biodiversity on land in the region — a conservation covenant, which binds the land REGARDLESS OF WHO OWNS IT IN FUTURE, or a binding land management agreement with Auckland Council or the Department of Conservation, alongside the national QEII option. USE IT: two Auckland-specific things are worth knowing. The council route is a genuine alternative to a national covenant and may move faster for a local site. And single trees can be protected — the portal carries the guidelines and nomination form for the region's NOTABLE TREE SCHEDULE, which is a real lever when a development turns on removing mature trees rather than clearing a whole site. The portal also lists conservation projects by area if you are looking for people already active near you.

trackers.name: Zelena akcija / FoE Croatia — prostorno planiranje guide
trackers.desc: Croatia's oldest environmental association, active since 1990 and running on campaigns, nonviolent direct action and public participation. WHO TO ENLIST when a spatial plan, incinerator or waste facility is being pushed through against a neighbourhood — they have fought exactly these, from the Rebro medical-waste incinerator to Sisak landfill expansion. You CAN: use their free Priručnik on spatial planning and why public participation matters, and draw on an organisation that shares expertise with other groups, individuals and communities. For activists: the practical route into Croatia's planning consultation process, plus a partner with SLAPP experience.

trackers.name: Justice and Environment — European green-law network
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the European network of environmental-law NGOs, whose national member here is Zelena akcija. Its fifteen members act as the environmental-law service point in their own countries, taking cases and intervening in legislative processes, while the network defends communities and nature in court and lodges infringement complaints against member-state governments. Its standing themes are access to justice under the Aarhus Convention, environmental assessment and pollution control. WHO IT SUITS: anyone who does not yet know which lawyer to call — knock on Zelena akcija's door first, and use the network only if your problem crosses a border. The network itself does not take individual cases; its members do.

trackers.name: Pro Natura — Verbandsbeschwerderecht
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Switzerland's oldest nature-protection organisation, holder of the Verbandsbeschwerderecht and steward of over 700 nature reserves. Under article 12 NHG and article 55 USG a closed list of about thirty organisations, designated by the Federal Council, can challenge permits for projects affecting nature — and their appeals succeed three to four times more often than private parties'. WHO IT SUITS: you, only through them. The right was deliberately built NOT to be a popular action: it is restricted to bodies active across the whole of Switzerland, purely non-commercial in purpose, and working in that legal field for at least ten years, which excludes any committee formed for a single case. So take your project to a listed organisation early. Two traps: in several cantons an Einsprache during the permit procedure is a precondition for appealing later, and since 2024 the right no longer reaches small residential projects inside the building zone.

trackers.name: Natuurpunt — aankoop van natuurgebieden (Flanders)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: buys land outright and holds it as nature reserve across Flanders, at real scale — 798.5 hectares bought in 2024 alone for €32.6M, bringing the area under its management to just under 30,000 hectares. Roughly 70 percent of a purchase comes from Flemish acquisition subsidy and 30 percent from its own funds. It also takes land by gift: a parcel next to an existing reserve becomes reserve, and one elsewhere can seed a new reserve or be exchanged for strategically located ground. USE IT: but read the limit it states plainly itself — the subsidy tapers away as the price rises, so it CANNOT outbid farmers, developers or estate agents, and can only really act on parcels less attractive for other uses. If a developer wants your site badly, this is not the tool. Its local afdelingen buy in their own right and it trains volunteers in how to do it, so approach the afdeling, not only the head office.

trackers.name: Natuur en Bos — subsidie aankoop gronden (Flanders)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the Flemish government's nature agency runs the public subsidy scheme behind most private nature-reserve purchases in the region — money to buy land with a view to its recognition as a nature reserve. This is the primary source sitting underneath what the conservation associations do, so it is worth reading directly rather than through them. USE IT: to check the current scheme and conditions for yourself before assuming an association can act, and to see what a municipality or other public body could apply for. Flanders only — Wallonia and Brussels run their own arrangements.

trackers.name: Natagora — achat de réserves naturelles (Wallonie & Bruxelles)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: buys land and holds it as nature reserve across Wallonia and Brussels — over 6,200 hectares on more than 200 protected sites — and says openly that it often has to move fast to buy ground that is threatened or left to speculators. The economics are favourable: Wallonia funds half the purchase price of land destined to become a réserve naturelle agréée, and gifts to Natagora carry a Belgian tax deduction, so a donation buys more reserve than its face value. It buys jointly with the Département de la Nature et des Forêts on some programmes. USE IT: the direct route is the one it advertises — if you are SELLING land that could host biodiversity and become a reserve, contact them before you list it. For a community, that means finding the owner and getting Natagora in front of them early, because once a site is on the open market the timetable belongs to someone else.

trackers.name: Quercus — ONGA nacional / ação popular ambiental
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: read the standing rule first, because Portugal's is the most open in Europe. Article 52(3) of the Constitution gives everyone — personally or through an association — the right of ação popular, naming preservation of the environment expressly, and Lei 83/95 regulates it. It is not a special procedure but a species of active standing: you can bring ANY action, in ANY court, including interim measures, to defend diffuse interests, WITHOUT having to show a personal and direct interest or any connection to the matter. A citizen can act alone. WHO IT SUITS: everyone, which is the point — but an association carries weight and evidence a citizen cannot, and Quercus is the national environmental NGO of public utility, founded 1985. Note the screen for associations under article 3: legal personality, the interest in your statutes, and no professional activity competing with firms or liberal professionals.

trackers.name: Landvernd — landgræðslu- og umhverfisverndarsamtök Íslands
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Iceland's environmental association, which wins at the environment and natural resources appeals committee often enough to publish an archive of the rulings. It got Skútustaðahreppur's construction permit for the Kröflulína 4 power line annulled — a result it calls precedent-setting because the committee recognised nature-protection considerations as bearing on the decision — and obtained an interim ruling halting works on Þeistareykjalína 1 and Kröflulína 4. The committee has also upheld its claims over changes to the Kjalvegur road and a new hotel building in Kerlingarfjöll, and it filed jointly with three other conservation groups to stop the Hvalá hydropower scheme. WHO IT SUITS: communities facing power lines, hydropower, roads and highland tourism development. It appeals in its own name, so you do not need standing of your own to get a decision reviewed — but you do need to reach it inside the one-month appeal window.

trackers.name: Úrskurðarnefnd umhverfis- og auðlindamála (ÚUA) — environmental appeals committee
trackers.desc: The independent administrative committee that rules on appeals against environmental and natural-resource decisions in Iceland — the venue where a construction or operating permit actually gets overturned. WHO TO ENLIST: nobody; you file here yourself. You CAN: appeal as an environmental, outdoor-recreation or interest organisation WITHOUT having to show a legally protected interest of your own, which is how Iceland implements the Aarhus access-to-justice requirement, and the committee can suspend a decision's effect so work stops while it decides. For activists: the deadline is the thing. You generally have ONE MONTH from when you knew or should have known of the decision, running from publication where the decision is publicly notified. Say which decision you are appealing, how it touches your interests and what you want — usually annulment. Every appellant must sign or give written authority, and note that a lawyer's ordinary court mandate does NOT carry here; a separate authorisation is needed.

trackers.name: Centre for Environmental Justice (CEJ)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Sri Lanka's most active environmental litigator — files fundamental-rights and writ petitions in the Supreme Court and Court of Appeal against deforestation, sand mining, quarrying, wetland filling, hazardous waste, coastal reclamation and defective land-use decisions, and publishes its ongoing and completed case lists. It forced the return of illegally imported waste containers to the UK and litigates the X-Press Pearl marine pollution disaster. It also files comments on EIAs and runs a scoring tool for reading them. WHO IT SUITS: a Sri Lankan community facing clearing, mining, filling or a project approved on a weak EIA — CEJ takes strategic cases, usually as petitioner or co-petitioner, and is not a general legal-aid service.

trackers.name: Environmental Foundation (Guarantee) Limited (EFL)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Sri Lanka's oldest environmental litigator, founded in 1981 and incorporated under the Companies Act precisely so that it would have standing to sue in its own name — a paired legal and science operation in which researchers build the technical case the lawyers then argue. Its own site records more than 100 cases filed; reported wins include keeping Galle Face Green a public space, the Eppawala phosphate and Kandalama hotel cases, and the air-pollution case that made vehicle emissions testing mandatory. WHO IT SUITS: a community whose fight turns on evidence as much as argument. EFL is known for a deliberately neutral, non-campaigning posture, which serves a technical challenge well and an outright confrontation less well than a movement litigator would.

trackers.name: Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association (BELA)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the organisation whose 1997 case persuaded Bangladesh's Supreme Court to recognise public-interest litigation at all, opening standing to representative civil-society organisations and to individual public-interested litigants. That precedent is the single most important lever in the country for anyone without a personal stake in a project. Founded in 1992, BELA has filed more than 350 PILs on river and industrial pollution, wetland encroachment, hill cutting, ship-breaking and compensation for losses inflicted by development projects, and was joint winner of the Tang Prize in Rule of Law in 2020. WHO IT SUITS: individuals or communities affected by an environmental problem — and unusually, there is a published intake route. Its legal cell takes applications by email, replies within 15 days, then meets the applicant, scrutinises documents and conducts a field verification before deciding whether to file. Screened, but genuinely open.

trackers.desc: Uruguayan civil-society organisation promoting the right of access to public information and transparency. Publishes the Active Transparency Online Index (ITAeL) assessing public bodies' compliance, and monitors press freedom and freedom of expression.

trackers.name: Vida Silvestre Uruguay — Refugios de vida silvestre
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a civil association founded in 1995 running the Refugios de vida silvestre programme since 2011 — a national network of voluntary private reserves, which matters in Uruguay because almost all the natural grassland, native woodland, wetland, sierra and coast sits on private land outside the state protected-area system. Refugios now protect over 500 plant, 300 invertebrate and 362 vertebrate species, many of them in no SNAP area at all. USE IT: if you own or work rural land in Uruguay and want it recognised and mapped as a refugio; the programme has its own sign-up route and works with landowners who keep farming.

trackers.name: REDES — Amigos de la Tierra Uruguay
trackers.desc: Founded in 1988 and the Friends of the Earth member group in Uruguay, working alongside the social movements affected by a project rather than for them. What it supplies is capacity and evidence: participatory research run jointly with faculties of the Universidad de la República, training and institutional strengthening for affected movements, and — through its Programa Uruguay Sustentable with the Comisión Nacional en Defensa del Agua y la Vida — a territorial GIS information system built for water-basin campaigning. It has fought the Neptuno-Arazatí water project, arguing the contract breached the Escazú Agreement on access to information and participation, and offshore hydrocarbon prospecting. WHO IT SUITS: organised groups already in a fight who need research, mapping and national coordination. It campaigns and researches; it does not litigate.

trackers.name: CEJIS — Centro de Estudios Jurídicos e Investigación Social
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Bolivian non-profit founded in 1978 that has accompanied the titling of 24 indigenous territories in the lowlands and helped write indigenous rights into the 2009 Constitution. It now works on agrarian recovery of ancestral land, territorial autonomies, and control and defence of territory, with offices in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Trinidad, Riberalta and La Paz. WHO IT SUITS: indigenous and peasant organisations of the Amazon, Chiquitanía and Chaco, and the Movimiento Sin Tierra — it works through representative organisations, not individual households. You CAN also use its territorial-monitoring guide and heat-spot reporting, which documents fire inside titled territories and is usable evidence when the state says nothing is happening.

trackers.name: COICA — Coordinadora de las Organizaciones Indígenas de la Cuenca Amazónica
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the basin-wide confederation of Amazonian Indigenous organisations, founded to act for 511 Indigenous peoples across the nine Amazon countries, around 66 of them in voluntary isolation or initial contact. It works through one national member organisation per country — in this country that is CIDOB, Confederación de Pueblos Indígenas de Bolivia — and its governing Council brings those presidents together. Its standing work areas are territorial rights and natural resources, human and sociocultural rights, and international law, and it has issued a formal declaration on the defence of Amazonian Indigenous defenders. USE IT: go to CIDOB first — COICA is the regional weight behind a national organisation, not a direct service. It is the route to carry a territorial case or a threat against leaders from your community into regional and international forums.

trackers.name: FUNDESNAP — Fundación para el Desarrollo del Sistema Nacional de Áreas Protegidas
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: Bolivia's protected-areas fund, and the national operator of Conserva Aves — a Bezos Earth Fund-backed initiative led by American Bird Conservancy, Audubon, BirdLife, Birds Canada and RedLAC — running open public convocatorias with Asociación Armonía as technical partner. WHO IT SUITS: the calls co-finance proposals to CREATE OR EXPAND subnational protected areas, and the eligible categories are unusually wide — departmental, municipal, indígena originario campesina, and private natural-heritage reserves. So a community or municipality wanting to declare an area is squarely in scope, not just one already managing one. The site must fall inside the published priority areas, which are shown on a geographic viewer with the call documents. HOW IT DIFFERS: it funds the act of protecting a place, rather than the running costs of a place already protected.

trackers.desc: National right-to-information authority; El Salvador’s IAIP is the guarantor body under the LAIP (2011) — resolving access appeals, training officials and overseeing the Portal de Transparencia, El Salvador.

trackers.name: FIAES — Fondo de la Iniciativa para las Américas El Salvador
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a debt-for-nature fund created by Legislative Decree 585 of 1993 under the Enterprise for the Americas agreement with the United States and extended in 2001 by the Tropical Forest Conservation Act. It funds work in protected areas, the coastal-marine ecosystem and their buffer zones, prioritising by national poverty index as well as biodiversity. WHO IT SUITS: NGOs and ADESCOs — legally recognised community development associations — acting as organizaciones ejecutoras; individuals cannot apply. HOW IT DIFFERS: its council is chaired by the environment minister, so it is quasi-public money with published operating manuals you can read before applying.

trackers.name: UNES — Unidad Ecológica Salvadoreña
trackers.desc: El Salvador's principal environmental organisation working alongside community groups defending territory — indigenous communities in resistance in the Sensunapán-Banderas river basin, mangrove management on the coast, and the long fight over metallic mining. It accompanies and strengthens local committees rather than acting for them, and it articulates nationally with the Juzgado Ambiental, the human rights ombudsman (PDDH) and municipal governments, which is the practical value: it knows which of those doors to use. It has also run a strategic environmental litigation diploma with the Universidad de El Salvador. WHO IT SUITS: organised community committees and campesino and indigenous groups; UNES accompanies and trains, it does not litigate your case for you.

trackers.name: Fundación Moisés Bertoni — reservas bajo dominio privado
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: works with landowners who want part of their property declared a private nature reserve recognised by the Paraguayan state, handling the technical justification, the declaration and the subsequent management. Private conservation became a formal category with the SINASIP in 1994; the Reserva Natural del Bosque Mbaracayú was created by Ley 112/91 as Paraguay's first private reserve, and Reserva Tapytá was recognised by Decreto 5831 of 2005 as protected in perpetuity. USE IT: to convert threatened Atlantic Forest, Cerrado or Chaco land into a declared reserve — the technical dossier is the bottleneck, and this is who writes it.

trackers.name: Guyra Paraguay — Conservación de Sitios
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: has been acquiring land for conservation in perpetuity since 2001 and now runs four conservation units, including the Guyra Retã complex of over 6,000 hectares inside the Tekoha Guasu / San Rafael national park reserve, Cañada El Carmen created by Ley 2073/05, Campo Iris and Tobich in the Chaco. Its private reserve category runs under Resolución SEAM 200 of 2001 within Ley 352/94 on protected areas. Critically, it buys land for Indigenous territorial reclamation as well as for conservation: in 2008 it bought 548 hectares in socio-environmental condominium under a deed committing it to cede the land outright after ten years, and in 2023 it transferred that title to the Mbya Guaraní community of Tapy Kanguekua–Arroyo Morotí. USE IT: where an Atlantic Forest or Chaco property is for sale over ancestral territory and the community needs a buyer that will hand the title on.

trackers.name: FAPI — Federación por la Autodeterminación de los Pueblos Indígenas
trackers.desc: An autonomous third-level Indigenous federation of 13 member organisations across both regions of Paraguay, registered since 2007 and recognised as a legitimate interlocutor before the Paraguayan state. Its most directly usable output is tierrasindigenas.org.py, the interactive platform it coordinates with UCINY, CLIBCH, Tierraviva, GAT and others, which maps Indigenous lands and territories against forest-change and fire data — most Indigenous territory is absent from official maps, so the platform exists to make it visible and to drive territorial restitution. Its member associations also drafted the national free, prior and informed consent protocol over nine years. WHO IT SUITS: Indigenous communities in Paraguay working through their own association — FAPI acts through its 13 members, not for individual claimants.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Natural Justice: Lawyers for Communities and the Environment
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an African public-interest law organisation — lawyers and paralegals working with communities facing mining, oil and gas, logging and large infrastructure, combining legal empowerment, community protocols, policy work and litigation. Hubs in Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, staff in Madagascar, Botswana and Guinea, and country programmes in Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal and South Africa. It also runs the Environmental Lawyers Collective for Africa and an EIA Process Tracker. WHO IT SUITS: an Indigenous or rural community whose land, water or customary rights are threatened by an extractive or infrastructure project. It takes selected cases and works project-to-project outside its programme countries, so expect an approach-and-assess conversation rather than open intake.

trackers.name: African Environmental Defenders Fund (emergency grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the African Environmental Defenders Fund — an emergency grant fund run by Natural Justice with the International Land Coalition Africa, ICCA Consortium, PACJA, Oxfam Novib, FEMNET and others, giving up to US$5,000 to land and environmental defenders anywhere in Africa who are under threat because of their activism. It can cover the cost of legal representation where a defender is arrested, summoned or prosecuted, plus relocation and other short-term transitional costs. WHO IT SUITS: an individual frontline defender who is a citizen or legal resident of an African country, facing an imminent threat, and not already supported by another body — it is not project or core funding, and routine office and administrative costs are excluded. HOW IT DIFFERS: applications are rolling, by email or helpline, not to a grant round. Natural Justice's own site names Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa and Botswana as its country programmes, which is where this entry is placed; the fund's stated eligibility is any African country, so apply from elsewhere on the continent too.

trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the largest environmental legal centre in the Australia-Pacific region, whose Pasifika-led programme works on extractive industries, forestry, marine protection and climate across Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Fiji, Vanuatu and Tuvalu. WHO IT SUITS: an in-country organisation rather than an individual — EDO works predominantly through partner organisations (CELCOR in PNG, the Landowners Advocacy and Legal Support Unit and the Solomon Islands Environmental Law Association, the Fiji Environmental Law Association and the Vanuatu Environmental Law Association), supplying strategic legal capacity, co-authored law-reform papers and litigation support. Approach your national environmental law association first; its free advice hotline is for Australia only.

It has co-authored policy and law papers on marine protected areas and Fiji's coastal fisheries. WHO IT SUITS: a Fijian community or landowning unit facing a coastal development, extraction or fisheries decision — advice is given in matters that meet the association's casework guidelines, so it is a screened service rather than open legal aid.

trackers.name: Environmental Defenders Office — Pasifika Program
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the largest environmental legal centre in the Australia-Pacific region, whose Pasifika-led programme works on extractive industries, forestry, marine protection and climate across Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Fiji, Vanuatu and Tuvalu. WHO IT SUITS: an in-country organisation rather than an individual — EDO works predominantly through partner organisations (CELCOR in PNG, the Landowners Advocacy and Legal Support Unit and the Solomon Islands Environmental Law Association, the Fiji Environmental Law Association and the Vanuatu Environmental Law Association), supplying strategic legal capacity, co-authored law-reform papers and litigation support. Approach your national environmental law association first; its free advice hotline is for Australia only.

trackers.name: Centre for Environmental Law & Community Rights (CELCOR)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Papua New Guinea's public-interest environmental law NGO, established in 2000 — legal advice and representation for customary landowners, community organisations and NGOs facing logging, mining, oil palm, other extractives and marine development, alongside community legal education, paralegal training and mediation. It has intervened in most of PNG's provinces and supported the Mesulam v Joku ruling on the public's right to project information. WHO IT SUITS: a customary landowning group or CBO facing a resource project on its land — assistance to landowners is the core mandate, but this is a nine-person office working from Port Moresby only, so travel and capacity limit what it can take.

trackers.name: Friends of the Earth Asia Pacific
trackers.desc: The Asia Pacific regional structure of Friends of the Earth International, formed in 2008, whose member groups work on community-based struggles against destructive projects, particularly mining and other extractive industries, alongside Indigenous peoples, peasant farmers, fisherfolk and trade unions. WHO TO ENLIST: the national member group nearest the project. In this region Friends of the Earth International's own directory names groups in Bangladesh (BELA, the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers' Association), India, Indonesia (WALHI), Japan, Malaysia (Sahabat Alam Malaysia), Nepal, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines (the Legal Rights and Natural Resources Center), South Korea and Sri Lanka. You CAN: reach an organisation that already works community-side in your own country, and draw regional weight onto a local fight. For activists: in several of these countries the Friends of the Earth affiliate is the most experienced community-side environmental body there is.

trackers.name: Office of the Auditor-General
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Papua New Guinea, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Papua New Guinea — Department of Treasury

trackers.name: TEMA Vakfı — hukuk mücadelesi ve il temsilcilikleri
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Turkish foundation that has been suing the state over land since 1997, when it took the Prime Ministry and the Forestry Ministry to the Council of State to strike down part of a regulation. Its biggest win was legislative — the Pasture Law, stalled for 38 years and lapsed four times, passed unanimously in 1998 after its campaign. It brings annulment actions against environmental plans and ÇED (impact assessment) decisions, including two cases against the 1/100,000 Mersin-Adana environmental plan covering the nuclear site. WHO IT SUITS: any community anywhere in the country, because of the thing that makes it unusual — it publishes a directory of provincial representatives, named individuals with phone numbers and emails, and it operates in all 81 provinces. Start with the temsilci for your province, not the head office. Be realistic about the odds: its 2014 action to annul the positive ÇED decision for the Akkuyu nuclear plant was dismissed and construction proceeded. This is a large mainstream foundation that litigates steadily and does not win everything.

trackers.name: TEMA Vakfı — Adana il temsilciliği
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: TEMA Vakfı's provincial representative for Adana. TEMA publishes a temsilcilikler directory of named İl Temsilcisi with phone numbers, email addresses and in many cases a street address, and it operates in all 81 provinces — which makes this the rare case where a land defender gets a person to ring in their own province rather than a head office. The foundation behind them has sued the state over land since 1997, brings annulment actions against environmental plans and ÇED decisions, and drove the Pasture Law through parliament in 1998. WHO IT SUITS: anyone in Adana facing a mine, quarry, plan or permit. Two honest caveats: representative posts fall vacant and TEMA periodically advertises for them, so check the directory rather than assuming Adana is currently staffed; and these are volunteers, not staff lawyers — they route you to the foundation's legal work, they do not conduct it.

trackers.name: Information & Data Protection Commissioner (IDPC)
trackers.desc: Information & Data Protection Commissioner (IDPC) — Malta’s national data-protection / information authority, overseeing how public bodies handle personal data and enforcing access and privacy rights. — Holds to account: officials handling public information & personal data — find rulings, guidance and complaint channels.

trackers.name: Parliamentary Ombudsman of Malta
trackers.desc: Malta’s Parliamentary Ombudsman, investigating complaints against public bodies and monitoring places of detention.

trackers.name: Din l-Art Ħelwa — National Trust of Malta
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the National Trust of Malta, founded 1965, which does two things a community needs. It holds around seventeen sites under Deeds of Guardianship with the government or in trust from the ecclesiastical authorities, restoring and opening them — so it can take on a threatened site. And its Heritage and Environment Protection sub-committee reads the list of planning applications published WEEKLY IN THE GOVERNMENT GAZETTE, which is how you find out at all, and files objections at scale: 1,500 in one year against 9,599 applications. It built DLHAlert so the public can follow objections. WHO IT SUITS: everyone in Malta and Gozo, but understand the ladder before you climb it. Objecting is cheap; appealing is not. By its own account an appeal costs €200 to €1,000, needs a written case citing the policies and legislation, and runs to three or four sittings with photomontages, surveys, drawing analysis and expert affidavits, all rebutted and then defended in person — with a court appeal beyond that. It is volunteer-run with professionals acting pro bono, so it prioritises hard, and it cannot appeal everything it objects to.
