WHO TO ENLIST: the place to start when the threat is a dam, a reservoir or placer gold mining in a river basin. It runs independent hydropower assessments, maps threatened basins including the Selenga, Kherlen, Onon and the Mongolian Great Lakes, and tracks where mining licences sit relative to water-protection zones. You CAN: draw on its river-by-river document files and on its record of backing Mongolian herder movements pressing for enforcement of the 2009 law restricting mining near rivers, headwaters and forests. trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Kazakhstan's veteran environmental-rights organisation, which litigates and publishes an annual review of its own court practice so you can see exactly what it runs and how it fares. It files in the Specialised Inter-district Administrative Court in Almaty both for itself and — the lever worth knowing — in defence of an indeterminate circle of persons, which is how an association carries a claim for a community that could not bring one alone. WHO IT SUITS: anyone refused environmental information or facing a project pushed through without disclosure. It is Almaty-based and small, so expect reach to be strongest there.

trackers.desc: A youth-led Cambodian environmental rights movement, active since 2012, which stopped a Chinese-led hydroelectric dam threatening an Indigenous community in the Areng Valley and helped end the sand-export trade that was destroying the Koh Kong estuaries. Right Livelihood Award, 2023. It was deregistered as an NGO by the Ministry of Interior in 2017 and has continued without legal registration. For activists: association carries real risk. Five members have been imprisoned since July 2024 on plotting and lese-majeste charges, bail refused by both the Appeal and Supreme Courts, and dozens more have been arrested since 2015.

trackers.name: Fishermen and Friends of the Sea (FFOS)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a non-profit formed by fishers and citizens in 1996 and incorporated in 2000, with the strongest public-interest litigation record in the country — three separate appeals to the Privy Council, over a Certificate of Environmental Clearance for a highway beside the Aripo Savannas, over water pollution fees and the polluter-pays principle, and over judicial review time limits. It also runs a public route to report an environmental emergency. WHO IT SUITS: fishing communities and coastal residents facing oil spills, seismic survey, port or highway projects. Structurally it matters because section 5(6) of the Judicial Review Act lets a bona fide third party bring judicial review for people who cannot file themselves because of poverty or disadvantage. Courts have been strict on the duty to act promptly, so make contact early.

trackers.name: Caribbean Biodiversity Fund (CBF)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a regional environmental endowment established in 2012 which disburses mainly through partner National Conservation Trust Funds and runs open calls under its Ecosystem-based Adaptation window. WHO IT SUITS — READ THIS FIRST: this country is NOT a core eligible country for the EbA facility. CBF's own trustee report lists it among territories that can benefit ONLY where they are included in a regional project in which eligible countries form a three-quarters majority. So the realistic route is joining a regional consortium led from an eligible country, not applying alone. HOW IT DIFFERS: long-horizon endowment money for sustained ecosystem management, not campaign funding.

trackers.name: CANARI — Caribbean Natural Resources Institute
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional technical non-profit founded in 1989, headquartered in Trinidad and legally registered as a non-profit in this country, working with grassroots and community-based organisations directly involved in natural resource management. What it actually supplies is capacity rather than representation: coaching, mentoring and training of trainers, facilitated multi-stakeholder dialogues for planning and policymaking, participatory research, and unusual practical tools — participatory GIS mapping, three-dimensional modelling, participatory video and photojournaling — for communities that need to evidence their own case. It also channels funding and technical support to civil society organisations. WHO IT SUITS: community organisations and CSOs that need to be equipped to hold their ground in a planning or policy process. It is not a litigator, and its re-granting runs through time-limited donor projects rather than a standing open call — ask what is currently running.

trackers.name: Association of Indigenous Village Leaders in Suriname (VIDS)
trackers.desc: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname — founded in 1992 and representing the traditional leaders of all 51 Indigenous villages in Suriname (Kaliña, Lokono, Trio, Wayana and others). It promotes and defends Indigenous peoples’ rights nationally and internationally, campaigns for the legal recognition of collective land and territorial rights and free, prior and informed consent (FPIC), and presses Suriname to honour its obligations under the binding rulings of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights; it was awarded the inaugural EU Human Rights Award for the region.

trackers.name: Caribbean Biodiversity Fund — regional conservation finance
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a regional umbrella environmental fund providing continuous finance for conservation, through an Endowment Fund and a Climate Change Program whose Ecosystem-based Adaptation Facility runs competitive calls for proposals — around 100 projects funded. WHO IT SUITS: Caribbean community and conservation groups. HOW IT DIFFERS: mostly you do NOT apply to CBF directly — partner National Conservation Trust Funds lead the grantmaking in each country, so find your national trust fund first. CBF states it works across 14 Caribbean countries; check its 'Where We Work' map for yours.

trackers.name: COICA — Coordinadora de las Organizaciones Indígenas de la Cuenca Amazónica
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the basin-wide confederation of Amazonian Indigenous organisations, founded to act for 511 Indigenous peoples across the nine Amazon countries, around 66 of them in voluntary isolation or initial contact. It works through one national member organisation per country — in this country that is OIS, Organizaciones Indígenas de Surinam — and its governing Council brings those presidents together. Its standing work areas are territorial rights and natural resources, human and sociocultural rights, and international law, and it has issued a formal declaration on the defence of Amazonian Indigenous defenders. USE IT: go to OIS first — COICA is the regional weight behind a national organisation, not a direct service. It is the route to carry a territorial case or a threat against leaders from your community into regional and international forums.

trackers.name: ACT Suriname — Amazon Conservation Team Suriname
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a Surinamese foundation established under Surinamese law in September 2002, working in partnership with Indigenous and Maroon communities of the southern interior. Its flagship is the Amazon Conservation Rangers programme, launched in Suriname in 2007: community-appointed rangers, 42 currently active, trained and equipped to monitor their own territory — reviewing satellite imagery for deforestation, testing water quality, and detecting illegal intruders such as loggers and gold miners. It also facilitates Community Life Plans, territorial management documents a village can put in front of a government agency or a company. USE IT: in a country that still has no legal recognition of Indigenous land rights, this is the practical substitute — evidence and governance documents a community controls itself.

trackers.desc: National budget authority; monitors State revenues & expenditures and prepares the State budget (Staatsbegroting), Suriname. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Suriname.

trackers.name: Suriname — Kamer van Koophandel en Fabrieken (KKF)

trackers.name: Access to Information Unit (Office of the Prime Minister)
trackers.desc: Jamaica's Access to Information Unit, which administers the ATI Act 2002 and is secretariat to the Access to Information Appeal Tribunal. You CAN get: any official document held by a public authority — correspondence, budgets, maps, photographs, computerised records — with acknowledgement within 7 working days and a decision within 30 days, extendable once by a further 30. If refused or ignored you have an internal review within 60 days, then an appeal to the Tribunal within 60 days of the decision or of the date the answer was due. The Tribunal can inspect the document itself and overrule the authority, and critically THE BURDEN IS ON THE PUBLIC AUTHORITY to prove its refusal was justified, not on you to prove it was wrong. You may appear yourself; a lawyer is optional. You CAN'T get: free copies — reproduction is charged, though viewing and inspecting are free — or documents an authority never created, since it need not make a record to answer you. trackers.name: Associação Projecto Vitó
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a Cape Verdean environmental association that began on Fogo as a volunteer effort after a sea-turtle rescue and now works on Fogo, Brava, Santo Antão, São Nicolau and Santiago, and in the Reserva Natural Integral dos Ilhéus do Rombo. It supports management of the Parque Natural do Fogo and the operationalisation of the Fogo Biosphere Reserve, working through citizen science and transferring technical knowledge to civil society. The first environmental NGO awarded Cape Verde's Medal of Merit, First Class. USE IT: as the organisation with standing and field presence inside Cape Verde's protected-area network — the route to getting a site monitored, documented and argued for. It is a conservation and education body, not a campaigning or legal one.

trackers.name: Biosfera
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a Cape Verdean NGO working on coastal and marine species and their habitats from São Vicente, with long-running field operations on the uninhabited island of Santa Luzia. It states a dual mission — conservation, and mobilising Cape Verdean civil society for the protection of the environment — and its strategic objectives include protecting coastal and marine habitats, promoting responsible artisanal fishing and reducing pollution that disturbs species and habitats. USE IT: as the coastal counterpart to the protected-area bodies. It is the organisation to approach about a shoreline, a fishery or a marine habitat under pressure, and the one in Cape Verde that most explicitly treats mobilising the public as part of its job.

trackers.desc: Togo's first NGO wholly dedicated to environmental protection, founded on 20 June 1990 and formally recognised as an association the following year, and the Togolese member of Friends of the Earth International. Its work spans biodiversity, climate, desertification, water and sanitation, chemicals, mining and scrutiny of public decision-making, delivered largely through community dialogues, agro-ecology training and youth education from its Lome office. WHO TO ENLIST: a first port of call for a Togolese community rather than a litigator — ADT-Togo is a focal point for the national civil-society networks on climate and energy, so it is the quickest route to finding who else already works on a site. trackers.name: ADN — Associació per a la Defensa de la Natura (Andorra)
trackers.desc: Andorra's nature-defence association, founded in 1986, working on conservation, research and public information across the whole country. WHO TO ENLIST when a development touches a valley, a river or a protected area — its record is the reason to: it made the first proposal to protect the Madriu valley in 1997, a valley now inscribed as World Heritage, and it still publishes the documents from that campaign. You CAN: use its Denúncies channel to report an environmental breach, and draw on its practice of naming areas that ought to be protected and pressing for their designation, which is the lever in a country with little formal land-protection machinery. It also runs river monitoring through Projecte Rius, so it can supply baseline water data. For activists: this is a volunteer scientific association, not a law firm — expect evidence, designation proposals and a public voice rather than representation.

trackers.name: CANARI — Caribbean Natural Resources Institute

COVERAGE NOTE: CANARI is not registered as a non-profit in this country, but has delivered sub-grants to communities here under its Caribbean ecosystem-restoration work, so it does operate here — ask what is currently running. It is not a litigator and its re-granting is tied to donor projects.

USE IT: to propose a threatened Bahamian site for national-park status or trust acquisition, and to check whether land a developer wants already sits inside a park boundary.

trackers.name: Caribbean Biodiversity Fund (CBF)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a regional environmental endowment established in 2012 which disburses mainly through partner National Conservation Trust Funds and runs open calls under its Ecosystem-based Adaptation window. WHO IT SUITS — READ THIS FIRST: this country is NOT a core eligible country for the EbA facility. CBF's own trustee report lists it among territories that can benefit ONLY where they are included in a regional project in which eligible countries form a three-quarters majority. So the realistic route is joining a regional consortium led from an eligible country, not applying alone. HOW IT DIFFERS: long-horizon endowment money for sustained ecosystem management, not campaign funding.

trackers.name: CANARI — Caribbean Natural Resources Institute
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional technical non-profit founded in 1989, headquartered in Trinidad and legally registered as a non-profit in this country, working with grassroots and community-based organisations directly involved in natural resource management. What it actually supplies is capacity rather than representation: coaching, mentoring and training of trainers, facilitated multi-stakeholder dialogues for planning and policymaking, participatory research, and unusual practical tools — participatory GIS mapping, three-dimensional modelling, participatory video and photojournaling — for communities that need to evidence their own case. It also channels funding and technical support to civil society organisations. WHO IT SUITS: community organisations and CSOs that need to be equipped to hold their ground in a planning or policy process. It is not a litigator, and its re-granting runs through time-limited donor projects rather than a standing open call — ask what is currently running.

trackers.name: MAR Fund — Small Grants Program (Mesoamerican Reef)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: an ecoregional fund created in 2004 by the national conservation funds of Belize, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, running a Small Grants Program by competitive Call for Proposals — now past its 17th call — with two windows, the Traditional Window and the Reef Rescue Initiative. WHO IT SUITS: civil-society groups working on coastal and marine protected areas anywhere in the Mesoamerican Reef System. HOW IT DIFFERS: transnational by design, so a project spanning the reef across two countries is a fit here where a national funder would balk.

WHO IT SUITS: Caribbean community and conservation groups. HOW IT DIFFERS: mostly you do NOT apply to CBF directly — partner National Conservation Trust Funds lead the grantmaking in each country, so find your national trust fund first. CBF states it works across 14 Caribbean countries; check its 'Where We Work' map for yours.

trackers.name: Protected Areas Conservation Trust (PACT)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a statutory trust created by the PACT Act 1996 and given legal power by the 2015 amendment to set priorities for and allocate financing across Belize's National Protected Areas System. Since 2018 it invests through a Conservation Investment Program rather than annual grants, and is Belize's Adaptation Fund implementing entity and a Green Climate Fund direct-access entity. WHO IT SUITS: co-managers and community groups working in or beside a declared protected area — an unprotected parcel is a much harder ask. HOW IT DIFFERS: statutory public money with a duty to fund the system, not discretionary philanthropy.

trackers.name: Ya'axché Conservation Trust
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: founded in 1998 by community leaders in Toledo District to secure the Golden Stream Corridor Preserve — a 15,000-acre private protected area it owns and manages — and now co-manages Bladen Nature Reserve, the most intact protected area in Belize and the watershed feeding the Barrier Reef. It works across the Maya Golden Landscape, a mosaic of protected areas, private and Maya community land linking the Maya Mountains to the sea, and it set up Belize's first agroforestry concession. USE IT: in southern Belize, for a partner that already holds land under private protection and runs extension officers into the buffer communities — nine Maya communities work with it on land use, cacao and honey, so it is a route to defending a corridor through what people farm rather than against it.

WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the only IUCN member in the Comoros, founded in 2013, with around sixty staff working alongside communities on Anjouan and Grande Comore. Its central instrument is the INDIVIDUAL CONSERVATION AGREEMENT: a farmer contracts with Dahari for a fixed term not to clear forest or cut native trees on their plot, and receives payments calculated by the area preserved, checked by periodic inspection of the parcel. Management of the Moya forest zone has been delegated to Dahari by the national protected-areas network, and it has supported fishers in establishing the country's first permanent community-managed marine reserve. USE IT: if you hold or farm land carrying native forest, the conservation agreement is a way to make leaving it standing pay; if you fish, the marine programme is the route to a community-managed no-take zone.

trackers.name: Les Mêmes Droits Pour Tous (MDT)
trackers.desc: Guinea’s leading prisoner legal-aid organisation (“Same Rights For All”), founded in 2005 and specialising in criminal justice. Under a standing agreement with the Ministry of Justice it has unrestricted access to all of Guinea’s prisons — where the great majority of detainees are held in prolonged pretrial detention — and provides free legal and judicial assistance to people deprived of liberty, having won the release of hundreds who were illegally or unlawfully detained. It documents prison conditions, assists victims of torture and gender-based violence and communities affected by mining projects, and works from its Conakry headquarters and regional offices in N’Zérékoré and Kankan; it holds ECOSOC observer status.

trackers.name: Natural Justice: Lawyers for Communities and the Environment
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an African public-interest law organisation — lawyers and paralegals working with communities facing mining, oil and gas, logging and large infrastructure, combining legal empowerment, community protocols, policy work and litigation. Hubs in Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, staff in Madagascar, Botswana and Guinea, and country programmes in Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal and South Africa. It also runs the Environmental Lawyers Collective for Africa and an EIA Process Tracker. WHO IT SUITS: an Indigenous or rural community whose land, water or customary rights are threatened by an extractive or infrastructure project. It takes selected cases and works project-to-project outside its programme countries, so expect an approach-and-assess conversation rather than open intake.

trackers.name: African Environmental Defenders Fund (emergency grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the African Environmental Defenders Fund — an emergency grant fund run by Natural Justice with the International Land Coalition Africa, ICCA Consortium, PACJA, Oxfam Novib, FEMNET and others, giving up to US$5,000 to land and environmental defenders anywhere in Africa who are under threat because of their activism. It can cover the cost of legal representation where a defender is arrested, summoned or prosecuted, plus relocation and other short-term transitional costs. WHO IT SUITS: an individual frontline defender who is a citizen or legal resident of an African country, facing an imminent threat, and not already supported by another body — it is not project or core funding, and routine office and administrative costs are excluded. HOW IT DIFFERS: applications are rolling, by email or helpline, not to a grant round. Natural Justice's own site names Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa and Botswana as its country programmes, which is where this entry is placed; the fund's stated eligibility is any African country, so apply from elsewhere on the continent too.

trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: an NGO working to conserve Príncipe Island with and for its people, with a team of nearly fifty, more than 90 per cent of them local, running marine conservation, terrestrial conservation and community-engagement programmes in partnership with the regional authorities and local communities. Its terrestrial work documents species and the threats to them, builds protection initiatives with communities, and trains technicians in local government institutions and guide associations. USE IT: start with LEAP if you want an area near you protected and locally run; use its protected-area staff if you need the technical case for why a site matters. It sits on government committees and taskforces and in the Citizen Engagement Platform Seychelles, so it has standing in consultations — but it works with government rather than against it, and will not fight a project for you.

It supports STATES in preparing Protected Areas Network site plans and protected-area management plans, with the stated aim of building each state's own capacity rather than managing on its behalf, and runs a Private Lands Initiative extending conservation onto land outside the state system. USE IT: if your state or village wants a conservation area recognised and managed, PCS is the body that helps write and run the plan. It implements national policy rather than opposing it, and says openly that what it can take on is limited by staff and funding.

Areas enter the network at the initiative of state governments, traditional leaders and individuals who have protected land or reef inside their own boundaries; the Fund then supports the running of those sites, including enforcement coordination and conservation training. WHO IT SUITS: states, traditional leaders and landholders whose area is a PAN site or could become one. This is money for managing a designated protected area, not a grant for campaigning against a project. HOW IT DIFFERS: it is financed by a visitor arrival fee rather than by donor cycles, which makes it far steadier than most conservation money in the region.

trackers.name: AccessInfo.hk — FOI requests (HKG)
trackers.desc: You CAN get: information held by Hong Kong government bureaux and departments, and by the public agencies listed at Annex A of the Code on Access to Information — requested through this volunteer-run platform, which files on your behalf and publishes every request and reply openly, so past answers are searchable before you ask. Anyone may request, resident or not, and requests can be oral or written. Land-relevant precedent exists: the Lands Department has answered requests about specific land grants here. You CAN'T get: a legal right. HONG KONG HAS NO FREEDOM-OF-INFORMATION STATUTE — the Code is an administrative instrument only, with no legal protection of the right, and the Ombudsman has criticised departments for refusing on grounds the Code does not contain. It does not reach the many statutory and advisory bodies that decide policy. Refusal grounds are broad — security, external affairs, administration of justice — subject to a public-interest test the department applies itself. For activists: if refused, ask for internal review, then complain to the Ombudsman. But note the limit that bites hardest on a development fight — the Ombudsman is statutorily barred from investigating the imposition or variation of LAND GRANT CONDITIONS, and will not take a complaint more than two years old.

trackers.name: Ålands Natur & Miljö
trackers.desc: Åland's independent environmental folkrörelse, with around a thousand members in a population of just over thirty thousand — proportionally one of the deepest memberships of any body in this file, which is why it is taken seriously in a small polity. WHO TO ENLIST when a wind farm, a plan or a permit lands on the islands. You CAN: use it as a formal consultee — it gives utlåtanden in impact-assessment procedures, including on whether Finland should take part in the transboundary assessment of an offshore wind expansion. It also sits on the monitoring committee for Åland's structural fund programme and its CAP interventions, so it has a seat where the money is allocated, not only where the permit is decided. For activists: it owns its own forest in the archipelago at Nötö and had it professionally surveyed as untouched natural forest, so it holds land as well as opinions. Expect campaigning, consultation responses and evidence rather than litigation.

trackers.name: Te Ipukarea Society (TIS)
trackers.desc: The Cook Islands' first environmental NGO, registered as an incorporated society in 1996, membership-based, working across biodiversity, climate, eco-sustainable development and waste, and a member of IUCN and BirdLife International. WHO TO ENLIST: TIS when a development is being framed as opportunity — its record is campaigning to protect Suwarrow, opposing destructive fishing practices, and challenging deep seabed mining, including calling for a pause while independent baseline research is done. You CAN draw on an unusual piece of standing: TIS was the first national NGO in the Pacific accepted as an observer at the International Seabed Authority, which lets it make statements in ISA Assembly and Council meetings on behalf of a Cook Islands view. For activists: it acts alongside Kōrero O Te ‘Ōrau and Ocean Ancestors, so an approach to one tends to reach the others.
